title: 14  Span and linear independence
text:
14.1 Build intuition
Core
Builds on Chapter 2, Chapter 12.
The column picture of Chapter 10 turned every system of equations into a question about vectors: can \(\vect{b}\) be made by combining the columns of \(\M{A}\), and if so, in how many ways? Part III gives these questions names and develops the language for answering them. This chapter introduces the two central ideas. The span of some vectors is everything they can make. They are linearly independent if none of them is wasted: none can be made from the others.
From here on, it helps to name the spaces that vectors live in. \(\R^n\) (said “R n”) stands for the set of all vectors with \(n\) real-number entries. So \(\R^2\) is the plane, \(\R^3\) is ordinary space, and \(\R^n\) for larger \(n\) is the same idea with more entries, even though it can’t be drawn.
The app shows up to three vectors in space, the set of every point they can reach (their span), and a target \(\vect{b}\). Use the sliders to make combinations of the vectors, and the use boxes to switch vectors on and off.
Things to try:

title: 14  Span and linear independence
text:
Open the span explorer in its own tab



In A plane, move the sliders. Can the green combination ever leave the plane? Now switch on \(\vect{v}_3\). What happens to the span?
In Parallel: a line, the two vectors point along the same line. Why can’t they reach anything off it?
In Three in a plane, there are three vectors but the span is still only a plane. Change one entry of \(\vect{v}_3\) by a small amount, and watch what happens.

title: 14  Span and linear independence
text:
14.2 The ideas

Span
A linear combination of vectors \(\vect{v}_1, \dots, \vect{v}_k\) is any vector \[
c_1\vect{v}_1 + c_2\vect{v}_2 + \dots + c_k\vect{v}_k
\] with numbers \(c_1, \dots, c_k\), as in Chapter 2. The span of the vectors, written \(\operatorname{span}\{\vect{v}_1, \dots, \vect{v}_k\}\), is the set of all their linear combinations: every point you can reach by scaling them and adding.
In three dimensions the possibilities are:



The vectors
Their span




one non-zero vector
a line through the origin


two vectors, not along the same line
a plane through the origin


three vectors, not all in one plane
all of \(\R^3\)



Every span contains the origin (take all the \(c_i = 0\)), so a span is always a line, plane or space through the origin, never one that misses it.
Deciding whether \(\vect{b}\) is in the span is exactly the question of Chapter 10. Put the vectors in the columns of a matrix \(\M{A}\). Then \(\M{A}\vect{c} = c_1\vect{v}_1 + \dots + c_k\vect{v}_k\), so






ImportantSpan and systems



\(\vect{b}\) is in the span of the columns of \(\M{A}\) exactly when \(\M{A}\vect{c} = \vect{b}\) has a solution. The solution gives the coefficients.


To test it, compare ranks (Chapter 12): \(\vect{b}\) is in the span exactly when \(\operatorname{rank}[\M{A} \mid \vect{b}] = \operatorname{rank}\M{A}\).






NoteExample 1: is it in the span?



Let \(\vect{v}_1 = (1, 2, 1)\T\) and \(\vect{v}_2 = (0, 1, 2)\T\). Is \((1, 5, 7)\T\) in their span? Is \((1, 5, 5)\T\)?
Solution. We need \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) with \(c_1\vect{v}_1 + c_2\vect{v}_2 = \vect{b}\). Reduce the augmented matrix for both right-hand sides at once: \[
\amat{rr|rr}{1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 5 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 & 7 & 5}
\xrightarrow[R_3 \,\leftarrow\, R_3 - R_1]{R_2 \,\leftarrow\, R_2 - 2R_1}
\amat{rr|rr}{1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 6 & 4}
\xrightarrow{R_3 \,\leftarrow\, R_3 - 2R_2}
\amat{rr|rr}{1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -2}.
\] For \((1, 5, 7)\T\) (the first right-hand column) the last row reads \(0 = 0\), so it is in the span, with \(c_1 = 1\) and \(c_2 = 3\). Check: \((1, 2, 1)\T + 3(0, 1, 2)\T = (1, 5, 7)\T\). ✓
For \((1, 5, 5)\T\) the last row reads \(0 = -2\), so it is not in the span. The two vectors span a plane, and \((1, 5, 5)\T\) lies off it.




Linear independence
Some sets of vectors contain a passenger: a vector that is already a combination of the others, and so adds nothing to the span. In Three in a plane, \(\vect{v}_3 = \vect{v}_2 - 2\vect{v}_1\), so \(\vect{v}_3\) lies in the plane that \(\vect{v}_1\) and \(\vect{v}_2\) already span. Moving everything to one side gives a dependence relation, \[
2\vect{v}_1 - \vect{v}_2 + \vect{v}_3 = \zerovec,
\] a combination of the vectors that adds up to zero without all the coefficients being zero.
The vectors \(\vect{v}_1, \dots, \vect{v}_k\) are linearly independent if the only way to combine them to make \(\zerovec\) is the trivial way: \[
c_1\vect{v}_1 + \dots + c_k\vect{v}_k = \zerovec \quad\text{only when}\quad c_1 = c_2 = \dots = c_k = 0.
\] Otherwise they are linearly dependent. The two descriptions match: vectors are dependent exactly when at least one of them is a combination of the others. (If \(c_j \neq 0\) in a dependence relation, divide by \(c_j\) and rearrange to write \(\vect{v}_j\) in terms of the rest.)
Geometrically:

two vectors are dependent exactly when they lie along the same line (one is a multiple of the other);
three vectors in \(\R^3\) are dependent exactly when they lie in one plane through the origin.



Testing for independence
With the vectors as the columns of \(\M{A}\), a dependence relation is a non-zero solution of \(\M{A}\vect{c} = \zerovec\). So, using Chapter 12:

the columns are independent exactly when \(\M{A}\vect{c} = \zerovec\) has only the solution \(\vect{c} = \zerovec\), that is, when there is a pivot in every column: \(\operatorname{rank}\M{A} = k\);
if they are dependent, the free variables of \(\M{A}\vect{c} = \zerovec\) give the dependence relations.

For \(n\) vectors in \(\R^n\), \(\M{A}\) is square, and there is a quicker test: the vectors are independent exactly when \(\det\M{A} \neq 0\) (Chapter 6). A non-zero determinant means the unit cube is mapped to a box of non-zero volume, so the columns point in genuinely different directions.
Two facts follow straight away:

Any set containing \(\zerovec\) is dependent, because \(1 \cdot \zerovec = \zerovec\) is a dependence relation.
More than \(n\) vectors in \(\R^n\) are always dependent. \(\M{A}\vect{c} = \zerovec\) then has more unknowns than equations, so it has non-zero solutions (Chapter 12, Exercise 6). Four vectors in \(\R^3\) can never be independent.







NoteExample 2: finding a dependence relation



Are \(\vect{v}_1 = (1, 0, 1)\T\), \(\vect{v}_2 = (2, 1, 0)\T\) and \(\vect{v}_3 = (0, 1, -2)\T\) independent?
Solution. Solve \(c_1\vect{v}_1 + c_2\vect{v}_2 + c_3\vect{v}_3 = \zerovec\) by reducing the matrix with these columns: \[
\mat{1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & -2}
\xrightarrow{R_3 \,\leftarrow\, R_3 - R_1}
\mat{1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & -2}
\xrightarrow{R_3 \,\leftarrow\, R_3 + 2R_2}
\mat{1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0}.
\] There is no pivot in column 3, so \(c_3\) is free and the vectors are dependent. Take \(c_3 = 1\). Then row 2 gives \(c_2 = -1\), and row 1 gives \(c_1 = -2c_2 = 2\). So \[
2\vect{v}_1 - \vect{v}_2 + \vect{v}_3 = \zerovec,
\] which you can check entry by entry. The three vectors lie in one plane, the one spanned by \(\vect{v}_1\) and \(\vect{v}_2\). This is the Three in a plane example in the app.








NoteExample 3: three independent vectors



Show that \((1, 1, 0)\T\), \((0, 1, 1)\T\) and \((1, 0, 1)\T\) are independent, and that they span \(\R^3\).
Solution. Three vectors in \(\R^3\) make a square matrix, so use the determinant. Expanding along the first row, \[
\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}
= 1(1 - 0) - 0 + 1(1 - 0) = 2 \neq 0.
\] So the vectors are independent. And since \(\det\M{A} \neq 0\), \(\M{A}\vect{c} = \vect{b}\) has a solution for every \(\vect{b}\) (Chapter 7), so every vector in \(\R^3\) is in their span.




Why independence matters
If the vectors are independent, every vector in their span can be made from them in exactly one way. For if \[
\vect{b} = c_1\vect{v}_1 + \dots + c_k\vect{v}_k = d_1\vect{v}_1 + \dots + d_k\vect{v}_k,
\] then subtracting gives \((c_1 - d_1)\vect{v}_1 + \dots + (c_k - d_k)\vect{v}_k = \zerovec\), and independence forces every \(c_i = d_i\). With dependent vectors, there are always infinitely many ways (the app shows this in Parallel: a line). This is the idea behind coordinates, in Chapter 15.


Subspaces
Spans have a special property. Adding two combinations of \(\vect{v}_1, \dots, \vect{v}_k\) gives another combination of them, and so does multiplying one by a number. A set of vectors with these properties (containing \(\zerovec\), and closed under adding and scaling) is called a subspace. In \(\R^3\), the subspaces are the origin on its own, lines and planes through the origin, and all of \(\R^3\). Every span is a subspace, and every subspace is a span. The subspaces attached to a matrix are the subject of Chapter 16.

title: 14  Span and linear independence
text:
14.3 In code

Run this chapter’s code yourself: open the notebook in Colab, or download the Jupyter notebook or the MATLAB script.

Both tests come down to rank. To find a dependence relation, find the solutions of \(\M{A}\vect{c} = \zerovec\): SciPy’s null_space and MATLAB’s null do this. They return a vector of length 1, so divide by one of its entries to get tidier numbers.

PythonMATLAB



import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import null_space

v1, v2, v3 = [1, 0, 1], [2, 1, 0], [0, 1, -2]
A = np.column_stack([v1, v2, v3])          # the vectors as columns
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(A))            # 2 < 3, so dependent

c = null_space(A)                          # solutions of A c = 0
print(c.ravel() / c[2, 0])                 # scaled so that c3 = 1

b = [1, 2, 3]                              # is b in the span?
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(A), np.linalg.matrix_rank(np.column_stack([A, b])))

2
[ 2. -1.  1.]
2 3


The rank is 2, so the three vectors are dependent, with \(2\vect{v}_1 - \vect{v}_2 + \vect{v}_3 = \zerovec\) as in Example 2. Adding \(\vect{b}\) raises the rank to 3, so \(\vect{b}\) is not in their span.


v1 = [1; 0; 1]; v2 = [2; 1; 0]; v3 = [0; 1; -2];
A = [v1 v2 v3];            % the vectors as columns
rank(A)                    % 2 < 3, so dependent

c = null(A);               % solutions of A c = 0
c = c / c(3)               % scaled so that c3 = 1

b = [1; 2; 3];             % is b in the span?
[rank(A), rank([A b])]
ans =

     2

c =

     2
    -1
     1

ans =

     2     3
The rank is 2, so the three vectors are dependent, with \(2\vect{v}_1 - \vect{v}_2 + \vect{v}_3 = \zerovec\) as in Example 2. Adding \(\vect{b}\) raises the rank to 3, so \(\vect{b}\) is not in their span. In MATLAB, null(A, 'r') gives tidy whole-number answers directly.

title: 14  Span and linear independence
text:
14.4 Check your understanding






TipWhat is the span of \((1, 2)\T\) and \((-2, -4)\T\)?





The line through the origin in the direction \((1, 2)\T\): the second vector is \(-2\) times the first, so it adds nothing.









TipCan four vectors in \(\R^3\) be linearly independent?





No. More than \(n\) vectors in \(\R^n\) are always dependent.









TipCan a plane that doesn’t pass through the origin be the span of some vectors?





No. Every span contains \(\zerovec\).

title: 14  Span and linear independence
text:
14.5 Key ideas

The span of a set of vectors is all their linear combinations. \(\vect{b}\) is in the span of the columns of \(\M{A}\) exactly when \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) has a solution.
Vectors are linearly independent when no one of them is a combination of the others: the only way to make \(\zerovec\) is with all the amounts zero.
To test, put the vectors in the columns of a matrix and row reduce. They are independent exactly when every column has a pivot (the rank equals the number of vectors).
A dependence relation can be read from the solutions of \(\M{A}\vect{c} = \zerovec\).
A subspace is a set of vectors closed under addition and scaling, such as a line or plane through the origin. Every span is a subspace.

title: 14  Span and linear independence
text:
14.7 In practice

Redundant sensors: if one sensor’s readings are always a fixed combination of others’ (say, a total flow meter that reads the sum of three branch meters), the measurement vectors are dependent. That redundancy is useful for spotting a faulty sensor, but it adds no new information about the system.
Statistics: in regression, if one explanatory variable is (nearly) a combination of the others, the columns of the data matrix are (nearly) dependent. This is called multicollinearity. The fit can still predict well, but the individual coefficients become unreliable, because many combinations explain the data almost equally well.
Colour: screens mix red, green and blue light. The three colours are independent, so different mixes give different colours, and together they span the colours the screen can show. A fourth primary would always be a combination of the first three.
Structures: the members meeting at a joint of a frame must point in enough independent directions to hold it in place. If they all lie in one plane, the joint can move out of that plane.

title: 14  Span and linear independence
text:
14.8 Going further

Vectors don’t have to be lists of numbers. Anything that can be added and scaled, following the rules of Chapter 2, forms a vector space: polynomials, functions, signals, images. The functions \(1\), \(x\) and \(x^2\) are linearly independent (no combination of them is zero for every \(x\) unless all the coefficients are zero), and their span is all quadratics. Fourier series write a signal as a combination of the independent functions \(\sin x, \cos x, \sin 2x, \cos 2x, \dots\)
Independence is fragile in floating-point arithmetic: a tiny change can turn dependent vectors into independent ones, as the app shows. In practice, the question is often how close to dependent the vectors are, which the singular value decomposition answers (Chapter 21).
The largest number of independent vectors in a subspace, and the smallest number that span it, turn out to be the same number: its dimension (Chapter 15).

title: 15  Basis, dimension and change of basis
text:
15.1 Build intuition
Core
Builds on Chapter 7, Chapter 14.
Coordinates are not built into a vector. They depend on the directions you measure along. Measuring along \(\ui\) and \(\uj\) is natural for a page, but for a reflection it is more natural to measure along the mirror and at right angles to it, and for a rotating body, along its axis. In the right directions, a complicated matrix often becomes very simple. This chapter shows how to choose directions (a basis), how to find a vector’s coordinates in them, and how to rewrite a matrix in them. It is the groundwork for eigenvalues and diagonalisation in Part IV.
The green vector \(\vect{v}\) stays fixed while you choose a new pair of basis vectors \(\vect{b}_1\) and \(\vect{b}_2\). The purple grid is the grid they make, and the readout gives \(\vect{v}\)’s coordinates in the usual basis and in the new one.
Things to try:

Open the basis grids app in its own tab



In the Example 2 preset, count along the purple grid to check the new coordinates of \(\vect{v}\).

crumbs: 15  Basis, dimension and change of basis

title: 15  Basis, dimension and change of basis
text:
15.2 The ideas

Basis
A basis for a subspace (Chapter 14) is a set of vectors that

spans the subspace, so every vector in it can be made from them, and
is linearly independent, so none of them is wasted.

Together these say that every vector in the subspace can be written as a combination of the basis vectors in exactly one way (Chapter 14). The standard basis of \(\R^n\) is \(\ue{1}, \dots, \ue{n}\), the columns of the identity matrix; in \(\R^2\) and \(\R^3\) these are \(\ui\), \(\uj\) and \(\uk\). But there are infinitely many other bases. Any two vectors in \(\R^2\) that don’t lie along the same line form a basis for \(\R^2\).


Dimension
A subspace has many different bases, but they all have the same number of vectors (a proof is in Section C.8). That number is the dimension of the subspace:

a line through the origin has dimension 1;
a plane through the origin has dimension 2;
\(\R^n\) has dimension \(n\), since the standard basis has \(n\) vectors;
the subspace containing only \(\zerovec\) has dimension 0, with the empty set as its basis.

So dimension makes the everyday idea precise. It also gives useful shortcuts in \(\R^n\):

any \(n\) independent vectors in \(\R^n\) form a basis (they automatically span);
any \(n\) vectors that span \(\R^n\) form a basis (they are automatically independent);
fewer than \(n\) vectors can’t span \(\R^n\), and more than \(n\) can’t be independent.



Finding a basis for a span
Given some vectors, put them in the columns of a matrix \(\M{A}\) and reduce it to echelon form. The pivot columns tell you which of the vectors to keep: the original vectors in the pivot columns form a basis for their span, and the others are combinations of them. (Row operations change the vectors but not the relationships between them, which is why you go back to the original columns, as in the proof in Section C.6.) So the dimension of the span is the rank of \(\M{A}\).






NoteExample 1: a basis for a span



Find a basis for the span of \((1, 2, 1)\T\), \((2, 4, 2)\T\), \((1, 0, 1)\T\) and \((0, 2, 0)\T\), and its dimension.
Solution. Reduce the matrix with these columns: \[
\mat{1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 0}
\xrightarrow[R_3 \,\leftarrow\, R_3 - R_1]{R_2 \,\leftarrow\, R_2 - 2R_1}
\mat{1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0}.
\] The pivots are in columns 1 and 3, so \((1, 2, 1)\T\) and \((1, 0, 1)\T\) form a basis, and the span has dimension 2: it is a plane. The other two vectors are combinations of these: \((2, 4, 2)\T\) is twice the first, and \((0, 2, 0)\T\) is the first minus the second.




Coordinates
If \(\vect{b}_1, \dots, \vect{b}_n\) is a basis for \(\R^n\), each vector \(\vect{v}\) can be written in exactly one way as \[
\vect{v} = c_1\vect{b}_1 + \dots + c_n\vect{b}_n.
\] The numbers \(c_1, \dots, c_n\) are the coordinates of \(\vect{v}\) in this basis, written \([\vect{v}]_B\). The usual entries of \(\vect{v}\) are just its coordinates in the standard basis.
Put the basis vectors in the columns of a matrix \(\M{P}\). By the column view of multiplication, \[
\vect{v} = \M{P}\,[\vect{v}]_B
\qquad\text{and so}\qquad
[\vect{v}]_B = \M{P}^{-1}\vect{v}.
\tag{15.1}\] \(\M{P}\) is invertible because its columns are independent. Multiplying by \(\M{P}\) converts new coordinates to standard ones; multiplying by \(\M{P}^{-1}\), or better, solving \(\M{P}\vect{c} = \vect{v}\), converts the other way.






NoteExample 2: coordinates in a new basis



Show that \(\vect{b}_1 = (1, 1)\T\) and \(\vect{b}_2 = (1, -1)\T\) form a basis for \(\R^2\), and find the coordinates of \(\vect{v} = (5, 1)\T\) in it.
Solution. The vectors don’t lie along the same line (\(\det\mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1} = -2 \neq 0\)), so they are independent, and two independent vectors in \(\R^2\) form a basis. Solve \(c_1\vect{b}_1 + c_2\vect{b}_2 = \vect{v}\): \[
\begin{aligned}
c_1 + c_2 &= 5 \\
c_1 - c_2 &= 1
\end{aligned}
\] Adding gives \(2c_1 = 6\), so \(c_1 = 3\) and \(c_2 = 2\): \([\vect{v}]_B = (3, 2)\T\). Check: \(3(1, 1)\T + 2(1, -1)\T = (5, 1)\T\). ✓ This is Example 2 in the app.




A transformation in a new basis
Suppose \(\M{A}\) is the matrix of a transformation in standard coordinates. What is its matrix in the basis \(B\)? Start with a vector’s new coordinates \([\vect{x}]_B\), and follow three steps, each a matrix multiplication:

convert to standard coordinates: multiply by \(\M{P}\);
apply the transformation: multiply by \(\M{A}\);
convert back to new coordinates: multiply by \(\M{P}^{-1}\).

So the matrix of the same transformation in the new basis is \[
\M{B} = \M{P}^{-1}\M{A}\M{P}.
\tag{15.2}\] Read it from right to left, as with any composition (Chapter 5). Turned round, \(\M{A} = \M{P}\M{B}\M{P}^{-1}\): this lets you build a matrix by describing what it does in a convenient basis, as Example 3 shows.
Two matrices related by \(\M{B} = \M{P}^{-1}\M{A}\M{P}\) for some invertible \(\M{P}\) are called similar. Similar matrices describe the same transformation in different coordinates, so they share everything that doesn’t depend on the coordinates. For example, they have the same determinant (the same area or volume scale factor): \[
\det\M{B} = \det\M{P}^{-1}\,\det\M{A}\,\det\M{P} = \det\M{A}.
\] They also have the same eigenvalues (Chapter 18).






NoteExample 3: a reflection built in a convenient basis



Find the matrix of the reflection in the line \(y = 2x\).
Solution. In the right basis, this reflection is easy to describe. Take \(\vect{b}_1 = (1, 2)\T\) along the mirror and \(\vect{b}_2 = (-2, 1)\T\) at right angles to it (Figure 15.1). The reflection leaves \(\vect{b}_1\) alone and reverses \(\vect{b}_2\), so in this basis its matrix is \[
\M{B} = \mat{1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1}.
\] With \(\M{P} = \mat{1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1}\), whose determinant is 5, the inverse is \(\M{P}^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{5}\mat{1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1}\), and so \[
\M{A} = \M{P}\M{B}\M{P}^{-1} = \mat{1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1} \cdot \frac{1}{5}\mat{1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1} = \frac{1}{5}\mat{-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3}.
\] Check: \(\M{A}(1, 2)\T = \tfrac{1}{5}(5, 10)\T = (1, 2)\T\), so the mirror line is fixed. ✓ This agrees with the reflection formula in Chapter 4.






Figure 15.1: The convenient basis for the reflection in \(y = 2x\): \(\vect{b}_1\) lies along the mirror and is left alone, and \(\vect{b}_2\) is at right angles to it and is reversed.











NoteExample 4: a matrix that becomes diagonal



In Chapter 9, the matrix \(\M{A} = \mat{3 & 1 \\ 2 & 2}\) had invariant lines along \((1, 1)\T\), stretched by 4, and \((1, -2)\T\), fixed. Find its matrix in the basis of these two vectors.
Solution. With \(\M{P} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2}\), first compute \(\M{A}\M{P}\), whose columns are the images of the basis vectors: \[
\M{A}\M{P} = \mat{4 & 1 \\ 4 & -2}.
\] Column 1 is \(4\vect{b}_1\) and column 2 is \(1\vect{b}_2\), so in the new basis the images have coordinates \((4, 0)\T\) and \((0, 1)\T\): \[
\M{P}^{-1}\M{A}\M{P} = \mat{4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1}.
\] In the basis of its invariant lines, the matrix is diagonal: it just stretches each new coordinate. This is the idea behind diagonalisation (Chapter 19), and the Invariant lines preset in the app shows this basis.

title: 15  Basis, dimension and change of basis
text:
15.4 Check your understanding






TipDo \((1, 0, 0)\T\) and \((0, 1, 0)\T\) form a basis for \(\R^3\)?





No: two vectors can’t span \(\R^3\), which has dimension 3. They form a basis for the \(xy\)-plane.









TipIf \(\vect{b}_1\) is doubled in length, what happens to the first coordinate of every vector?





It halves: you need half as many of the longer steps.









TipCan two similar matrices have different determinants?





No: similar matrices describe the same transformation, and \(\det(\M{P}^{-1}\M{A}\M{P}) = \det\M{A}\).
crumbs: 15  Basis, dimension and change of basis

title: 15  Basis, dimension and change of basis
text:
15.5 Key ideas

A basis is a set of independent vectors that spans a space. Every vector in the space can then be written as a combination of them in exactly one way.
Every basis of a space has the same number of vectors, its dimension.
The pivot columns of a matrix form a basis for the span of its columns.
The coordinates of \(\vect{x}\) in the basis that makes up the columns of \(\M{P}\) are \(\M{P}^{-1}\vect{x}\).
In that basis, the transformation \(\M{A}\) has the matrix \(\M{P}^{-1}\M{A}\M{P}\). Choosing a convenient basis can make a matrix simple, even diagonal.

title: 15  Basis, dimension and change of basis
text:
15.7 In practice

Finite element analysis: each beam or panel in a structure is easiest to describe in its own local coordinates, along and across the member. The program converts each member’s stiffness matrix to the global coordinates of the whole structure with a change of basis, \(\M{P}\M{K}\M{P}\T\), before assembling them.
Robotics and graphics: a robot arm or an animated character is a chain of parts, each with its own coordinate frame. Positions are passed along the chain by multiplying change-of-basis matrices (Chapter 34).
Crystals and materials: properties such as stiffness or electrical conductivity are simplest along a crystal’s own axes, and are converted to laboratory axes by a change of basis.
Data: principal component analysis (Chapter 21) finds a new basis in which a cloud of data points is described most efficiently.
crumbs: 15  Basis, dimension and change of basis

title: 15  Basis, dimension and change of basis
text:
15.8 Going further

Bases exist for any vector space, not just \(\R^n\). The polynomials of degree at most 2 have the basis \(1, x, x^2\), so they form a space of dimension 3. Some spaces, such as the space of all continuous functions, have no finite basis at all, and are infinite-dimensional.
A transformation between abstract vector spaces, such as differentiation of polynomials, has a matrix once a basis is chosen for each space, and changing the bases changes the matrix as in Equation 15.2.
Proof that every basis of a subspace has the same number of vectors: Section C.8.

title: 16  Column space, null space and rank–nullity
text:
16.1 Build intuition
Core
Builds on Chapter 12, Chapter 15.
Every \(m \times n\) matrix comes with four subspaces. Two of them have appeared already without names: the right-hand sides \(\vect{b}\) for which \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) can be solved, and the solutions of \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec\) (Chapter 10). This chapter names all four, finds bases for them by row reduction, and shows how their dimensions are tied together by the rank. Together they answer every question about \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\): whether it has a solution, and if so, what all the solutions are.
The span explorer is showing the three columns of \[
\M{A} = \mat{1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 3}.
\] Their span is the column space of \(\M{A}\): all the vectors \(\M{A}\vect{x}\) that the matrix can produce.

crumbs: 16  Column space, null space and rank–nullity

title: 16  Column space, null space and rank–nullity
text:
16.2 The ideas

The column space
The column space of \(\M{A}\), written \(C(\M{A})\), is the span of its columns. Since \(\M{A}\vect{x}\) is a combination of the columns with coefficients from \(\vect{x}\), it is the set of all vectors \(\M{A}\vect{x}\). It is a subspace of \(\R^m\) (the columns have \(m\) entries), and






ImportantSolvability



\(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) has a solution exactly when \(\vect{b}\) is in the column space of \(\M{A}\).


A basis for \(C(\M{A})\) is given by the pivot columns of \(\M{A}\) itself (not of its echelon form), as in Chapter 15. So the dimension of the column space is the rank \(r\).


The null space
The null space of \(\M{A}\), written \(N(\M{A})\), is the set of all solutions of \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec\). It is a subspace of \(\R^n\) (the solutions have \(n\) entries): adding two solutions, or scaling one, gives another solution (Chapter 10, Exercise 5). It contains every dependence relation between the columns, and it is \(\{\zerovec\}\) exactly when the columns are independent.
To find a basis, reduce \(\M{A}\) to reduced row echelon form, and write the solutions in terms of the free variables as in Chapter 12: \[
\vect{x} = s\,\vect{h}_1 + t\,\vect{h}_2 + \cdots,
\] with one vector \(\vect{h}_i\) for each free variable. These vectors are a basis for \(N(\M{A})\). (They are independent because each has a 1 in the position of its own free variable, where the others have 0.) So the dimension of the null space, called the nullity, is the number of free variables, \(n - r\).


Rank–nullity
Every column of \(\M{A}\) either has a pivot or belongs to a free variable. Counting the columns both ways gives the rank–nullity theorem: \[
\operatorname{rank}\M{A} + \operatorname{nullity}\M{A} = n,
\tag{16.1}\] the number of columns. In terms of the transformation \(\vect{x} \mapsto \M{A}\vect{x}\) from \(\R^n\) to \(\R^m\): the dimensions that are kept (\(r\), the dimension of the column space) plus the dimensions that are squashed to nothing (the nullity) add up to the dimensions you started with. A \(3 \times 3\) matrix of rank 2 squashes space onto a plane, and a whole line, its null space, is squashed onto the origin.






NoteExample 1: counting with rank–nullity



A \(5 \times 7\) matrix has rank 4. What are the dimensions of its four subspaces? Can \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) be solved for every \(\vect{b}\)?
Solution. With \(m = 5\), \(n = 7\) and \(r = 4\): the column space and row space have dimension 4, the null space has dimension \(7 - 4 = 3\), and the left null space has dimension \(5 - 4 = 1\). The column space is a 4-dimensional subspace of \(\R^5\), not all of it, so \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) has no solution for most \(\vect{b}\). When it does have one, it has infinitely many, with 3 free parameters.




The row space and the left null space
Applying the same ideas to \(\M{A}\T\) gives two more subspaces.

The row space \(C(\M{A}\T)\) is the span of the rows of \(\M{A}\), a subspace of \(\R^n\). Row operations replace rows by combinations of rows, so they don’t change it, and the non-zero rows of the echelon form are a basis. So the row space also has dimension \(r\): the number of independent rows equals the number of independent columns. This is not obvious at all, but it falls out of elimination.
The left null space \(N(\M{A}\T)\) is the set of solutions of \(\M{A}\T\vect{y} = \zerovec\), a subspace of \(\R^m\). Each such \(\vect{y}\) is a combination of the rows of \(\M{A}\) that adds up to zero, a dependence relation between the rows. By rank–nullity for \(\M{A}\T\), its dimension is \(m - r\).

NoteExample 2: all four subspaces



Find bases for the four fundamental subspaces of \[
\M{A} = \mat{1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 & 5},
\] and check the dimensions against the table.
Solution. Here \(m = 3\) and \(n = 4\). Reduce: \[
\M{A}
\xrightarrow[R_3 \,\leftarrow\, R_3 - 3R_1]{R_2 \,\leftarrow\, R_2 - 2R_1}
\mat{1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2}
\xrightarrow{R_3 \,\leftarrow\, R_3 - R_2}
\mat{1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0}.
\] This is already the reduced form. The pivots are in columns 1 and 3, so \(r = 2\).

Column space: the pivot columns of \(\M{A}\), \((1, 2, 3)\T\) and \((0, 1, 1)\T\). Dimension 2: a plane in \(\R^3\).
Null space: the free variables are \(x_2 = s\) and \(x_4 = t\), and the rows give \(x_1 = -2s - t\) and \(x_3 = -2t\). So \[
\vect{x} = s\mat{-2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0} + t\mat{-1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 1},
\] and these two vectors are a basis. Dimension \(n - r = 2\).
Row space: the non-zero rows of the echelon form, \((1, 2, 0, 1)\) and \((0, 0, 1, 2)\). Dimension 2.
Left null space: row 3 of \(\M{A}\) is row 1 plus row 2, so \(\vect{y} = (1, 1, -1)\T\) gives \(\M{A}\T\vect{y} = \zerovec\). Dimension \(m - r = 1\), so this vector is a basis.

Check the right angles: \((1, 2, 0, 1) \cdot (-2, 1, 0, 0) = 0\) and \((0, 0, 1, 2) \cdot (-1, 0, -2, 1) = 0\), and similarly for the other two pairs. And \((1, 1, -1) \cdot (1, 2, 3) = 0\) and \((1, 1, -1) \cdot (0, 1, 1) = 0\). ✓




Right angles between the subspaces
Write out \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec\) row by row. Each equation says that a row of \(\M{A}\), dotted with \(\vect{x}\), gives zero. So every vector in the null space is perpendicular to every row, and so to every combination of rows, as Figure 16.1 shows for a \(2 \times 3\) matrix:






ImportantOrthogonality



The null space of \(\M{A}\) is at right angles to the row space of \(\M{A}\). In the same way, the left null space is at right angles to the column space.




Show the code for this figure
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

r1, r2 = np.array([1, 1, 2]), np.array([1, 2, 3])
n = np.array([-1, -1, 1])
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 5))
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")
u1 = r1 / np.linalg.norm(r1)                     # two perpendicular directions in the plane
u2 = np.cross(n, r1); u2 = u2 / np.linalg.norm(u2)
s, t = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-2.2, 2.2, 2), np.linspace(-2.2, 2.2, 2))
X, Y, Z = (s[..., None] * u1 + t[..., None] * u2).transpose(2, 0, 1)
ax.plot_surface(X, Y, Z, color="#0a7050", alpha=0.25)
for r, lab in ((r1, "row 1"), (r2, "row 2")):
    ax.quiver(0, 0, 0, *r, color="#0a7050", arrow_length_ratio=0.12, lw=2)
    ax.text(*(r * 1.08), lab, color="#0a7050")
ax.plot(*np.outer([-2.2, 2.2], n).T, color="#2153b8", lw=3)
ax.text(*(n * 2.3), "null space", color="#2153b8")
ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("y"); ax.set_zlabel("z")
for f in (ax.set_xlim, ax.set_ylim, ax.set_zlim):
    f(-2.5, 2.5)
ax.set_box_aspect((1, 1, 1))                     # equal scales, so right angles look right
ax.view_init(elev=25, azim=-70)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 16.1: For the matrix with rows (1, 1, 2) and (1, 2, 3), the row space (the green plane spanned by the two rows) and the null space (the blue line along (−1, −1, 1)) meet at right angles. Every vector in space splits into a piece in each.





Because the dimensions add up (\(r + (n - r) = n\)), the row space and the null space together fill \(\R^n\): every vector splits uniquely into a piece in the row space and a piece in the null space (Chapter 17 makes this precise). Similarly the column space and left null space split \(\R^m\). These four subspaces, and the right angles between them, are the subject of the “fundamental theorem of linear algebra”.


The structure of every solution
Putting this together with Equation 10.1: if \(\vect{b}\) is in the column space, then every solution of \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) is \[
\vect{x} = \vect{x}_p + \vect{x}_n,
\] a particular solution \(\vect{x}_p\) plus any vector \(\vect{x}_n\) in the null space. The solution is unique exactly when the null space is just \(\{\zerovec\}\), that is, when \(r = n\).






NoteExample 3: every solution



For \(\M{A}\) in Example 2, solve \(\M{A}\vect{x} = (1, 4, 5)\T\).
Solution. First, is \(\vect{b} = (1, 4, 5)\T\) in the column space? It must be at right angles to the left null space, and \((1, 1, -1) \cdot (1, 4, 5) = 0\), so it is. (Equivalently, \(b_3 = b_1 + b_2\), matching the relation between the rows.) Reducing \([\M{A} \mid \vect{b}]\) with the same steps gives \[
\amat{rrrr|r}{1 & 2 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0}.
\] Setting the free variables to zero gives the particular solution \(\vect{x}_p = (1, 0, 2, 0)\T\). So every solution is \[
\vect{x} = \mat{1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ 0} + s\mat{-2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0} + t\mat{-1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 1},
\] a particular solution plus the null space: a plane of solutions in \(\R^4\).

title: 16  Column space, null space and rank–nullity
text:
16.3 In code

Run this chapter’s code yourself: open the notebook in Colab, or download the Jupyter notebook or the MATLAB script.

SciPy’s null_space and orth, and MATLAB’s null and orth, return bases for the null space and column space. They give orthonormal bases (perpendicular vectors of length 1, Chapter 17), computed from the singular value decomposition, so they look different from the bases found by hand. They span the same subspaces, which you can check by testing that \(\M{A}\) times each null space vector is zero.

PythonMATLAB



import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import null_space, orth

A = np.array([[1, 2, 0, 1],
              [2, 4, 1, 4],
              [3, 6, 1, 5]])
r = np.linalg.matrix_rank(A)
N = null_space(A)                  # columns: a basis for N(A)
print("rank", r, " nullity", N.shape[1], " n =", A.shape[1])
print(np.round(A @ N, 12) + 0)     # zero: they really solve Ax = 0
print(orth(A).shape[1])            # dimension of the column space
print(null_space(A.T).ravel())     # left null space: a multiple of (1, 1, -1)

The exact value of norm(A * N) depends on your computer; it is always tiny. null(A, 'r') gives the whole-number basis found by hand.

title: 16  Column space, null space and rank–nullity
text:
16.4 Check your understanding






TipA \(4 \times 4\) matrix has a null space of dimension 1. What is its rank? Is it invertible?





Rank \(4 - 1 = 3\), so it is not invertible.









TipWhy is every vector in the null space perpendicular to every row?





\(\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec\) says, row by row, that each row dotted with \(\vect{x}\) is zero.









TipCan a \(3 \times 5\) matrix have a column space of dimension 4?





No. The column space lives in \(\R^3\), and its dimension is the rank, which is at most 3.
crumbs: 16  Column space, null space and rank–nullity

title: 16  Column space, null space and rank–nullity
text:
16.5 Key ideas

Every matrix has four fundamental subspaces: the column space and the null space of \(\M{A}\), and the row space and the left null space, which are the column space and null space of \(\M{A}\T\).
The column space is the set of reachable right-hand sides \(\vect{b}\); its basis is the pivot columns of \(\M{A}\).
The null space is the set of solutions of \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec\); its basis comes from the free variables.
Rank–nullity: for an \(m \times n\) matrix, the rank plus the dimension of the null space equals \(n\), the number of unknowns.
The row space and the null space are at right angles. Every solution of \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) is a particular solution plus any vector in the null space.

title: 16  Column space, null space and rank–nullity
text:
16.7 In practice

Structures and mechanisms: the equilibrium equations of a pin-jointed frame relate the forces in its bars to the loads at its joints. A non-zero vector in the null space of the matrix that maps joint movements to bar stretches is a way the frame can move without stretching any bar: a mechanism, which an engineer must design out. A non-zero vector in the null space of the equilibrium matrix is a set of bar forces that balances with no load at all: a self-stress, as in a pre-tensioned cable net.
Chemical reactions: the null space of a matrix of atom counts (as in Chapter 12, Example 3) gives the balanced reactions. For a network of reactions, the left null space gives the quantities that are conserved, such as the total number of atoms of each element.
Networks and circuits: for the matrix that records which nodes each link of a network joins, the null space describes flows around closed loops, and the left null space reflects the network’s connected pieces (Chapter 32).
Data: when the columns of a data matrix are dependent, the null space describes exactly which combinations of the measured variables carry no information.
crumbs: 16  Column space, null space and rank–nullity

title: 16  Column space, null space and rank–nullity
text:
16.8 Going further

Taking right angles seriously turns the four subspaces into a complete picture of a matrix. The singular value decomposition (Chapter 21) gives orthonormal bases for all four at once, matched up so that \(\M{A}\) sends each row-space basis vector to a multiple of a column-space basis vector.
When \(\vect{b}\) is not in the column space, there is no solution, but the closest vector in the column space gives the best approximate one: least squares (Chapter 17).
Proof of the rank–nullity theorem, and that row rank equals column rank: Section C.9.

title: 17  Orthogonality and least squares
text:
17.1 Build intuition
Core
Builds on Chapter 7, Chapter 16, and the dot product from the Refresher.
Measured data never fits a model exactly. Five measurements of a spring under five loads give five equations for two unknowns (its natural length and its stretchiness), and because every measurement has a small error, no straight line passes through all five points. The system has no solution. But giving up would be absurd: there is clearly a best line. This chapter makes “best” precise, as the line that makes the total squared error as small as possible, and finds it with one linear system, the normal equations. The key idea is a right angle, so the chapter starts with dot products.
Adjust the blue line to fit the points as well as you can by eye. Each vertical dashed line is the error at one point, and the shaded squares show those errors squared. The least-squares line is the one with the smallest total area of squares.
Things to try:

text:
Open the line of best fit app in its own tab



How small can you make the error by moving the sliders? Then show the least-squares line. Was your line close?
Drag one point a long way up. How much does the least-squares line move? Try One outlier.

title: 17  Orthogonality and least squares
text:
17.2 The ideas

Lengths, angles and right angles in \(\R^n\)
The dot product of the Refresher works for vectors of any length: \[
\vect{x} \cdot \vect{y} = x_1y_1 + x_2y_2 + \dots + x_ny_n = \vect{x}\T\vect{y}.
\] The second form, a row times a column, is how it usually appears in matrix calculations. From it come:

the length (or norm) \(\lVert\vect{x}\rVert = \sqrt{\vect{x} \cdot \vect{x}}\), Pythagoras in \(n\) dimensions;
the distance between \(\vect{x}\) and \(\vect{y}\), which is \(\lVert\vect{x} - \vect{y}\rVert\);
the angle \(\theta\) between \(\vect{x}\) and \(\vect{y}\), from \(\vect{x} \cdot \vect{y} = \lVert\vect{x}\rVert\,\lVert\vect{y}\rVert\cos\theta\).

That last formula needs \(\lvert\vect{x} \cdot \vect{y}\rvert \le \lVert\vect{x}\rVert\,\lVert\vect{y}\rVert\), so that \(\cos\theta\) lies between \(-1\) and 1. This is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, and it holds in any number of dimensions (a proof is in Section C.10).
Two vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular) when \(\vect{x} \cdot \vect{y} = 0\). For orthogonal vectors, Pythagoras’ theorem holds: \[
\lVert\vect{x} + \vect{y}\rVert^2 = (\vect{x} + \vect{y}) \cdot (\vect{x} + \vect{y}) = \lVert\vect{x}\rVert^2 + 2\,\vect{x} \cdot \vect{y} + \lVert\vect{y}\rVert^2 = \lVert\vect{x}\rVert^2 + \lVert\vect{y}\rVert^2.
\]


Projection onto a line
The closest point to \(\vect{b}\) on the line through the origin in the direction \(\vect{a}\) is found by dropping a perpendicular. Call it \(\vect{p} = \hat{x}\,\vect{a}\). The error \(\vect{e} = \vect{b} - \vect{p}\) must be at right angles to \(\vect{a}\) (Figure 17.1): \[
\vect{a} \cdot (\vect{b} - \hat{x}\,\vect{a}) = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\hat{x} = \frac{\vect{a} \cdot \vect{b}}{\vect{a} \cdot \vect{a}},
\qquad
\vect{p} = \frac{\vect{a} \cdot \vect{b}}{\vect{a} \cdot \vect{a}}\,\vect{a}.
\tag{17.1}\] This \(\vect{p}\) is the projection of \(\vect{b}\) onto the line. It really is the closest point: any other point \(\vect{q}\) on the line gives \(\vect{b} - \vect{q} = \vect{e} + (\vect{p} - \vect{q})\), a sum of two orthogonal vectors, so by Pythagoras \(\lVert\vect{b} - \vect{q}\rVert^2 = \lVert\vect{e}\rVert^2 + \lVert\vect{p} - \vect{q}\rVert^2\), which is bigger. You met this as the “shadow” of one vector on another in the dot product view of the vector explorer.






Figure 17.1: Projecting \(\vect{b}\) onto the line through \(\vect{a}\). The projection \(\vect{p}\) is the closest point on the line, and the error \(\vect{e} = \vect{b} - \vect{p}\) is at right angles to the line.









NoteExample 1: projection onto a line



Project \(\vect{b} = (3, 1)\T\) onto the line through \(\vect{a} = (1, 2)\T\), and find the distance from \(\vect{b}\) to the line.
Solution. \(\vect{a} \cdot \vect{b} = 3 + 2 = 5\) and \(\vect{a} \cdot \vect{a} = 1 + 4 = 5\), so by Equation 17.1, \(\vect{p} = \tfrac{5}{5}\vect{a} = (1, 2)\T\). The error is \(\vect{e} = \vect{b} - \vect{p} = (2, -1)\T\). Check that it is at right angles to the line: \(\vect{e} \cdot \vect{a} = 2 - 2 = 0\). ✓ The distance from \(\vect{b}\) to the line is \(\lVert\vect{e}\rVert = \sqrt{5}\).




Projection onto a subspace
Now project \(\vect{b}\) onto a bigger subspace: the column space of a matrix \(\M{A}\) with independent columns (Chapter 16). The closest point is \(\vect{p} = \M{A}\hat{\vect{x}}\) for some \(\hat{\vect{x}}\), and the same argument says the error \(\vect{e} = \vect{b} - \M{A}\hat{\vect{x}}\) must be at right angles to the whole subspace (Figure 17.2), so to every column of \(\M{A}\). Dotting with every column at once is multiplying by \(\M{A}\T\): \[
\M{A}\T(\vect{b} - \M{A}\hat{\vect{x}}) = \zerovec
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\M{A}\T\M{A}\,\hat{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\T\vect{b}.
\tag{17.2}\] These are the normal equations (“normal” is another word for perpendicular). \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\) is a square matrix, with one row and column for each column of \(\M{A}\), and it is invertible exactly when the columns of \(\M{A}\) are independent (Chapter 16, Exercise 6). Then the projection is \[
\vect{p} = \M{A}\hat{\vect{x}} = \M{A}(\M{A}\T\M{A})^{-1}\M{A}\T\vect{b}.
\] The matrix \(\M{P} = \M{A}(\M{A}\T\M{A})^{-1}\M{A}\T\) is the projection matrix onto the column space. Projecting twice is the same as projecting once, so \(\M{P}^2 = \M{P}\).






Figure 17.2: Projecting \(\vect{b}\) onto the column space of \(\M{A}\), here a plane spanned by the columns \(\vect{a}_1\) and \(\vect{a}_2\). The error \(\vect{e}\) is at right angles to the whole plane.





Least squares
Suppose \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) has no solution, because \(\vect{b}\) is not in the column space. The least-squares solution is the \(\hat{\vect{x}}\) that makes \(\M{A}\hat{\vect{x}}\) as close as possible to \(\vect{b}\): it minimises \[
\lVert\M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b}\rVert^2 = \text{the sum of the squares of the errors in each equation}.
\] The closest point of the column space to \(\vect{b}\) is its projection, so the least-squares solution is the solution of the normal equations Equation 17.2. When \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) does have a solution, the normal equations give it, with zero error.
The most common use is fitting a model to data. To fit a straight line \(y = c + mt\) to points \((t_1, y_1), \dots, (t_k, y_k)\), ask for every point to lie on the line: \[
\mat{1 & t_1 \\ 1 & t_2 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & t_k}\mat{c \\ m} = \mat{y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_k}.
\] With more points than unknowns, this generally has no solution, and least squares gives the line of best fit. The method works for any model in which the unknown coefficients appear linearly, even if the model is curved. A parabola \(y = c_0 + c_1t + c_2t^2\) just needs a third column, holding \(t_i^2\).
Why squares, rather than the plain size of the errors? Squaring makes every error count as positive, gives a smooth quantity that calculus can minimise (Chapter 22 finds the normal equations that way too), and matches the geometry of distance. It has one weakness, which the app shows: a single wild point has a large squared error, so it can pull the line a long way.






NoteExample 2: calibrating a spring



A spring is hung with loads of 0, 1, 2 and 3 newtons, and its length is measured as 1, 2, 4 and 5 cm. Fit the straight line \(y = c + mt\), where \(t\) is the load and \(y\) the length.
Solution. Asking every point to lie on the line gives four equations for two unknowns: \[
\M{A} = \mat{1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3},
\qquad
\vect{y} = \mat{1 \\ 2 \\ 4 \\ 5}.
\] The normal equations need \[
\M{A}\T\M{A} = \mat{4 & 6 \\ 6 & 14},
\qquad
\M{A}\T\vect{y} = \mat{12 \\ 25}.
\] (The entries are the number of points, the sum of the \(t_i\), the sum of the \(t_i^2\), the sum of the \(y_i\) and the sum of the \(t_iy_i\).) Solving \(4c + 6m = 12\) and \(6c + 14m = 25\) gives \(c = 0.9\) and \(m = 1.4\), so the line of best fit is \[
y = 0.9 + 1.4t.
\] The spring is about 0.9 cm long unloaded, and stretches about 1.4 cm per newton. The errors are \(\vect{e} = \vect{y} - \M{A}\hat{\vect{x}} = (0.1, -0.3, 0.3, -0.1)\T\), so the sum of squared errors is \(0.01 + 0.09 + 0.09 + 0.01 = 0.2\). As the theory says, \(\vect{e}\) is at right angles to both columns: its entries add up to 0, and \(0(0.1) + 1(-0.3) + 2(0.3) + 3(-0.1) = 0\). This is the Spring example in the app.




Orthonormal bases and Gram–Schmidt
Vectors \(\vect{q}_1, \dots, \vect{q}_k\) are orthonormal if each has length 1 and each pair is orthogonal. Put them in the columns of a matrix \(\M{Q}\). The entries of \(\M{Q}\T\M{Q}\) are the dot products \(\vect{q}_i \cdot \vect{q}_j\), so orthonormality says exactly \[
\M{Q}\T\M{Q} = \M{I}.
\] (A square \(\M{Q}\) like this is an orthogonal matrix, as in Chapter 7.) Orthonormal bases make everything easy:

the coordinates of \(\vect{v}\) in an orthonormal basis are just dot products, \(c_i = \vect{q}_i \cdot \vect{v}\), with no system to solve;
the normal equations become \(\hat{\vect{x}} = \M{Q}\T\vect{b}\), and the projection onto the column space is \(\vect{p} = \M{Q}\M{Q}\T\vect{b} = (\vect{q}_1 \cdot \vect{b})\vect{q}_1 + \dots + (\vect{q}_k \cdot \vect{b})\vect{q}_k\), a sum of projections onto lines.

The Gram–Schmidt process turns any independent vectors \(\vect{a}_1, \dots, \vect{a}_k\) into orthonormal ones with the same span. Take each vector in turn, subtract its projections onto the orthonormal vectors found so far, and scale what is left to length 1: \[
\vect{v}_j = \vect{a}_j - (\vect{q}_1 \cdot \vect{a}_j)\,\vect{q}_1 - \dots - (\vect{q}_{j-1} \cdot \vect{a}_j)\,\vect{q}_{j-1},
\qquad
\vect{q}_j = \frac{\vect{v}_j}{\lVert\vect{v}_j\rVert}.
\] What is left, \(\vect{v}_j\), is the part of \(\vect{a}_j\) at right angles to all the earlier vectors. Recording the numbers used along the way writes \(\M{A} = \M{Q}\M{R}\), with \(\M{R}\) upper triangular, the QR factorisation. It is the reliable way to solve least-squares problems on a computer (Chapter 30).






NoteExample 3: Gram–Schmidt, and a projection onto a plane



Find an orthonormal basis for the plane spanned by \(\vect{a}_1 = (1, 1, 0)\T\) and \(\vect{a}_2 = (1, 0, 1)\T\), and use it to project \(\vect{b} = (1, 2, 3)\T\) onto the plane.
Solution. First, \(\lVert\vect{a}_1\rVert = \sqrt{2}\), so \(\vect{q}_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1, 0)\T\). Next, remove from \(\vect{a}_2\) its projection onto \(\vect{q}_1\). Since \(\vect{q}_1 \cdot \vect{a}_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), \[
\vect{v}_2 = \vect{a}_2 - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\vect{q}_1 = (1, 0, 1)\T - \tfrac{1}{2}(1, 1, 0)\T = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}, 1\right)\T.
\] Its length is \(\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{4} + \tfrac{1}{4} + 1} = \sqrt{\tfrac{3}{2}}\), so \(\vect{q}_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(1, -1, 2)\T\). Check: \(\vect{q}_1 \cdot \vect{q}_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{12}}(1 - 1 + 0) = 0\). ✓
With an orthonormal basis, the projection is a sum of projections onto lines. \(\vect{q}_1 \cdot \vect{b} = \tfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(\vect{q}_2 \cdot \vect{b} = \tfrac{5}{\sqrt{6}}\), so \[
\vect{p} = \tfrac{3}{2}(1, 1, 0)\T + \tfrac{5}{6}(1, -1, 2)\T = \left(\tfrac{7}{3}, \tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac{5}{3}\right)\T.
\] The error \(\vect{b} - \vect{p} = \tfrac{4}{3}(-1, 1, 1)\T\) is at right angles to both \(\vect{a}_1\) and \(\vect{a}_2\), as it should be.

title: 17  Orthogonality and least squares
text:
17.3 In code

Run this chapter’s code yourself: open the notebook in Colab, or download the Jupyter notebook or the MATLAB script.

For least squares, use a solver that works on \(\M{A}\) directly rather than forming \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\): NumPy’s lstsq, or MATLAB’s backslash, which automatically gives the least-squares solution when \(\M{A}\) has more rows than columns. They use the QR factorisation, which is more accurate (Chapter 30). For fitting polynomials there is also polyfit, which lists the coefficients from the highest power down.

PythonMATLAB



import numpy as np

t = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3])
y = np.array([1, 2, 4, 5])
A = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(t), t])        # columns: 1 and t

x, sse, rank, sv = np.linalg.lstsq(A, y, rcond=None)
print(x, sse)                                    # c and m, and the sum of squared errors

print(np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A, A.T @ y))         # the normal equations: same answer
print(np.polyfit(t, y, 1))                       # slope first, then intercept

Q, R = np.linalg.qr(np.array([[1, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1]]))
print(np.round(Q, 4) + 0)                        # orthonormal columns (Example 3, up to sign)

[0.9 1.4] [0.2]
[0.9 1.4]
[1.4 0.9]
[[-0.7071  0.4082]
 [-0.7071 -0.4082]
 [ 0.      0.8165]]




t = [0; 1; 2; 3];
y = [1; 2; 4; 5];
A = [ones(4, 1), t];       % columns: 1 and t

x = A \ y                  % least squares, because A is tall
sum((y - A*x).^2)          % the sum of squared errors
p = polyfit(t, y, 1)       % slope first, then intercept

[Q, R] = qr([1 1; 1 0; 0 1], 0);
Q                          % orthonormal columns (Example 3, up to sign)
x =

    0.9000
    1.4000

ans =

    0.2000

p =

    1.4000    0.9000

Q =

   -0.7071    0.4082
   -0.7071   -0.4082
         0    0.8165



The QR factorisation may give \(-\vect{q}_1\) or \(-\vect{q}_2\) instead of \(\vect{q}_1\) or \(\vect{q}_2\). Either sign is an equally good orthonormal basis.

title: 17  Orthogonality and least squares
text:
17.4 Check your understanding






TipWhat is the projection of \(\vect{b}\) onto a line if \(\vect{b}\) is already on the line? If \(\vect{b}\) is at right angles to the line?





\(\vect{b}\) itself; and \(\zerovec\).









TipWhy does the least-squares error vector have to be at right angles to every column of \(\M{A}\)?





If it weren’t, moving \(\M{A}\hat{\vect{x}}\) a little along that column would bring it closer to \(\vect{b}\), so it wouldn’t be the closest point.









TipIf the columns of \(\M{Q}\) are orthonormal, what is \(\M{Q}\T\M{Q}\)?





The identity matrix.

title: 17  Orthogonality and least squares
text:
17.5 Key ideas

The dot product measures length, \(\lVert\vect{v}\rVert = \sqrt{\vect{v}\cdot\vect{v}}\), and angle, \(\cos\theta = \vect{u}\cdot\vect{v}/(\lVert\vect{u}\rVert\lVert\vect{v}\rVert)\), in any number of dimensions. Vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero.
Projecting \(\vect{b}\) onto a line or subspace gives its closest point there, and the error is at right angles to the subspace.
When \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) has no solution, the least-squares solution solves the normal equations \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\hat{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\T\vect{b}\), and makes \(\M{A}\hat{\vect{x}}\) the projection of \(\vect{b}\) onto the column space.
Fitting a line or curve to data is a least-squares problem.
Gram–Schmidt turns any basis into an orthonormal one, in which coordinates and projections are just dot products.

title: 17  Orthogonality and least squares
text:
17.6 Exercises
Exercises marked † are harder: they take longer, or need an idea that the worked examples don’t show.

Solution to exercise 1

(Hint: use \((\M{X}\M{Y})\T = \M{Y}\T\M{X}\T\), and note that \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\) is symmetric, so its inverse is too. For \(\M{P}^2\), multiply out and cancel \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\) against its inverse.)

Code. A ball is thrown upwards, and its height \(h\) in metres is measured at times \(t = 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5\) seconds as \(2.1, 7.6, 11.3, 11.8, 10.5, 6.2\). title: 17  Orthogonality and least squares
text:
17.7 In practice

Calibration: instruments from thermometers to strain gauges are calibrated by fitting a line or curve to readings at known values, exactly as in Example 2.
Statistics: linear regression is least squares. Each row of \(\M{A}\) is one observation, each column one explanatory variable, and \(\hat{\vect{x}}\) holds the estimated effects (Chapter 37).
GPS: a receiver measures its distance to more satellites than it strictly needs, with small errors in each. It finds its position by least squares (after a step that makes the equations linear, Chapter 28), and the extra satellites improve the accuracy.
Surveying and image processing: networks of measured angles and distances are adjusted by least squares so that they fit together consistently, and least squares underlies many methods for removing blur and noise from images.

title: 17  Orthogonality and least squares
text:
17.8 Going further

Weighted least squares gives more reliable measurements more influence, by minimising \(\sum w_i e_i^2\) with weights \(w_i\). Robust methods reduce the influence of outliers, for example by minimising \(\sum \lvert e_i\rvert\) instead.
Forming \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\) squares the condition number of the problem (Chapter 24), so it can lose accuracy when the columns of \(\M{A}\) are nearly dependent. The QR factorisation avoids this (Chapter 30).
When the columns of \(\M{A}\) are dependent, there are many least-squares solutions. The singular value decomposition picks the shortest one, through the pseudo-inverse (Chapter 21).
Orthogonality works for functions too, with the dot product replaced by an integral, \(\int f(t)g(t)\,dt\). Fourier series are projections onto orthogonal sines and cosines.
Proofs of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, that the normal equations give the minimum, and that Gram–Schmidt works: Section C.10.

title: 18  Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
text:
18.1 Build intuition
Core
Builds on Chapter 6, Chapter 9, Chapter 16.
Chapter 9 found the lines that a \(2 \times 2\) matrix maps onto themselves, with a formula that only works in two dimensions. Along such a line the matrix just stretches: \(\M{A}\vect{v} = \lambda\vect{v}\). The vectors \(\vect{v}\) are eigenvectors and the stretch factors \(\lambda\) are eigenvalues. This chapter gives the method that works for a square matrix of any size.
Eigenvalues are among the most useful numbers in applied mathematics. They give the natural frequencies of a vibrating structure, the growth rate of a population, the stability of a control system, the principal stresses in a loaded beam and the most important directions in a data set. The rest of Part IV is built on them.
The invariant line finder from Chapter 9 shows the same idea. Turn the vector \(\vect{v}\) and watch for the directions where \(\M{A}\vect{v}\) lines up with \(\vect{v}\). Each such direction is an eigenvector, and the stretch factor shown is its eigenvalue.
Things to try:

title: 18  Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
text:
18.2 The ideas

Directions that are only stretched
A non-zero vector \(\vect{v}\) is an eigenvector of the square matrix \(\M{A}\), with eigenvalue \(\lambda\), if \[
\M{A}\vect{v} = \lambda\vect{v}.
\] The matrix sends \(\vect{v}\) to a multiple of itself, so it stays on the same line through the origin. The meaning of \(\lambda\) is as in Chapter 9: points along that line are stretched (\(\lambda > 1\)), shrunk (\(0 < \lambda < 1\)), left alone (\(\lambda = 1\)), squashed to the origin (\(\lambda = 0\)) or flipped (\(\lambda < 0\)).
The zero vector is not allowed as an eigenvector (it would satisfy the equation for every \(\lambda\)), but \(\lambda = 0\) is a perfectly good eigenvalue. Any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is also an eigenvector, with the same eigenvalue, so it is really a direction that is being found. Together with \(\zerovec\), all the eigenvectors for one eigenvalue form a subspace (Chapter 14), called its eigenspace.


The characteristic equation
Rewrite \(\M{A}\vect{v} = \lambda\vect{v}\) as \(\M{A}\vect{v} - \lambda\M{I}\vect{v} = \zerovec\), that is, \[
(\M{A} - \lambda\M{I})\vect{v} = \zerovec.
\] This homogeneous system has a non-zero solution exactly when \(\M{A} - \lambda\M{I}\) is singular (Chapter 10), so the eigenvalues are the solutions of the characteristic equation \[
\det(\M{A} - \lambda\M{I}) = 0.
\tag{18.1}\] For an \(n \times n\) matrix, \(\det(\M{A} - \lambda\M{I})\) is a polynomial in \(\lambda\) of degree \(n\), the characteristic polynomial. So an \(n \times n\) matrix has exactly \(n\) eigenvalues, provided you count repeated ones as often as they repeat and allow complex numbers.
For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(\M{A} = \mat{a & b \\ c & d}\), \[
\det\mat{a - \lambda & b \\ c & d - \lambda} = \lambda^2 - (a + d)\lambda + (ad - bc).
\] The coefficient \(a + d\) is the trace of \(\M{A}\), written \(\operatorname{tr}\M{A}\): the sum of its diagonal entries. So \[
\lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr}\M{A})\,\lambda + \det\M{A} = 0.
\tag{18.2}\] This gives a useful check in any size: the eigenvalues add up to the trace, and multiply to give the determinant (a proof is in Section C.11).






WarningWatch out: row reduction changes eigenvalues



Find the eigenvalues from \(\M{A}\) itself. Row operations change them: \(\mat{2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3}\) has eigenvalues 2 and 3, but halving its first row gives \(\mat{1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3}\), with eigenvalues 1 and 3. Row reduce only \(\M{A} - \lambda\M{I}\), once you know \(\lambda\), to find the eigenvectors.




Finding the eigenvectors
For each eigenvalue \(\lambda\), the eigenvectors are the non-zero solutions of \((\M{A} - \lambda\M{I})\vect{v} = \zerovec\): the null space of \(\M{A} - \lambda\M{I}\) (Chapter 16). Row reduce, and read the solutions off in terms of free variables, as in Chapter 12. Because \(\M{A} - \lambda\M{I}\) is singular, there is always at least one free variable. If there isn’t, the eigenvalue is wrong.






NoteExample 1: a \(2 \times 2\) matrix



Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(\M{A} = \mat{4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3}\).
Solution. The trace is 7 and the determinant is \(12 - 2 = 10\), so by Equation 18.2, \[
\lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (\lambda - 5)(\lambda - 2) = 0,
\] giving \(\lambda_1 = 5\) and \(\lambda_2 = 2\). Check: \(5 + 2 = 7\), the trace, and \(5 \times 2 = 10\), the determinant. ✓
For \(\lambda_1 = 5\): \(\M{A} - 5\M{I} = \mat{-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2}\). Both rows say \(x = y\), so \(\vect{v}_1 = (1, 1)\T\).
For \(\lambda_2 = 2\): \(\M{A} - 2\M{I} = \mat{2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1}\). Both rows say \(2x + y = 0\), so \(\vect{v}_2 = (1, -2)\T\).
Check: \(\M{A}(1, -2)\T = (4 - 2, 2 - 6)\T = (2, -4)\T = 2(1, -2)\T\). ✓




Quick facts
Some eigenvalues can be seen without any calculation.

A triangular matrix (including a diagonal one) has its diagonal entries as its eigenvalues, because \(\M{A} - \lambda\M{I}\) is triangular and its determinant is the product of its diagonal entries.
\(\lambda = 0\) is an eigenvalue exactly when \(\M{A}\) is singular, since then \(\M{A}\vect{v} = 0\vect{v}\) has a non-zero solution.
If \(\M{A}\vect{v} = \lambda\vect{v}\), then \(\M{A}^2\vect{v} = \M{A}(\lambda\vect{v}) = \lambda^2\vect{v}\), and in general \(\M{A}^k\) has eigenvalue \(\lambda^k\) with the same eigenvector. If \(\M{A}\) is invertible, \(\M{A}^{-1}\) has eigenvalue \(1/\lambda\).
\(\M{A}\) and \(\M{A}\T\) have the same eigenvalues (but usually different eigenvectors), since a matrix and its transpose have the same determinant.



Repeated eigenvalues
When an eigenvalue is a repeated root of the characteristic polynomial, its eigenspace may or may not have as many dimensions as the repeat count. The identity matrix \(\M{I}\) has \(\lambda = 1\) twice, and every vector is an eigenvector: a whole plane of them. But the shear \(\mat{1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1}\) also has \(\lambda = 1\) twice, and only the \(x\)-axis is an eigenvector direction (Chapter 9, Example 4).
The number of times \(\lambda\) repeats as a root is its algebraic multiplicity; the dimension of its eigenspace is its geometric multiplicity. The geometric multiplicity is always at least 1 and never more than the algebraic multiplicity. A matrix where it is smaller, like the shear, is called defective: it doesn’t have enough independent eigenvectors to make a basis, which matters in Chapter 19.






NoteExample 2: a \(3 \times 3\) matrix with a repeated eigenvalue



Find the eigenvalues and eigenspaces of \(\M{A} = \mat{2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2}\).
Solution. Expanding \(\det(\M{A} - \lambda\M{I})\) directly is possible, but a shortcut is quicker. \(\M{A} - \M{I}\) has every entry equal to 1, so it has rank 1 and is singular: \(\lambda = 1\) is an eigenvalue, and its eigenspace has dimension \(3 - 1 = 2\). So \(\lambda = 1\) appears at least twice. The trace is 6, so the third eigenvalue is \(6 - 1 - 1 = 4\). (Check with the determinant: \(1 \times 1 \times 4 = 4 = \det\M{A}\).)
For \(\lambda = 1\): \((\M{A} - \M{I})\vect{v} = \zerovec\) is the single equation \(x + y + z = 0\). With \(y\) and \(z\) free, a basis is \((-1, 1, 0)\T\) and \((-1, 0, 1)\T\): the eigenspace is a plane.
For \(\lambda = 4\): \(\M{A} - 4\M{I} = \mat{-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -2}\), whose rows each add up to zero, so \(\vect{v} = (1, 1, 1)\T\) works. The eigenspace is the line through it.
The repeated eigenvalue has a two-dimensional eigenspace, so this matrix is not defective. (Notice also that \((1, 1, 1)\) is at right angles to the whole plane \(x + y + z = 0\). That is no accident: \(\M{A}\) is symmetric, Chapter 20.)








NoteExample 3: a defective matrix



Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the shear \(\M{H} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1}\).
Solution. It is triangular, so its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries: \(\lambda = 1\), twice. \(\M{H} - \M{I} = \mat{0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0}\) says \(y = 0\), so the eigenvectors are the multiples of \((1, 0)\T\) only. The algebraic multiplicity is 2 but the geometric multiplicity is 1: \(\M{H}\) is defective.




Complex eigenvalues
The rotation \(\M{R}(\theta) = \mat{\cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta}\) turns every direction, so for \(\theta\) other than \(0°\) or \(180°\) it has no real eigenvectors. Its characteristic equation is \[
\lambda^2 - 2\cos\theta\,\lambda + 1 = 0,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\lambda = \cos\theta \pm i\sin\theta = e^{\pm i\theta},
\] a pair of complex numbers (see the Refresher for complex numbers). Their angle is the angle of rotation, and their size, \(\lvert\lambda\rvert = 1\), says that lengths don’t change.
In general, a real matrix with complex eigenvalues has them in conjugate pairs, \(\alpha \pm i\beta\), because the characteristic polynomial has real coefficients. For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, such a pair means the matrix acts like a rotation through the angle of \(\lambda\) combined with a stretch by \(\lvert\lambda\rvert = \sqrt{\alpha^2 + \beta^2}\), as seen in suitable coordinates. The eigenvectors are complex too. You won’t need them in this book except in passing, but the eigenvalues themselves are vital: in Chapter 23 they become oscillation frequencies.






NoteExample 4: complex eigenvalues



Find the eigenvalues of \(\M{A} = \mat{1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1}\) and interpret them.
Solution. The trace is 2 and the determinant is 2, so \(\lambda^2 - 2\lambda + 2 = 0\), and \[
\lambda = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 8}}{2} = 1 \pm i.
\] Each has size \(\lvert\lambda\rvert = \sqrt{2}\) and angle \(45°\). Indeed \(\M{A} = \sqrt{2}\,\M{R}(45°)\): it rotates by \(45°\) and stretches by \(\sqrt{2}\). No real direction is left on its own line, so there are no real eigenvectors.

title: 18  Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
text:
18.3 In code

Run this chapter’s code yourself: open the notebook in Colab, or download the Jupyter notebook or the MATLAB script.

np.linalg.eig and MATLAB’s eig return the eigenvalues, and the eigenvectors as the columns of a matrix in the same order, each scaled to length 1. They don’t use the characteristic polynomial, which would be slow and inaccurate for large matrices. Instead they use the QR algorithm of Chapter 29. The order of the eigenvalues, and the sign of each eigenvector, may differ from a hand calculation.

PythonMATLAB



import numpy as np

A = np.array([[4, 1], [2, 3]])
values, vectors = np.linalg.eig(A)
values, vectors = values.real, vectors.real   # recent NumPy returns complex numbers
print(values)
print(vectors)                   # columns: (1, 1) and (1, -2), scaled to length 1

print(np.allclose(A @ vectors, vectors * values))   # A v = lambda v for each column

print(np.linalg.eigvals(np.array([[1, -1], [1, 1]])))   # complex: 1 + i and 1 - i

The columns of V are \((1, 1)\T\) and \((1, -2)\T\) scaled to length 1, with the second multiplied by \(-1\). Either sign describes the same direction.

title: 18  Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
text:
18.4 Check your understanding






TipA \(3 \times 3\) matrix has eigenvalues 2, 2 and \(-1\). What are its trace and determinant?





Trace \(2 + 2 - 1 = 3\); determinant \(2 \times 2 \times (-1) = -4\).









TipIf 0 is an eigenvalue of \(\M{A}\), what can you say about \(\M{A}\)?





It is singular: it has no inverse, and \(\det\M{A} = 0\).









TipCan a real \(3 \times 3\) matrix have no real eigenvalues?





No. Complex eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs, so with three eigenvalues at least one must be real. (Geometrically: every rotation of space has an axis.)
crumbs: Part IV: Eigenvalues and matrix calculus

title: 18  Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
text:
18.5 Key ideas

An eigenvector of \(\M{A}\) is a non-zero vector whose direction \(\M{A}\) doesn’t change: \(\M{A}\vect{v} = \lambda\vect{v}\), where \(\lambda\) is its eigenvalue.
The eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic equation \(\det(\M{A} - \lambda\M{I}) = 0\). The eigenvectors for each \(\lambda\) form the null space of \(\M{A} - \lambda\M{I}\).
The eigenvalues add up to the trace and multiply to the determinant, which makes a quick check.
A repeated eigenvalue may have fewer independent eigenvectors than its multiplicity; such a matrix is called defective.
Complex eigenvalues of a real matrix come in conjugate pairs, and describe a rotation combined with a stretch.

title: 18  Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
text:
18.7 In practice

Vibration: every structure, from a guitar string to a bridge or an aircraft wing, has natural frequencies at which it vibrates freely, found from the eigenvalues of its stiffness and mass matrices. Engineers keep them away from the frequencies of wind, traffic, engines or footsteps, to avoid resonance. The Millennium Bridge in London swayed on its opening day in 2000 because a sideways natural frequency matched the rhythm of people walking.
Stability: whether a control system, an electrical network or an ecosystem returns to equilibrium after a disturbance depends on the eigenvalues of its linearised equations (Chapter 23).
Principal stresses: the eigenvalues of the stress matrix at a point of a loaded material are the largest and smallest normal stresses there, and the eigenvectors are their directions (Chapter 20).
Rankings: Google’s original PageRank was the eigenvector, with eigenvalue 1, of a huge matrix describing the links between web pages (Chapter 35).
Quantum mechanics: the possible energies of an atom or molecule are the eigenvalues of a matrix (or operator) called the Hamiltonian (Chapter 38).
crumbs: Part IV: Eigenvalues and matrix calculus

title: 18  Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
text:
18.8 Going further

Never compute eigenvalues of large matrices from the characteristic polynomial: the roots of a polynomial can be extremely sensitive to tiny changes in its coefficients. Chapter 29 describes the methods that software uses instead.
Gershgorin’s theorem gives a quick estimate: every eigenvalue lies within a distance \(\sum_{j \neq i}\lvert a_{ij}\rvert\) of some diagonal entry \(a_{ii}\).
Defective matrices can’t be diagonalised, but they have a Jordan form, which is almost diagonal (Chapter 19).
Proofs that the eigenvalues add to the trace and multiply to the determinant: Section C.11.
crumbs: Part IV: Eigenvalues and matrix calculus

title: 19  Diagonalisation and matrix powers
text:
19.1 Build intuition
Core
Builds on Chapter 15, Chapter 18.
Many processes repeat the same linear step over and over: next year’s population from this year’s, tomorrow’s distribution of hire bikes from today’s, the next pair of Fibonacci numbers from the last pair. After \(k\) steps the state is \(\M{A}^k\vect{x}_0\). Multiplying out \(\M{A}^k\) for large \(k\) is slow and gives no insight. But in the basis of its eigenvectors, \(\M{A}\) is just a diagonal matrix (Chapter 15, Example 4), and powers of a diagonal matrix are easy. This chapter turns that observation into a method, and uses it to predict what happens in the long run.
Start from a vector and multiply by the same matrix again and again. The dashed lines are the eigenvector directions, labelled with their eigenvalues.
Things to try:

title: 19  Diagonalisation and matrix powers
text:
Open the matrix powers app in its own tab



In Grows along a line, press Play. Which eigenvector line does the vector end up along, and how fast does it grow at each step? Drag the starting point and try again. Can you find a starting point where it doesn’t end up along that line?
In Bike share, what does the vector settle down to?

In Spiral, the eigenvalues are complex. What happens instead?
