title: 19  Diagonalisation and matrix powers
text:
19.2 The ideas

Diagonalisation
Suppose the \(n \times n\) matrix \(\M{A}\) has \(n\) independent eigenvectors \(\vect{v}_1, \dots, \vect{v}_n\), with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n\). Put the eigenvectors in the columns of \(\M{P}\), and the eigenvalues, in the same order, on the diagonal of \(\M{D}\). The equations \(\M{A}\vect{v}_i = \lambda_i\vect{v}_i\), side by side, say \[
\M{A}\M{P} = \M{P}\M{D}.
\] \(\M{P}\) is invertible because its columns are independent, so \[
\M{A} = \M{P}\M{D}\M{P}^{-1}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\M{D} = \M{P}^{-1}\M{A}\M{P}.
\tag{19.1}\] This is diagonalisation. By Chapter 15, it says exactly what you would hope: in the basis of eigenvectors, \(\M{A}\) is the diagonal matrix \(\M{D}\), which just stretches each coordinate by its own eigenvalue.
When is it possible? Exactly when \(\M{A}\) has \(n\) independent eigenvectors.

If the \(n\) eigenvalues are all different, it always is: eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are independent (a proof is in Section C.12).
If some eigenvalue is repeated, it is possible exactly when each eigenspace has as many dimensions as its eigenvalue repeats (Chapter 18, Example 2 is fine). A defective matrix, such as the shear, can’t be diagonalised.
Complex eigenvalues are allowed, but then \(\M{P}\) and \(\M{D}\) contain complex numbers.







NoteExample 1: a matrix that can’t be diagonalised



Find \(\M{H}^k\) for the shear \(\M{H} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1}\).
Solution. \(\M{H}\) is defective (Chapter 18, Example 3), so Equation 19.2 can’t be used. But multiplying out a few powers shows the pattern: \(\M{H}^2 = \mat{1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1}\), \(\M{H}^3 = \mat{1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1}\), and in general \[
\M{H}^k = \mat{1 & k \\ 0 & 1}.
\] Both eigenvalues are 1, yet the entries grow, steadily rather than exponentially. The eigenvalues alone don’t tell the whole story for a defective matrix.




Powers
The middle factors cancel when a diagonalised matrix is multiplied by itself: \[
\M{A}^2 = \M{P}\M{D}\M{P}^{-1}\M{P}\M{D}\M{P}^{-1} = \M{P}\M{D}^2\M{P}^{-1},
\] and in general \[
\M{A}^k = \M{P}\M{D}^k\M{P}^{-1},
\tag{19.2}\] where \(\M{D}^k\) is diagonal with entries \(\lambda_1^k, \dots, \lambda_n^k\). This gives a formula for \(\M{A}^k\) with \(k\) as a variable, so it says how the entries grow, not just what they are for one \(k\).






NoteExample 2: a formula for \(\M{A}^k\)



Diagonalise \(\M{A} = \mat{4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3}\), and find a formula for \(\M{A}^k\).
Solution. From Chapter 18, Example 1, the eigenvalues are 5 and 2, with eigenvectors \((1, 1)\T\) and \((1, -2)\T\). So \[
\M{P} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2},
\] \[
\M{D} = \mat{5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2},
\] \[
\M{P}^{-1} = \frac{1}{3}\mat{2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1}.
\] Then \(\M{A}^k = \M{P}\M{D}^k\M{P}^{-1}\), which multiplies out to \[
\M{A}^k = \frac{1}{3}\mat{2 \cdot 5^k + 2^k & 5^k - 2^k \\ 2 \cdot 5^k - 2 \cdot 2^k & 5^k + 2 \cdot 2^k}.
\] Check with \(k = 1\): \(\tfrac{1}{3}\mat{12 & 3 \\ 6 & 9} = \M{A}\). ✓ For large \(k\), the \(5^k\) terms dominate, so every entry grows by a factor of about 5 per step.








NoteExample 3: Fibonacci numbers



The Fibonacci numbers \(0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, \dots\) obey \(F_{k+1} = F_k + F_{k-1}\). Find a formula for \(F_k\).
Solution. Put two neighbouring numbers in a vector. Then \[
\mat{F_{k+1} \\ F_k} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0}\mat{F_k \\ F_{k-1}},
\] a process with \(\M{A} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0}\). Its trace is 1 and determinant \(-1\), so \(\lambda^2 - \lambda - 1 = 0\), and \[
\lambda_1 = \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2} \approx 1.618,
\qquad
\lambda_2 = \frac{1 - \sqrt{5}}{2} \approx -0.618.
\] (\(\lambda_1\) is the golden ratio, \(\varphi\).) For each eigenvalue, \(\M{A} - \lambda\M{I}\) has first row \((1 - \lambda, 1)\), so the eigenvectors are \(\vect{v}_i = (\lambda_i, 1)\T\). The starting vector \((F_1, F_0)\T = (1, 0)\T\) is \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(\vect{v}_1 - \vect{v}_2)\), as you can check, so by Equation 19.3, reading off the second entry, \[
F_k = \frac{\lambda_1^k - \lambda_2^k}{\sqrt{5}}.
\] Since \(\lvert\lambda_2\rvert < 1\), the second term shrinks quickly, and \(F_k\) is just \(\lambda_1^k/\sqrt{5}\) rounded to the nearest whole number. For example, \(\varphi^{30}/\sqrt{5} \approx 832\,040.0000002\), and indeed \(F_{30} = 832\,040\). The ratio of neighbouring Fibonacci numbers tends to \(\varphi\), as the Fibonacci preset in the app shows.




Repeated steps: \(\vect{x}_{k+1} = \M{A}\vect{x}_k\)
For a process that applies \(\M{A}\) at each step, write the starting vector in the eigenvector basis, \(\vect{x}_0 = c_1\vect{v}_1 + \dots + c_n\vect{v}_n\) (the coefficients are \(\vect{c} = \M{P}^{-1}\vect{x}_0\), as in Chapter 15). Each step multiplies each eigenvector by its eigenvalue, so \[
\vect{x}_k = \M{A}^k\vect{x}_0 = c_1\lambda_1^k\vect{v}_1 + c_2\lambda_2^k\vect{v}_2 + \dots + c_n\lambda_n^k\vect{v}_n.
\tag{19.3}\] Each eigenvector is a mode of the process, evolving on its own by powers of its eigenvalue.
Now order the eigenvalues so that \(\lvert\lambda_1\rvert\) is the largest, the dominant eigenvalue, strictly larger than the others. As \(k\) grows, \(\lvert\lambda_1\rvert^k\) outgrows every other \(\lvert\lambda_i\rvert^k\), so (as long as \(c_1 \neq 0\)) \[
\vect{x}_k \approx c_1\lambda_1^k\,\vect{v}_1 \quad\text{for large } k.
\] Two things follow. The direction of \(\vect{x}_k\) settles along the dominant eigenvector, whatever the start. And the size changes by a factor of about \(\lvert\lambda_1\rvert\) per step: it grows without limit if \(\lvert\lambda_1\rvert > 1\), dies away if every \(\lvert\lambda_i\rvert < 1\), and settles to a steady state if \(\lambda_1 = 1\) and the others are smaller. The speed of settling is set by the ratio \(\lvert\lambda_2\rvert / \lvert\lambda_1\rvert\): the smaller it is, the faster the other modes fade.






NoteExample 4: where do the bikes end up?



A bike-hire scheme has two docking stations, A and B. Each day, 90% of the bikes at A end the day at A and 10% at B; of those at B, 20% end at A and 80% stay at B (Figure 19.1). If all the bikes start at A, what happens in the long run?






Figure 19.1: The daily movement of bikes in Example 4. The two numbers leaving each station add up to 1.



Solution. Let \(\vect{x}_k\) hold the fractions of bikes at A and at B after \(k\) days. Then \(\vect{x}_{k+1} = \M{M}\vect{x}_k\) with \[
\M{M} = \mat{0.9 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.8}.
\] Each column adds up to 1, because every bike ends up somewhere. The trace is 1.7 and the determinant \(0.72 - 0.02 = 0.7\), so \(\lambda^2 - 1.7\lambda + 0.7 = 0\), giving \(\lambda_1 = 1\) and \(\lambda_2 = 0.7\).
For \(\lambda_1 = 1\): \(\M{M} - \M{I} = \mat{-0.1 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & -0.2}\) gives \(x = 2y\), so \(\vect{v}_1 = (2, 1)\T\). For \(\lambda_2 = 0.7\): \(\M{M} - 0.7\M{I} = \mat{0.2 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.1}\) gives \(\vect{v}_2 = (1, -1)\T\).
Starting from \(\vect{x}_0 = (1, 0)\T = \tfrac{1}{3}(2, 1)\T + \tfrac{1}{3}(1, -1)\T\), \[
\vect{x}_k = \frac{1}{3}\mat{2 \\ 1} + \frac{1}{3}(0.7)^k\mat{1 \\ -1}.
\] The second term dies away, so in the long run \(\tfrac{2}{3}\) of the bikes are at A and \(\tfrac{1}{3}\) at B, whatever the starting arrangement. After a week (\(k = 7\), \(0.7^7 \approx 0.08\)) the arrangement is already within 3 percentage points of this. This is the Bike share preset in the app.

Run this chapter’s code yourself: open the notebook in Colab, or download the Jupyter notebook or the MATLAB script.

The diagonalisation comes straight from eig. For powers with a specific \(k\), matrix_power (or A^k in MATLAB) multiplies efficiently by repeated squaring; the formula Equation 19.2 is most useful for understanding.

PythonMATLAB



import numpy as np

A = np.array([[4, 1], [2, 3]])
lam, P = np.linalg.eig(A)
lam, P = lam.real, P.real                       # recent NumPy returns complex numbers
D = np.diag(lam)
print(np.allclose(A, P @ D @ np.linalg.inv(P)))  # A = P D P^(-1)

k = 5
print(np.linalg.matrix_power(A, k))
print(np.round(P @ np.diag(lam**k) @ np.linalg.inv(P)))   # the same, from the eigenvalues

F = np.array([[1, 1], [1, 0]])
print(np.linalg.matrix_power(F, 30)[0, 1])      # the 30th Fibonacci number

text:
19.4 Check your understanding






TipA \(3 \times 3\) matrix has eigenvalues 1, 2 and 3. Can it be diagonalised?





Yes: three different eigenvalues give three independent eigenvectors.









TipIf \(\M{A} = \M{P}\M{D}\M{P}^{-1}\), what is \(\M{A}^{-1}\)?





\(\M{P}\M{D}^{-1}\M{P}^{-1}\), where \(\M{D}^{-1}\) has the reciprocals \(1/\lambda_i\) on its diagonal (if none of them is 0).









TipA process \(\vect{x}_{k+1} = \M{A}\vect{x}_k\) has eigenvalues 0.9 and 0.5. What happens to \(\vect{x}_k\)?





It shrinks to \(\zerovec\), eventually along the eigenvector for 0.9, shrinking by about 10% per step.

title: 19  Diagonalisation and matrix powers
text:
19.5 Key ideas

If \(\M{A}\) has \(n\) independent eigenvectors, then \(\M{A} = \M{P}\M{D}\M{P}^{-1}\), with the eigenvectors in the columns of \(\M{P}\) and the eigenvalues on the diagonal of \(\M{D}\).
Distinct eigenvalues guarantee this; a defective matrix can’t be diagonalised.
Powers become easy: \(\M{A}^k = \M{P}\M{D}^k\M{P}^{-1}\), and \(\M{D}^k\) just raises each eigenvalue to the power \(k\).
For a process \(\vect{x}_{k+1} = \M{A}\vect{x}_k\), the eigenvalue of largest size dominates in the long run: the process grows if it is bigger than 1 in size, dies away if it is smaller, and lines up with its eigenvector.

\] Find the dominant eigenvalue and its eigenvector. What is the long-run growth rate of the population, and what fraction of the animals is in each age group in the long run? Check by applying \(\M{L}\) 50 times to a starting population.

title: 19  Diagonalisation and matrix powers
text:
19.7 In practice

Population models: the dominant eigenvalue of a Leslie matrix is the long-run growth rate of a population, and its eigenvector the stable mix of ages. Conservation biologists use the model to see which life stage matters most for a threatened species (Chapter 36).
Markov chains: processes that move between states with fixed probabilities, like the bikes in Example 4, settle down to the eigenvector with eigenvalue 1. The same idea models customers switching brands, weather patterns, and the random web surfer of PageRank (Chapter 35).
Recurrences and signal processing: any recurrence like the Fibonacci one, such as a digital filter that computes each output from the last few, can be written as matrix powers. Its eigenvalues decide whether the filter is stable.
Decoupling: in the eigenvector basis, a set of interacting equations becomes independent ones, one per mode. This is how engineers analyse a vibrating structure one mode at a time (Chapter 23).

title: 19  Diagonalisation and matrix powers
text:
19.8 Going further

Every square matrix, even a defective one, can be written as \(\M{P}\M{J}\M{P}^{-1}\), where the Jordan form \(\M{J}\) is diagonal apart from some 1s just above the diagonal. Example 1’s shear is already in Jordan form. Jordan forms are fragile in floating-point arithmetic, so they are a tool for theory rather than computation.
Repeatedly multiplying by \(\M{A}\) and rescaling is itself a way to find the dominant eigenvector: the power method, which underlies PageRank (Chapter 29).
Diagonalisation lets you apply other functions to matrices, such as square roots and exponentials, by applying them to the eigenvalues: \(f(\M{A}) = \M{P}f(\M{D})\M{P}^{-1}\). The matrix exponential is the key to Chapter 23.
Proof that eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are independent: Section C.12.

title: 20  Symmetric and positive definite matrices
text:
20.1 Build intuition
Further
Builds on Chapter 17, Chapter 19.
Symmetric matrices (\(\M{A}\T = \M{A}\)) are the most common matrices in applications. They describe stiffness, energy, covariance, stress, distances and the normal equations \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\). They also have the best possible eigenvalues and eigenvectors: always real, always diagonalisable, and with eigenvectors at right angles to each other. That makes them both easier to understand and easier to compute with. This chapter explains why, and what the eigenvalues mean when the matrix describes a shape, a set of data or the stress in a material.
For a symmetric matrix \(\M{A}\), the quadratic form \(q(\vect{x}) = \vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x}\) gives a number at each point of the plane. The app shades it, with green where it is positive and orange where it is negative, and draws the curves \(q = 1\) and \(q = -1\).

title: 20  Symmetric and positive definite matrices
text:
20.2 The ideas

The spectral theorem






ImportantThe spectral theorem



If \(\M{A}\) is a real symmetric matrix, then

all its eigenvalues are real;
eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are perpendicular;
it has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, so it can be diagonalised as \[
\M{A} = \M{Q}\M{\Lambda}\M{Q}\T,
\] where the columns of the orthogonal matrix \(\M{Q}\) are the unit eigenvectors, and \(\M{\Lambda}\) (capital lambda) is diagonal with the eigenvalues.



Proofs of parts 1 and 2 are in Section C.13; part 3 follows by building up the basis one eigenvector at a time. Compare Chapter 19: for a symmetric matrix, \(\M{P}^{-1}\) is just \(\M{Q}\T\) (Chapter 7), and defective matrices never occur.
Multiplying out \(\M{Q}\M{\Lambda}\M{Q}\T\) column by row gives another useful form, \[
\M{A} = \lambda_1\vect{q}_1\vect{q}_1\T + \lambda_2\vect{q}_2\vect{q}_2\T + \dots + \lambda_n\vect{q}_n\vect{q}_n\T.
\] Each \(\vect{q}_i\vect{q}_i\T\) is the matrix that projects onto the line through \(\vect{q}_i\) (Chapter 17). So a symmetric matrix splits any vector into pieces along perpendicular axes, and scales each piece by its own eigenvalue.






NoteExample 1: orthogonal diagonalisation



Write \(\M{A} = \mat{2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2}\) as \(\M{Q}\M{\Lambda}\M{Q}\T\).
Solution. The trace is 4 and the determinant 3, so the eigenvalues are 3 and 1. For \(\lambda = 3\), \(\M{A} - 3\M{I} = \mat{-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1}\) gives \((1, 1)\T\); for \(\lambda = 1\), \(\M{A} - \M{I} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1}\) gives \((1, -1)\T\). They are perpendicular, as promised. Scaling them to length 1, \[
\M{Q} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1},
\qquad
\M{\Lambda} = \mat{3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1},
\] and \(\M{A} = \M{Q}\M{\Lambda}\M{Q}\T\). No inverse is needed: \(\M{Q}^{-1} = \M{Q}\T\).




Quadratic forms
A quadratic form is an expression like \[
q(x, y) = ax^2 + 2bxy + cy^2 = \mat{x & y}\mat{a & b \\ b & c}\mat{x \\ y} = \vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x},
\] with every term of degree 2. Each one has a symmetric matrix, with the squared coefficients on the diagonal and half of each cross-term coefficient off it. Quadratic forms appear as energies (the energy stored in a spring system is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\vect{x}\T\M{K}\vect{x}\)), as squared errors (Chapter 17), and as the second-order terms of any smooth function near a point (Chapter 22).
The cross term makes \(q\) hard to picture. But in the coordinates of the eigenvectors, \(\vect{y} = \M{Q}\T\vect{x}\), it disappears: \[
q = \vect{x}\T\M{Q}\M{\Lambda}\M{Q}\T\vect{x} = \vect{y}\T\M{\Lambda}\vect{y} = \lambda_1y_1^2 + \lambda_2y_2^2 + \dots + \lambda_ny_n^2.
\] So the eigenvectors are the principal axes of the form. In two dimensions, if both eigenvalues are positive, the curve \(q = 1\) is an ellipse with semi-axes \(1/\sqrt{\lambda_1}\) and \(1/\sqrt{\lambda_2}\) along the eigenvectors: the larger eigenvalue gives the shorter axis. If the eigenvalues have opposite signs, it is a hyperbola. On the unit circle (or sphere), \(q\) is largest along the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue, where it equals that eigenvalue, and smallest along the eigenvector of the smallest.






NoteExample 2: an ellipse and a saddle



Describe the curves (a) \(5x^2 + 4xy + 2y^2 = 6\) and (b) \(x^2 + 4xy + y^2 = 3\).
Solution. (a) The matrix is \(\mat{5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2}\), with trace 7 and determinant 6, so the eigenvalues are 6 and 1, with eigenvectors \((2, 1)\T\) and \((1, -2)\T\). In eigenvector coordinates the curve is \(6y_1^2 + y_2^2 = 6\), that is, \(y_1^2 + y_2^2/6 = 1\): an ellipse with semi-axis 1 along \((2, 1)\T\) and semi-axis \(\sqrt{6} \approx 2.45\) along \((1, -2)\T\). The form is positive definite. This is Ellipse in the app.

The matrix is \(\mat{1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1}\), with eigenvalues 3 and \(-1\) and eigenvectors \((1, 1)\T\) and \((1, -1)\T\). In eigenvector coordinates the curve is \(3y_1^2 - y_2^2 = 3\): a hyperbola crossing the \((1, 1)\) axis at distance 1 from the origin, never crossing the \((1, -1)\) axis. The form is indefinite, a saddle. This is Saddle in the app. Figure 20.1 shows both curves.







Figure 20.1: The curves of Example 2, with their eigenvector directions (dashed). (a) An ellipse, with semi-axes along the eigenvectors. (b) A hyperbola, which crosses the \((1, 1)\) axis, where the form is positive, and never crosses the \((1, -1)\) axis, where it is negative.







Positive definite matrices
A symmetric matrix \(\M{A}\) is positive definite if \(\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x} > 0\) for every \(\vect{x} \neq \zerovec\): its quadratic form is a bowl with its lowest point at the origin. From \(q = \sum \lambda_iy_i^2\), this happens exactly when every eigenvalue is positive. Similarly:








Eigenvalues
Name
Shape of \(q\)

positive definite
bowl, minimum at \(\zerovec\)


all \(\ge 0\), some \(= 0\)
positive semidefinite
valley, flat along some directions


some \(> 0\), some \(< 0\)
indefinite
saddle


all \(< 0\)
negative definite
upturned bowl



Finding eigenvalues is expensive, so in practice positive definiteness is usually tested another way. For a symmetric matrix these are all equivalent:

every eigenvalue is positive;
every pivot of Gaussian elimination without row swaps is positive;
every leading principal minor (the determinant of the top-left \(1 \times 1\), \(2 \times 2\), … block) is positive;
\(\M{A} = \M{L}\M{L}\T\) for a lower triangular \(\M{L}\) with positive diagonal entries: the Cholesky factorisation.

The Cholesky factorisation is the symmetric version of LU (Chapter 13), with half the work and storage. Computers test for positive definiteness by attempting it: it succeeds exactly when the matrix is positive definite. For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix the minor test is quickest: \(\mat{a & b \\ b & c}\) is positive definite exactly when \(a > 0\) and \(ac - b^2 > 0\).
One family is always at least semidefinite: for any matrix \(\M{A}\), \(\vect{x}\T\M{A}\T\M{A}\vect{x} = \lVert\M{A}\vect{x}\rVert^2 \ge 0\). So \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\) is positive semidefinite, and positive definite when the columns of \(\M{A}\) are independent. That is why the normal equations of Chapter 17 always have a unique solution in that case.






NoteExample 3: testing positive definiteness



Is \(\M{A} = \mat{4 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 6}\) positive definite? Find its Cholesky factor.
Solution. Eliminate without swaps: \(R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - \tfrac{1}{2}R_1\) and \(R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - \tfrac{1}{2}R_1\) give rows \((0, 4, 2)\) and \((0, 2, 5)\), then \(R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - \tfrac{1}{2}R_2\) gives \((0, 0, 4)\). The pivots are 4, 4 and 4, all positive, so \(\M{A}\) is positive definite.
For the Cholesky factor, look for \(\M{L} = \mat{\ell_{11} & 0 & 0 \\ \ell_{21} & \ell_{22} & 0 \\ \ell_{31} & \ell_{32} & \ell_{33}}\) with \(\M{L}\M{L}\T = \M{A}\), matching entries in order. \(\ell_{11}^2 = 4\) gives \(\ell_{11} = 2\); then \(2\ell_{21} = 2\) and \(2\ell_{31} = 2\) give \(\ell_{21} = \ell_{31} = 1\). Next \(1 + \ell_{22}^2 = 5\) gives \(\ell_{22} = 2\), and \(1 + 2\ell_{32} = 3\) gives \(\ell_{32} = 1\). Finally \(1 + 1 + \ell_{33}^2 = 6\) gives \(\ell_{33} = 2\). So \[
\M{L} = \mat{2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 2}.
\] (The diagonal entries are the square roots of the pivots.) Had any square root been of a negative number, the matrix would not have been positive definite.




Covariance matrices
Suppose \(n\) items are each measured on \(p\) variables, such as height, weight and age, and the measurements are stored in an \(n \times p\) data matrix \(\M{X}\), one row per item. Subtract each column’s mean, so that every column of \(\M{X}\) averages zero. The covariance matrix is \[
\M{C} = \frac{1}{n - 1}\M{X}\T\M{X}.
\] Its diagonal entries are the variances of the variables (how spread out each one is), and its off-diagonal entries are the covariances (how strongly pairs of variables rise and fall together). It is symmetric, and positive semidefinite because it has the form \(\M{X}\T\M{X}\).
Its quadratic form has a meaning too. Projecting every data point onto a unit vector \(\vect{u}\) gives one number per item, and the variance of those numbers is \(\vect{u}\T\M{C}\vect{u}\). So the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue is the direction in which the data are most spread out, and its eigenvalue is that spread. This is the starting point of principal component analysis (Chapter 21).


Stress in materials
At each point inside a loaded material, the forces between neighbouring pieces are described by a symmetric stress matrix (or stress tensor), \(3 \times 3\) in a solid and \(2 \times 2\) in a thin plate. Its diagonal entries are normal stresses, which pull (\(+\)) or push (\(-\)) straight across a surface, and its off-diagonal entries are shear stresses, which slide one side of a surface past the other.
Because the stress matrix is symmetric, there are always perpendicular directions in which there is no shear at all, only pure pulling or pushing. These are its eigenvectors, the principal directions, and the eigenvalues are the principal stresses. The largest principal stress is what a designer compares with a material’s strength, since brittle materials such as concrete and cast iron crack at right angles to it.






NoteExample 4: principal stresses



At a point on the surface of a loaded steel bracket, the stresses in megapascals (MPa) are a normal stress of 50 in the \(x\)-direction, \(-30\) in the \(y\)-direction (a push), and a shear stress of 30: \[
\M{\sigma} = \mat{50 & 30 \\ 30 & -30}.
\] Find the principal stresses and the direction of the largest.
Solution. The trace is 20 and the determinant \(-1500 - 900 = -2400\), so \(\lambda^2 - 20\lambda - 2400 = 0\), giving \(\lambda = 10 \pm \sqrt{100 + 2400} = 10 \pm 50\). The principal stresses are 60 MPa (tension) and \(-40\) MPa (compression). Both are larger in size than any entry of \(\M{\sigma}\): the shear has made the worst case worse than either the \(x\) or the \(y\) stress alone.
For \(\lambda = 60\), \(\M{\sigma} - 60\M{I} = \mat{-10 & 30 \\ 30 & -90}\) gives \(x = 3y\), so the direction is \((3, 1)\T\), at an angle of \(\tan^{-1}\tfrac{1}{3} \approx 18.4°\) to the \(x\)-axis. The compression acts at right angles to this (Figure 20.2).






Figure 20.2: Example 4. Left: a small square of material with a pull of 50 MPa across its \(x\) faces, a push of 30 MPa across its \(y\) faces, and a shear of 30 MPa along all four. Right: the same point, turned by \(18.4°\) to the principal directions, where there is no shear: a pull of 60 MPa and a push of 40 MPa.

20  Symmetric and positive definite matrices

title: 20  Symmetric and positive definite matrices
text:
20.3 In code

Run this chapter’s code yourself: open the notebook in Colab, or download the Jupyter notebook or the MATLAB script.

For symmetric matrices, use np.linalg.eigh rather than eig. It is faster, guarantees real eigenvalues (in increasing order) and orthonormal eigenvectors, and is not upset by tiny rounding errors that make a matrix very slightly unsymmetric. MATLAB’s eig detects symmetric matrices itself. Cholesky factorisation fails, with an error, exactly when a matrix is not positive definite, which makes it the standard test. Note that MATLAB’s chol returns the upper triangular factor \(\M{R} = \M{L}\T\).

PythonMATLAB



import numpy as np

A = np.array([[5, 2], [2, 2]])

20.4 Check your understanding






TipCan a symmetric matrix have eigenvalues \(2 + i\) and \(2 - i\)?





No: the eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix are always real.









TipWhat is the symmetric matrix of \(3x^2 - 8xy + y^2\)?





\(\mat{3 & -4 \\ -4 & 1}\): the cross-term coefficient \(-8\) is split equally between the two off-diagonal entries.









TipA symmetric matrix has a negative entry on its diagonal. Can it be positive definite?





No. If \(a_{ii} < 0\), then \(\ue{i}\T\M{A}\ue{i} = a_{ii} < 0\).

title: 20  Symmetric and positive definite matrices
text:
20.5 Key ideas

Spectral theorem: a symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and perpendicular eigenvectors, so \(\M{A} = \M{Q}\M{\Lambda}\M{Q}\T\) with \(\M{Q}\) orthogonal.
The eigenvectors are the principal axes of the quadratic form \(\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x}\), and the eigenvalues say how it curves along each axis.
A symmetric matrix is positive definite when \(\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x} > 0\) for every \(\vect{x} \neq \zerovec\). Equivalently, all its eigenvalues are positive, all its pivots are positive, or it has a Cholesky factorisation \(\M{A} = \M{L}\M{L}\T\).
For a covariance matrix, the eigenvectors are the directions of greatest spread in the data. For a stress matrix, they are the principal stress directions.

title: 20  Symmetric and positive definite matrices
text:
20.7 In practice

Structural engineering: stiffness matrices are symmetric and positive definite for any structure that is properly supported, so finite element programs solve their equations with the Cholesky factorisation. A failed factorisation is often the first sign that a model is missing a support and can move freely.
Material strength: principal stresses, found as eigenvalues, are the inputs to the failure criteria that engineers use to check whether a part will yield or crack.
Statistics and data science: covariance and correlation matrices are symmetric and positive semidefinite. Their eigenvectors give the directions of greatest variation, the basis of principal component analysis (Chapter 21).
Optimisation: a smooth function has a minimum at a stationary point where its matrix of second derivatives is positive definite (Chapter 22).
Physics: the inertia matrix of a rigid body is symmetric, and its eigenvectors are the principal axes about which the body spins steadily, the reason a rugby ball or a mobile phone spins smoothly about some axes and wobbles about another.

title: 20  Symmetric and positive definite matrices
text:
20.8 Going further

The Rayleigh quotient \(R(\vect{x}) = \dfrac{\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x}}{\vect{x}\T\vect{x}}\) of a symmetric matrix lies between its smallest and largest eigenvalues, reaching them at the corresponding eigenvectors. Many algorithms find eigenvalues by optimising it.
Generalised eigenproblems \(\M{K}\vect{v} = \lambda\M{M}\vect{v}\), with a stiffness matrix \(\M{K}\) and a mass matrix \(\M{M}\), give the natural frequencies of vibrating structures. When \(\M{M}\) is positive definite, its Cholesky factor turns them into ordinary symmetric eigenproblems.
Every square matrix is the sum of a symmetric and an antisymmetric matrix, \(\M{A} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\M{A} + \M{A}\T) + \tfrac{1}{2}(\M{A} - \M{A}\T)\), and only the symmetric part affects \(\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x}\).
Proofs that the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix are real and its eigenvectors perpendicular: Section C.13.

title: 21  The singular value decomposition and PCA
text:
21.1 Build intuition
Further
Builds on Chapter 17, Chapter 20.
Eigenvalues only make sense for square matrices, and even then they can be complex, or too few. The singular value decomposition (SVD) works for every matrix, of any shape, and always gives real, non-negative numbers and perpendicular directions. It says that every matrix, however complicated, does three simple things in turn: a rotation, a stretch along perpendicular axes, and another rotation. It is probably the most useful factorisation in applied linear algebra: it measures how close a matrix is to singular, finds the best low-rank approximation to a data set or an image, and is the engine of principal component analysis.
The app shows what a \(2 \times 2\) matrix does to the unit circle, one step at a time: the circle is turned, stretched into an ellipse, and turned again. The two stretch factors, shown as \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\), are the half-lengths of the ellipse’s longest and shortest axes; this chapter calls them the singular values. (The app’s second mode, Compressing a picture, comes back later in the chapter, once the idea behind it has been explained.)

title: 21  The singular value decomposition and PCA
text:
21.2 The ideas

Rotate, stretch, rotate






ImportantThe singular value decomposition



Every \(m \times n\) matrix \(\M{A}\) can be written as \[
\M{A} = \M{U}\M{\Sigma}\M{V}\T,
\] where \(\M{U}\) (\(m \times m\)) and \(\M{V}\) (\(n \times n\)) are orthogonal, and \(\M{\Sigma}\) (\(m \times n\)) is zero except for the singular values \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge 0\) down its main diagonal.


Read from right to left, as always (Chapter 5):

\(\M{V}\T\) turns space (a rotation, perhaps with a reflection), so that the columns \(\vect{v}_1, \vect{v}_2, \dots\) of \(\M{V}\) line up with the axes;
\(\M{\Sigma}\) stretches along the axes by \(\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \dots\);
\(\M{U}\) turns the result into place, so that the axes line up with the columns \(\vect{u}_1, \vect{u}_2, \dots\) of \(\M{U}\).

The unit circle (or sphere) becomes an ellipse (or ellipsoid) whose semi-axes are \(\sigma_1\vect{u}_1, \sigma_2\vect{u}_2, \dots\) (Figure 21.1).






Figure 21.1: The unit circle under \(\M{A} = \M{U}\M{\Sigma}\M{V}\T\), one factor at a time, for \(\M{V}\) a rotation by \(30°\), \(\M{\Sigma} = \operatorname{diag}(2, 0.6)\) and \(\M{U}\) a rotation by \(60°\). The right singular vectors \(\vect{v}_1\) and \(\vect{v}_2\) (blue and brown) end up as the semi-axes \(\sigma_1\vect{u}_1\) and \(\sigma_2\vect{u}_2\) of the ellipse.



Column by column, the decomposition says \[
\M{A}\vect{v}_i = \sigma_i\vect{u}_i.
\tag{21.1}\] Compare \(\M{A}\vect{v} = \lambda\vect{v}\): the right singular vectors \(\vect{v}_i\) are perpendicular directions in the input that \(\M{A}\) sends to perpendicular directions \(\vect{u}_i\) in the output (the left singular vectors), stretched by \(\sigma_i\). Unlike eigenvectors, the input and output directions can differ, which is what makes the SVD possible for every matrix.


Finding the SVD
Multiply \(\M{A}\) by its transpose: \[
\M{A}\T\M{A} = \M{V}\M{\Sigma}\T\M{U}\T\M{U}\M{\Sigma}\M{V}\T = \M{V}(\M{\Sigma}\T\M{\Sigma})\M{V}\T.
\] This is the orthogonal diagonalisation of the symmetric matrix \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\) (Chapter 20). So:

the right singular vectors \(\vect{v}_i\) are the eigenvectors of \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\);
the singular values are the square roots of its eigenvalues, \(\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}\) (which are never negative, since \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\) is positive semidefinite);
the left singular vectors follow from Equation 21.1: \(\vect{u}_i = \M{A}\vect{v}_i / \sigma_i\) for each \(\sigma_i > 0\).

By hand this works for small examples. Software uses more accurate methods, which avoid forming \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\).






NoteExample 1: an SVD by hand



Find the SVD of \(\M{A} = \mat{3 & 0 \\ 4 & 5}\).
Solution. First, \[
\M{A}\T\M{A} = \mat{3 & 4 \\ 0 & 5}\mat{3 & 0 \\ 4 & 5} = \mat{25 & 20 \\ 20 & 25},
\] with trace 50 and determinant \(625 - 400 = 225\), so its eigenvalues are 45 and 5, with eigenvectors \((1, 1)\T\) and \((1, -1)\T\). So \[
\sigma_1 = \sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5},
\qquad
\sigma_2 = \sqrt{5},
\qquad
\vect{v}_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1)\T,
\qquad
\vect{v}_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, -1)\T.
\] Then \(\vect{u}_1 = \M{A}\vect{v}_1/\sigma_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(3, 9)\T / (3\sqrt{5}) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(1, 3)\T\), and \(\vect{u}_2 = \M{A}\vect{v}_2/\sigma_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(3, -1)\T/\sqrt{5} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(3, -1)\T\). These are perpendicular, as they must be. So \[
\M{A} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\mat{1 & 3 \\ 3 & -1}\mat{3\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{5}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1}.
\] Check: \(\sigma_1\sigma_2 = 15 = \lvert\det\M{A}\rvert\). ✓ This is Example in the app.




What the singular values tell you

Rank. The number of non-zero singular values is the rank of \(\M{A}\). In floating-point arithmetic, tiny singular values signal a matrix that is nearly of lower rank, which is how matrix_rank and MATLAB’s rank decide (Chapter 12).
Size. \(\sigma_1\) is the largest factor by which \(\M{A}\) stretches any vector: \(\lVert\M{A}\vect{x}\rVert \le \sigma_1\lVert\vect{x}\rVert\).
Closeness to singular. For a square matrix, \(\lvert\det\M{A}\rvert = \sigma_1\sigma_2\cdots\sigma_n\), and the ratio \(\sigma_1/\sigma_n\), the condition number, measures how much errors can be magnified when solving \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) (Chapter 24).
The four subspaces. The first \(r\) columns of \(\M{V}\) are an orthonormal basis for the row space, the rest for the null space; the first \(r\) columns of \(\M{U}\) are an orthonormal basis for the column space, the rest for the left null space (Chapter 16). This is how null_space and orth work.



Low-rank approximation
Multiplying out \(\M{U}\M{\Sigma}\M{V}\T\) column by row writes \(\M{A}\) as a sum of simple pieces, \[
\M{A} = \sigma_1\vect{u}_1\vect{v}_1\T + \sigma_2\vect{u}_2\vect{v}_2\T + \dots + \sigma_r\vect{u}_r\vect{v}_r\T,
\] each a rank-1 matrix (a column times a row), in decreasing order of importance. Keeping only the first \(k\) terms gives a matrix \(\M{A}_k\) of rank \(k\). The Eckart–Young theorem says that this is the best possible: no matrix of rank \(k\) is closer to \(\M{A}\), measuring closeness by the square root of the sum of the squared differences of the entries. The error of the approximation is \(\sqrt{\sigma_{k+1}^2 + \dots + \sigma_r^2}\).
An \(m \times n\) greyscale image is a matrix of pixel brightnesses. Storing \(\M{A}_k\) needs only \(k\) columns \(\vect{u}_i\), \(k\) rows \(\vect{v}_i\T\) and \(k\) numbers \(\sigma_i\): \(k(m + n + 1)\) numbers instead of \(mn\). Natural images have singular values that fall off quickly, so a modest \(k\) gives a recognisable picture. (Real image formats such as JPEG use a related idea with fixed basis patterns, which is faster.)
The SVD explorer from the start of the chapter, in its second mode, builds a picture up one rank-1 term at a time.



Open the picture compression in its own tab

Things to try:

How many terms do you need before the picture looks right? How many numbers does that store, compared with the whole picture?
Watch the plot of singular values as you add terms. Where does the picture stop improving much?
Try Checks and Stripes. Why are so few terms enough? (Hint: how many genuinely different rows does each picture have, and what does that say about its rank?)







NoteExample 2: the best rank-1 approximation



Find the best rank-1 approximation to \(\M{A}\) in Example 1, and its error.
Solution. Keep the first term: \[
\M{A}_1 = \sigma_1\vect{u}_1\vect{v}_1\T = 3\sqrt{5} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\mat{1 \\ 3} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\mat{1 & 1} = \frac{3}{2}\mat{1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3}.
\] The error is \(\M{A} - \M{A}_1 = \mat{1.5 & -1.5 \\ -0.5 & 0.5}\), and the square root of the sum of its squared entries is \(\sqrt{2.25 + 2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25} = \sqrt{5} = \sigma_2\), exactly as the Eckart–Young theorem says.




Principal component analysis
Take a data set of \(n\) items measured on \(p\) variables, as an \(n \times p\) matrix \(\M{X}\) with each column’s mean subtracted (Chapter 20). Write its SVD as \(\M{X} = \M{U}\M{\Sigma}\M{V}\T\). Then the covariance matrix is \[
\M{C} = \frac{1}{n - 1}\M{X}\T\M{X} = \M{V}\,\frac{\M{\Sigma}\T\M{\Sigma}}{n - 1}\,\M{V}\T,
\] so the columns of \(\M{V}\) are the eigenvectors of \(\M{C}\): the directions of greatest spread in the data, called the principal components. The variance along the \(i\)th one is \(\sigma_i^2/(n - 1)\), and the fraction of the total variance it accounts for is \[
\frac{\sigma_i^2}{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \dots + \sigma_p^2}.
\] Principal component analysis (PCA) describes each item by its coordinates along the first few principal components, its scores \(\M{X}\vect{v}_i\), instead of by all \(p\) of its original variables. When the first few components explain most of the variance, little information is lost, and data with dozens of variables can be plotted in two or three dimensions.






NoteExample 3: principal components of a small data set



Five items are measured on two variables: \((1, 2)\), \((2, 3)\), \((3, 5)\), \((4, 4)\) and \((5, 6)\). Find the principal components and how much of the variance each explains.
Solution. The means are 3 and 4, so the centred data are \[
\M{X} = \mat{-2 & -2 \\ -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2},
\] and the covariance matrix is \[
\M{C} = \frac{1}{4}\M{X}\T\M{X} = \frac{1}{4}\mat{10 & 9 \\ 9 & 10}.
\] Its eigenvalues are \(\tfrac{19}{4}\) and \(\tfrac{1}{4}\), with eigenvectors \((1, 1)\T\) and \((1, -1)\T\). The first principal component is the direction \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1)\), explaining \(\tfrac{19}{20} = 95\%\) of the variance; the second, at right angles to it, explains the remaining 5%. The data lie close to a line through their mean in the direction \((1, 1)\), so describing each item by its single score along that line loses little.




The pseudoinverse
If \(\M{A}\) has rank \(r\), replacing each non-zero \(\sigma_i\) in \(\M{\Sigma}\) by \(1/\sigma_i\), and transposing, gives \(\M{\Sigma}^+\), and the pseudoinverse is \[
\M{A}^+ = \M{V}\M{\Sigma}^+\M{U}\T.
\] For an invertible matrix it is the ordinary inverse. For any \(\M{A}\), \(\hat{\vect{x}} = \M{A}^+\vect{b}\) is the least-squares solution of \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) (Chapter 17), and when there are many least-squares solutions, because the columns are dependent, it picks the shortest one.

text:
21.3 In code

Run this chapter’s code yourself: open the notebook in Colab, or download the Jupyter notebook or the MATLAB script.

np.linalg.svd returns \(\M{U}\), the singular values as a list, and \(\M{V}\T\) (not \(\M{V}\)). MATLAB’s svd returns \(\M{U}\), \(\M{\Sigma}\) and \(\M{V}\). With full_matrices=False, or 'econ' in MATLAB, a tall matrix gets only the columns of \(\M{U}\) that matter, which saves a lot of memory for data sets.

PythonMATLAB



import numpy as np

A = np.array([[3, 0], [4, 5]])
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A)
print(s)                                   # 3*sqrt(5) and sqrt(5)
print(U)
print(Vt)                                  # rows are v1 and v2 (signs may differ)

# PCA of Example 3
X = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 5], [4, 4], [5, 6]])
Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)                    # centre each column
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)
print(Vt[0])                               # first principal component
print(s**2 / np.sum(s**2))                 # fraction of variance explained

title: 21  The singular value decomposition and PCA
text:
21.5 Key ideas

Every matrix, of any shape, has a singular value decomposition \(\M{A} = \M{U}\M{\Sigma}\M{V}\T\): rotate, stretch along the axes, rotate.
The singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\), and they measure how much \(\M{A}\) stretches in each direction.
The number of non-zero singular values is the rank, and the ratio of the largest to the smallest is the condition number.
Keeping only the largest \(k\) singular values gives the best rank-\(k\) approximation to \(\M{A}\), the basis of compression.
Principal component analysis is the SVD of centred data: the right singular vectors are the principal directions, and the squared singular values measure the variance along each.

title: 21  The singular value decomposition and PCA
text:
21.7 In practice

Data science: PCA is one of the first steps in exploring a data set with many variables, from gene expression measurements to survey responses, both to visualise it and to reduce the number of variables before further modelling (Chapter 37).
Recommender systems: a table of users’ ratings of films or products is approximately low-rank, because tastes are driven by a few underlying factors. Low-rank approximations, close relatives of the truncated SVD, fill in the missing ratings to make recommendations.
Engineering: in measurements or simulations of fluid flow, structural vibration or heat, the SVD of a matrix of snapshots picks out the dominant patterns, called modes. Models built from a few modes can run thousands of times faster than the full simulation.
Numerical computing: the SVD gives reliable ranks, orthonormal bases for the four subspaces, condition numbers and least-squares solutions even when a matrix is nearly singular.
Signal and image processing: noise spreads over all the singular values, while the signal is concentrated in the first few, so dropping the small ones removes much of the noise.

title: 21  The singular value decomposition and PCA
text:
21.8 Going further

For very large matrices, randomised SVD finds the first few singular values and vectors by multiplying the matrix by a handful of random vectors, at a fraction of the cost of a full SVD.
A proof that every matrix has an SVD, from the spectral theorem applied to \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\), and of a form of the Eckart–Young theorem: Section C.14.
PCA results depend on the units of the variables. When variables are measured on different scales, they are usually standardised first (divided by their standard deviations), which amounts to using the correlation matrix instead of the covariance matrix.

title: 22  Derivatives with vectors and matrices
text:
22.1 Build intuition
Further
Builds on Chapter 17, Chapter 20, and partial derivatives.
Much of applied mathematics is about finding the best of something: the line that fits the data most closely, the design with the least weight, the model parameters with the smallest error. With one variable you set a derivative to zero. With many variables, the derivatives collect into vectors and matrices, and matrix notation turns pages of partial derivatives into a few lines. This chapter assumes you know how to take partial derivatives; everything else is built from there.
There is no app for this chapter. Instead, study Figure 22.1 below. It shows the contours (lines of constant height) of the quadratic function of Example 1, like the contour lines on a map of a valley, with arrows showing the gradient at points across the plane, and the path taken by gradient descent from \((-2, -1)\).
Show the code for this figure
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

A = np.array([[3.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]])
b = np.array([5.0, 5.0])
f = lambda x, y: 0.5 * (A[0, 0] * x**2 + 2 * A[0, 1] * x * y + A[1, 1] * y**2) - b[0] * x - b[1] * y

x, y = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-3, 5, 200), np.linspace(-2, 5, 200))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
ax.contour(x, y, f(x, y), levels=np.arange(-7, 40, 3), cmap="viridis", linewidths=1)

gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-2.5, 4.5, 9), np.linspace(-1.5, 4.5, 8))
grad = np.einsum("ij,jkl->ikl", A, np.array([gx, gy])) - b[:, None, None]
ax.quiver(gx, gy, -grad[0], -grad[1], color="0.55", angles="xy", scale=120, width=0.004)

path = [np.array([-2.0, -1.0])]
for _ in range(20):
    path.append(path[-1] - 0.4 * (A @ path[-1] - b))
path = np.array(path)
ax.plot(path[:, 0], path[:, 1], "o-", color="#c0392b", ms=4, lw=1.5)
ax.plot(1, 2, "k*", ms=12)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xlabel("$x_1$")
ax.set_ylabel("$x_2$")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 22.1: Contours of \(f(\vect{x}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b}\T\vect{x}\) with \(\M{A} = \mat{3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2}\) and \(\vect{b} = (5, 5)\T\). The grey arrows show the negative gradient \(-\nabla f\) (scaled down), and the red path is gradient descent with step size 0.4, starting from \((-2, -1)\) and reaching the minimum at \((1, 2)\).

title: 22  Derivatives with vectors and matrices
text:
22.2 The ideas

The gradient
For a scalar function \(f(\vect{x})\) of a vector \(\vect{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_n)\T\), the gradient is the column vector of its partial derivatives, \[
\nabla f = \mat{\partial f/\partial x_1 \\ \vdots \\ \partial f/\partial x_n}.
\] For a small change \(\Delta\vect{x}\), the change in \(f\) is approximately a dot product: \[
f(\vect{x} + \Delta\vect{x}) \approx f(\vect{x}) + \nabla f(\vect{x}) \cdot \Delta\vect{x}.
\tag{22.1}\] This one formula explains the gradient’s geometry. Moving along a contour leaves \(f\) unchanged, so \(\nabla f \cdot \Delta\vect{x} = 0\): the gradient is perpendicular to the contours. And among all steps of a given length, the dot product is largest when \(\Delta\vect{x}\) points along \(\nabla f\) (Chapter 17): the gradient points in the direction of steepest increase, and its length is the rate of increase in that direction.
At a minimum or maximum of a smooth function, no direction goes uphill to first order, so \(\nabla f = \zerovec\). Points where this happens are called stationary points.


Two gradients worth knowing
Two kinds of function come up again and again: linear functions \(\vect{a}\T\vect{x}\) and quadratic forms \(\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x}\) (Chapter 20).






ImportantGradients of linear and quadratic forms



\[
\nabla(\vect{a}\T\vect{x}) = \vect{a},
\qquad
\nabla(\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x}) = (\M{A} + \M{A}\T)\vect{x},
\] which is \(2\M{A}\vect{x}\) when \(\M{A}\) is symmetric.


These are the vector versions of \(\frac{d}{dx}(ax) = a\) and \(\frac{d}{dx}(ax^2) = 2ax\). You can check them in two dimensions by writing everything out: with \(\M{A} = \mat{a & b \\ b & c}\), \(\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x} = ax_1^2 + 2bx_1x_2 + cx_2^2\), whose partial derivatives are \(2ax_1 + 2bx_2\) and \(2bx_1 + 2cx_2\), the entries of \(2\M{A}\vect{x}\). The general proof is in Section C.15, and more formulas like these are collected in Appendix D.
A consequence is used all the time. If \(\M{A}\) is symmetric, the function \[
f(\vect{x}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b}\T\vect{x}
\] has gradient \(\M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b}\), so its stationary point solves the linear system \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\). If \(\M{A}\) is positive definite, the graph is a bowl and that point is its unique minimum. Solving a symmetric positive definite system and minimising a quadratic are the same problem, which is the starting point for several of the iterative methods in Chapter 27.






NoteExample 1: minimising a quadratic



Find the minimum of \(f(x_1, x_2) = \tfrac{3}{2}x_1^2 + x_1x_2 + x_2^2 - 5x_1 - 5x_2\), and take one step of gradient descent from \((-2, -1)\) with step size \(0.4\).
Solution. In matrix form, \(f = \tfrac{1}{2}\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b}\T\vect{x}\) with \[
\M{A} = \mat{3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2},
\qquad
\vect{b} = \mat{5 \\ 5}.
\] (Check: \(\tfrac{1}{2}\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x} = \tfrac{1}{2}(3x_1^2 + 2x_1x_2 + 2x_2^2)\).) The gradient is \(\M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b}\), and setting it to zero gives \(3x_1 + x_2 = 5\), \(x_1 + 2x_2 = 5\), so \(\vect{x}^* = (1, 2)\T\). The Hessian is \(\M{A}\), with trace 5 and determinant 5, so both eigenvalues are positive, \((5 \pm \sqrt{5})/2 \approx 3.62\) and \(1.38\): the point is a minimum.
At \((-2, -1)\), the gradient is \(\M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b} = (-7, -4)\T - (5, 5)\T = (-12, -9)\T\), so \[
\vect{x}_1 = \mat{-2 \\ -1} - 0.4\mat{-12 \\ -9} = \mat{2.8 \\ 2.6}.
\] The step overshoots, as the figure shows. Each error component along an eigenvector is multiplied by \(1 - 0.4\lambda\), about \(-0.45\) and \(0.45\), so the error shrinks by a factor of about 0.45 per step and falls below \(10^{-6}\) after 19 steps.




Least squares by calculus
In Chapter 17, the normal equations came from geometry: the error must be perpendicular to the column space. Calculus gets there too. Expand the squared error: \[
E(\vect{x}) = \lVert\M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b}\rVert^2 = (\M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b})\T(\M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b}) = \vect{x}\T\M{A}\T\M{A}\vect{x} - 2(\M{A}\T\vect{b})\T\vect{x} + \vect{b}\T\vect{b}.
\] The first term is a quadratic form with the symmetric matrix \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\), the second is linear, and the third is constant, so \[
\nabla E = 2\M{A}\T\M{A}\vect{x} - 2\M{A}\T\vect{b}.
\] Setting this to zero gives the normal equations \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\hat{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\T\vect{b}\), in three lines. The same method, writing the quantity to minimise in matrix form and setting its gradient to zero, derives the formulas behind ridge regression, Kalman filters and many other techniques.


The Jacobian
Now let \(\vect{f}\) be a function from \(\R^n\) to \(\R^m\): \(m\) outputs, each depending on \(n\) inputs. Applying Equation 22.1 to each output and stacking the results gives \[
\vect{f}(\vect{x} + \Delta\vect{x}) \approx \vect{f}(\vect{x}) + \M{J}(\vect{x})\,\Delta\vect{x},
\tag{22.2}\] where the Jacobian \(\M{J}\) is the \(m \times n\) matrix of partial derivatives, with \(J_{ij} = \partial f_i/\partial x_j\). Row \(i\) is the gradient of \(f_i\) written as a row; column \(j\) shows how all the outputs respond to the input \(x_j\).
Equation 22.2 says that, close to any point, a smooth nonlinear function looks like a linear transformation (Chapter 4), with the Jacobian as its matrix. Everything from Part I applies locally: in particular, \(\lvert\det\M{J}\rvert\) is the factor by which the function scales small areas or volumes (Chapter 6), which is why it appears when you change variables in a multiple integral.
The chain rule becomes matrix multiplication. If \(\vect{y} = \vect{g}(\vect{x})\) and \(\vect{z} = \vect{f}(\vect{y})\), then a small change passes through two linear approximations in turn, so \[
\M{J}_{\vect{f} \circ \vect{g}}(\vect{x}) = \M{J}_{\vect{f}}(\vect{y})\,\M{J}_{\vect{g}}(\vect{x}),
\] just as composing transformations multiplies their matrices (Chapter 5). Backpropagation, the algorithm that trains neural networks, is this product evaluated efficiently from left to right.






NoteExample 2: the Jacobian of polar coordinates



The map from polar to Cartesian coordinates is \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\). Find its Jacobian and its determinant, and use the Jacobian to estimate how \((x, y)\) moves when \((r, \theta)\) changes from \((2, \pi/6)\) by \((0.1, 0.05)\).
Solution. Differentiating each output with respect to each input, \[
\M{J} = \mat{\partial x/\partial r & \partial x/\partial\theta \\ \partial y/\partial r & \partial y/\partial\theta} = \mat{\cos\theta & -r\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & r\cos\theta},
\qquad
\det\M{J} = r\cos^2\theta + r\sin^2\theta = r.
\] This is the \(r\) in \(dA = r\,dr\,d\theta\) for integrals in polar coordinates: a small patch \(dr\) by \(d\theta\) has area about \(r\,dr\,d\theta\) (Figure 22.2). At \(r = 2\), \(\theta = \pi/6\), \[
\Delta\mat{x \\ y} \approx \mat{\sqrt{3}/2 & -1 \\ 1/2 & \sqrt{3}}\mat{0.1 \\ 0.05} \approx \mat{0.0366 \\ 0.1366}.
\] The exact change is \((0.0319, 0.1396)\), so the linear approximation is close.






Figure 22.2: A small polar patch. Its sides are \(dr\) along the radius and \(r\,d\theta\) around the arc, so its area is about \(r\,dr\,d\theta\): the determinant of the Jacobian is the factor \(r\).







The Hessian
The second derivatives of a scalar function \(f\) form the Hessian, the \(n \times n\) matrix \(\M{H}\) with \(H_{ij} = \partial^2 f/\partial x_i\partial x_j\). For smooth functions the order of differentiation doesn’t matter, so the Hessian is symmetric. It is the Jacobian of the gradient, and it gives the next term of the approximation: \[
f(\vect{x} + \Delta\vect{x}) \approx f(\vect{x}) + \nabla f(\vect{x}) \cdot \Delta\vect{x} + \tfrac{1}{2}\Delta\vect{x}\T\M{H}(\vect{x})\,\Delta\vect{x}.
\] At a stationary point the middle term vanishes, so the shape of \(f\) nearby is the shape of the quadratic form \(\Delta\vect{x}\T\M{H}\Delta\vect{x}\), which Chapter 20 classified by eigenvalues.






ImportantThe second derivative test



At a stationary point, where \(\nabla f = \zerovec\):

if \(\M{H}\) is positive definite (all eigenvalues positive), the point is a local minimum;
if \(\M{H}\) is negative definite (all eigenvalues negative), it is a local maximum;
if \(\M{H}\) has both positive and negative eigenvalues, it is a saddle point;
if some eigenvalues are zero and the rest have one sign, the test is inconclusive.



For a quadratic \(\tfrac{1}{2}\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b}\T\vect{x}\), the Hessian is \(\M{A}\) itself, the same at every point.






NoteExample 3: classifying stationary points



Find and classify the stationary points of \(f(x, y) = x^3 - 3x + y^2\).
Solution. The gradient is \(\nabla f = (3x^2 - 3, \; 2y)\T\), which is zero at \((1, 0)\) and \((-1, 0)\). The Hessian is \[
\M{H} = \mat{6x & 0 \\ 0 & 2}.
\] At \((1, 0)\), \(\M{H} = \mat{6 & 0 \\ 0 & 2}\) has eigenvalues 6 and 2, both positive: a local minimum, with \(f = -2\). At \((-1, 0)\), \(\M{H} = \mat{-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 2}\) has eigenvalues \(-6\) and 2: a saddle point, a maximum along the \(x\) direction and a minimum along the \(y\) direction (Figure 22.3).






Figure 22.3: Contours of \(f(x, y) = x^3 - 3x + y^2\). Around the minimum at \((1, 0)\) the contours are closed ovals; at the saddle \((-1, 0)\) the contour \(f = 2\) (brown) crosses itself.







Gradient descent
When setting \(\nabla f = \zerovec\) can’t be solved by hand, the simplest numerical method walks downhill. Starting from a guess \(\vect{x}_0\), repeat \[
\vect{x}_{k+1} = \vect{x}_k - \alpha\nabla f(\vect{x}_k),
\] taking a step of size \(\alpha\), the step size or learning rate, in the direction of steepest descent. For the quadratic above, the error \(\vect{e}_k = \vect{x}_k - \vect{x}^*\) obeys \(\vect{e}_{k+1} = (\M{I} - \alpha\M{A})\vect{e}_k\): a matrix power, exactly as in Chapter 19. Along each eigenvector of \(\M{A}\), the error is multiplied by \(1 - \alpha\lambda_i\) at every step. So:

the method converges only if \(\lvert 1 - \alpha\lambda_i\rvert < 1\) for every \(i\), which needs \(\alpha < 2/\lambda_{\max}\);
the step size must suit the steepest direction (largest \(\lambda\)), so progress along the shallowest one (smallest \(\lambda\)) is slow. The larger the ratio \(\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\), the more the path zigzags and the slower it gets.

That ratio is the condition number of \(\M{A}\), the same number that measures sensitivity to errors (Chapter 24). Near the minimum of any smooth function, the Hessian plays the role of \(\M{A}\). Newton’s method instead uses the Hessian to rescale each step, which removes the zigzag at the cost of solving a linear system per step (Chapter 28).

Run this chapter’s code yourself: open the notebook in Colab, or download the Jupyter notebook or the MATLAB script.

Getting gradients right by hand is error-prone, so it is worth checking them numerically: compare each entry with a finite difference \((f(\vect{x} + h\ue{i}) - f(\vect{x} - h\ue{i}))/(2h)\) for a small \(h\). In Python, the SymPy package (pip install sympy) can also find gradients, Jacobians and Hessians symbolically, as can MATLAB’s Symbolic Math Toolbox with gradient, jacobian and hessian.

PythonMATLAB

22.4 Check your understanding






TipWhat is the gradient of \(\lVert\vect{x}\rVert^2 = \vect{x}\T\vect{x}\)?





\(2\vect{x}\): it is \(\vect{x}\T\M{I}\vect{x}\), so the gradient is \(2\M{I}\vect{x}\). It points straight away from the origin, perpendicular to the circles $= $ constant.









TipWhat shape is the Jacobian of a function from \(\R^3\) to \(\R^2\)?





\(2 \times 3\): one row per output, one column per input.









TipWhat is the Jacobian of a linear function \(\vect{f}(\vect{x}) = \M{A}\vect{x}\)?





\(\M{A}\) itself, at every point: the best linear approximation to a linear function is the function.

title: 22  Derivatives with vectors and matrices
text:
22.5 Key ideas

The gradient \(\nabla f\) collects the partial derivatives of a scalar function, and points in the direction of steepest increase.
Two gradients cover most uses: \(\nabla(\vect{a}\T\vect{x}) = \vect{a}\), and \(\nabla(\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x}) = 2\M{A}\vect{x}\) for symmetric \(\M{A}\).
Setting the gradient of \(\lVert\M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b}\rVert^2\) to zero gives the normal equations of least squares.
The Jacobian of a vector function holds all its first partial derivatives, and gives its best linear approximation near a point.
The Hessian holds the second derivatives: at a stationary point, positive definite means a minimum, negative definite a maximum, and mixed signs a saddle. Gradient descent steps downhill along \(-\nabla f\).

title: 22  Derivatives with vectors and matrices
text:
22.7 In practice

Machine learning: training a model means minimising a loss function over millions of parameters by variants of gradient descent. Automatic differentiation software (as in PyTorch, JAX and TensorFlow) computes the gradients by applying the chain rule as a product of Jacobians.
Statistics: maximum likelihood estimation sets the gradient of the log-likelihood to zero, and the Hessian at the maximum gives the standard errors of the estimates.
Engineering design: optimising the shape of a structure or wing uses gradients of performance with respect to hundreds of design variables, often computed by solving one extra linear system, the adjoint method.
Robotics: the Jacobian of a robot arm maps joint speeds to the speed of its hand. Where it is singular, the arm loses the ability to move in some direction (Chapter 34).
Nonlinear equations: Newton’s method for systems repeatedly replaces the equations by their Jacobian linearisation and solves the resulting linear system (Chapter 28).

title: 22  Derivatives with vectors and matrices
text:
22.8 Going further

Proofs of the gradient formulas and the second derivative test: Section C.15. A longer list of gradients, including derivatives with respect to matrices, such as \(\partial \operatorname{tr}(\M{A}\M{X})/\partial\M{X}\), is in Appendix D.
Some books lay out derivatives as rows instead of columns (the “numerator layout”). The results are transposes of each other, so check which convention a source uses before copying a formula.
The method of Lagrange multipliers handles minimisation subject to constraints. For a quadratic objective with linear constraints it leads to a single symmetric linear system, which is how many structural and economic models are solved.

title: 23  Linear ODE systems and the matrix exponential
text:
23.1 Build intuition
Further
Builds on Chapter 18, Chapter 19, and first-order differential equations.
Two rooms lose heat to the outside and to each other; two masses on springs push and pull on each other; a drug passes from the gut into the blood and is then removed. In each case several quantities change at once, and the rate at which each one changes depends on all of them. When the dependence is linear, the whole system is one equation, \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\vect{x}\), where the dot means the derivative with respect to time. Chapter 19 solved \(\vect{x}_{k+1} = \M{A}\vect{x}_k\) for systems that change in steps; this chapter does the same for systems that change continuously, with the same tools. This chapter assumes you have met first-order differential equations such as \(\dot{x} = ax\).
The app draws the phase portrait of \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\vect{x}\): the paths that the state \(\vect{x}(t)\) traces out in the plane, from many starting points. Small arrows show the direction of motion at each point, and the chart on the right places the matrix by its trace and determinant.

title: 23  Linear ODE systems and the matrix exponential
text:
23.2 The ideas

Systems of differential equations
Suppose quantities \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) change with time \(t\), and each rate of change is a linear combination of all of them: \[
\begin{aligned}
\dot{x}_1 &= a_{11}x_1 + \dots + a_{1n}x_n, \\
&\;\;\vdots \\
\dot{x}_n &= a_{n1}x_1 + \dots + a_{nn}x_n.
\end{aligned}
\] In matrix form this is \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\vect{x}\), and together with a starting state \(\vect{x}(0) = \vect{x}_0\) it has exactly one solution. The origin is an equilibrium: if \(\vect{x} = \zerovec\), nothing changes.
Higher-order equations fit the same pattern. For a mass on a spring with damping, \(\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = 0\), take the position and the velocity as the two quantities, \(x_1 = x\) and \(x_2 = \dot{x}\). Then \(\dot{x}_1 = x_2\) and \(\dot{x}_2 = -kx_1 - cx_2\), so \[
\frac{d}{dt}\mat{x_1 \\ x_2} = \mat{0 & 1 \\ -k & -c}\mat{x_1 \\ x_2}.
\] Any linear equation of order \(n\) becomes a system of \(n\) first-order equations in this way, which is also how numerical ODE solvers expect equations to be written.


Eigenvector solutions
For one equation, \(\dot{x} = ax\) has solution \(x = e^{at}x_0\). So try \(\vect{x}(t) = e^{\lambda t}\vect{v}\) for a fixed vector \(\vect{v}\). Then \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \lambda e^{\lambda t}\vect{v}\) and \(\M{A}\vect{x} = e^{\lambda t}\M{A}\vect{v}\), and these are equal exactly when \(\M{A}\vect{v} = \lambda\vect{v}\). Every eigenvector gives a solution that stays on its line through the origin, growing if \(\lambda > 0\) and shrinking if \(\lambda < 0\).
The equation is linear, so sums of solutions are solutions. If \(\M{A}\) has \(n\) independent eigenvectors, write the starting state in terms of them, \(\vect{x}_0 = c_1\vect{v}_1 + \dots + c_n\vect{v}_n\) (Chapter 15). Then \[
\vect{x}(t) = c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}\vect{v}_1 + c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}\vect{v}_2 + \dots + c_ne^{\lambda_n t}\vect{v}_n.
\tag{23.1}\] Each term is a mode of the system, evolving independently of the others. This is Equation 19.3 of Chapter 19 with \(\lambda^k\) replaced by \(e^{\lambda t}\). In the long run, the mode with the largest \(\lambda\) dominates.






NoteExample 1: two rooms cooling



Two rooms, at temperatures \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) above the outside temperature, each lose heat to the outside and exchange heat with each other through a shared wall (Figure 23.1). With suitable units, \[
\dot{x}_1 = -x_1 - (x_1 - x_2),
\qquad
\dot{x}_2 = -x_2 - (x_2 - x_1).
\] Starting from \(\vect{x}_0 = (3, 1)\T\), find \(\vect{x}(t)\).






Figure 23.1: The two rooms of Example 1. Each loses heat to the outside at a rate equal to its temperature (brown), and heat flows through the shared wall at a rate equal to the difference in temperature (green).



Solution. The matrix is \(\M{A} = \mat{-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2}\), with trace \(-4\) and determinant 3, so \(\lambda^2 + 4\lambda + 3 = 0\) and \(\lambda = -1\) or \(-3\). Eigenvectors: \((1, 1)\T\) for \(\lambda = -1\) and \((1, -1)\T\) for \(\lambda = -3\). Writing \(\vect{x}_0 = (3, 1)\T = 2(1, 1)\T + 1(1, -1)\T\), \[
\vect{x}(t) = 2e^{-t}\mat{1 \\ 1} + e^{-3t}\mat{1 \\ -1}.
\] The modes have a physical meaning. In the first, both rooms are equally warm, so no heat crosses the wall and both cool at rate 1. In the second, one room is warmer than the other by as much as the other is cooler; heat also flows through the wall, so this difference dies away three times as fast. After a short time the temperatures are almost equal, and both fall together. This is Two rooms cooling in the app: paths first move parallel to \((1, -1)\) onto the line through \((1, 1)\), then slide along it to the origin.




Complex eigenvalues: oscillation
A real matrix can have complex eigenvalues \(\lambda = \alpha \pm \beta i\) (Chapter 18). Equation 23.1 still holds, and by Euler’s formula \[
e^{(\alpha + \beta i)t} = e^{\alpha t}(\cos\beta t + i\sin\beta t).
\] The imaginary parts cancel in the real solution, leaving combinations of \(e^{\alpha t}\cos\beta t\) and \(e^{\alpha t}\sin\beta t\). The imaginary part \(\beta\) sets the angular frequency of oscillation, and the real part \(\alpha\) decides whether the oscillation dies away (\(\alpha < 0\)), grows (\(\alpha > 0\)) or carries on for ever (\(\alpha = 0\)).






NoteExample 2: a damped spring



Solve \(\ddot{x} + 2\dot{x} + 5x = 0\) with \(x(0) = 1\), \(\dot{x}(0) = 0\), and describe the motion.
Solution. With \(x_1 = x\) and \(x_2 = \dot{x}\), the matrix is \(\M{A} = \mat{0 & 1 \\ -5 & -2}\), with trace \(-2\) and determinant 5. So \(\lambda^2 + 2\lambda + 5 = 0\), giving \(\lambda = -1 \pm 2i\). The solution is a combination of \(e^{-t}\cos 2t\) and \(e^{-t}\sin 2t\): \[
x(t) = e^{-t}(a\cos 2t + b\sin 2t).
\] From \(x(0) = 1\), \(a = 1\). Differentiating, \(\dot{x}(0) = -a + 2b = 0\), so \(b = \tfrac{1}{2}\), and \[
x(t) = e^{-t}\left(\cos 2t + \tfrac{1}{2}\sin 2t\right).
\] The mass oscillates with angular frequency 2, and the amplitude decays like \(e^{-t}\): a stable spiral in the phase plane, Damped spring in the app. Without damping (\(\ddot{x} + 4x = 0\), Undamped spring), the eigenvalues would be \(\pm 2i\) and the paths closed ellipses.




Stability
The equilibrium is stable if every solution tends to \(\zerovec\), and that depends only on the real parts of the eigenvalues.






ImportantStability of \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\vect{x}\)



Every solution tends to \(\zerovec\) if and only if every eigenvalue of \(\M{A}\) has negative real part. If any eigenvalue has positive real part, most solutions grow without limit.


Compare the discrete case of Chapter 19, where the test was \(\lvert\lambda\rvert < 1\): there the factor per step is \(\lambda\), here it is \(e^{\lambda}\) per unit time, and \(\lvert e^{\lambda}\rvert < 1\) exactly when the real part of \(\lambda\) is negative.
For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, the eigenvalues are the roots of \(\lambda^2 - \tau\lambda + \Delta = 0\), where \(\tau\) is the trace and \(\Delta\) the determinant (Chapter 18), so these two numbers decide the type of the phase portrait:








Condition
Eigenvalues
Phase portrait




\(\Delta < 0\)
real, opposite signs
saddle: unstable


\(\Delta > 0\), \(\tau^2 > 4\Delta\)
real, same sign
node: stable if \(\tau < 0\), unstable if \(\tau > 0\)


\(\Delta > 0\), \(\tau^2 < 4\Delta\), \(\tau \neq 0\)
complex
spiral: stable if \(\tau < 0\), unstable if \(\tau > 0\)


\(\Delta > 0\), \(\tau = 0\)
purely imaginary
centre: closed orbits



This is the chart in the app: the parabola \(\tau^2 = 4\Delta\) separates nodes from spirals, and the vertical axis separates stable from unstable.


The matrix exponential
For one equation the solution is \(e^{at}x_0\). For a system, define the matrix exponential by the same power series as \(e^x\): \[
e^{\M{A}t} = \M{I} + \M{A}t + \frac{(\M{A}t)^2}{2!} + \frac{(\M{A}t)^3}{3!} + \cdots
\] The series always converges, and differentiating term by term gives \(\frac{d}{dt}e^{\M{A}t} = \M{A}e^{\M{A}t}\) (Section C.16). So the solution of \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\vect{x}\), \(\vect{x}(0) = \vect{x}_0\), is \[
\vect{x}(t) = e^{\M{A}t}\vect{x}_0,
\] for every square matrix, diagonalisable or not. The matrix \(e^{\M{A}t}\) maps the state at time 0 to the state at time \(t\).
When \(\M{A} = \M{P}\M{D}\M{P}^{-1}\) is diagonalisable, every power is \(\M{A}^k = \M{P}\M{D}^k\M{P}^{-1}\) (Chapter 19), so the whole series factorises: \[
e^{\M{A}t} = \M{P}e^{\M{D}t}\M{P}^{-1},
\qquad
e^{\M{D}t} = \mat{e^{\lambda_1 t} & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & e^{\lambda_n t}}.
\] This is Equation 23.1 again, written as a single matrix.






WarningWatch out: exponentials of sums



For numbers, \(e^a e^b = e^{a + b}\). For matrices, \(e^{\M{A}}e^{\M{B}}\) equals \(e^{\M{A} + \M{B}}\) only when \(\M{A}\M{B} = \M{B}\M{A}\), because matrix multiplication is not commutative.








NoteExample 3: a matrix exponential



Find \(e^{\M{A}t}\) for the matrix of Example 1, and use it to find \(\vect{x}(1)\).
Solution. The unit eigenvectors are \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1)\T\) and \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, -1)\T\), and since \(\M{A}\) is symmetric, \(\M{P}^{-1} = \M{P}\T\) (Chapter 20). Then \[
e^{\M{A}t} = \M{P}\mat{e^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-3t}}\M{P}\T = \frac{1}{2}\mat{e^{-t} + e^{-3t} & e^{-t} - e^{-3t} \\ e^{-t} - e^{-3t} & e^{-t} + e^{-3t}}.
\] At \(t = 0\) this is \(\M{I}\), as it should be. At \(t = 1\), \[
\vect{x}(1) = e^{\M{A}}\mat{3 \\ 1} = \mat{2e^{-1} + e^{-3} \\ 2e^{-1} - e^{-3}} \approx \mat{0.7855 \\ 0.6860},
\] which agrees with Example 1.

23.3 In code

Run this chapter’s code yourself: open the notebook in Colab, or download the Jupyter notebook or the MATLAB script.

SciPy’s expm and MATLAB’s expm compute the matrix exponential directly, without needing eigenvectors, and work for any square matrix. For systems that are not linear, or not constant in time, numerical solvers such as solve_ivp and ode45 step the solution forward in time; they are worth trying on linear systems too, where you can check their answers.

PythonMATLAB



import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import expm
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

A = np.array([[-2, 1], [1, -2]])
x0 = np.array([3, 1])
print(expm(A * 1.0) @ x0)                  # x(1) for Example 1

# Example 2: the damped spring, solved numerically
S = np.array([[0, 1], [-5, -2]])
sol = solve_ivp(lambda t, x: S @ x, [0, 2], [1, 0], rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-12)
print(sol.y[:, -1])                        # position and velocity at t = 2
print(np.exp(-2) * (np.cos(4) + 0.5 * np.sin(4)))   # exact position
print(np.linalg.eigvals(S))                # -1 + 2i and -1 - 2i

title: 23  Linear ODE systems and the matrix exponential
text:
23.4 Check your understanding






TipA \(2 \times 2\) matrix has eigenvalues \(-1\) and \(2\). Is the origin stable?





No: it is a saddle. Paths along the eigenvector for \(-1\) go in, but almost every other path is eventually carried away along the eigenvector for 2.









TipWhat is \(e^{\M{A}t}\) when \(\M{A} = \M{0}\)?





\(\M{I}\), for every \(t\): nothing changes.









TipCan the trace alone tell you that a \(2 \times 2\) system is unstable?





Yes, if it is positive: the trace is the sum of the eigenvalues (or twice their real part), so at least one eigenvalue has positive real part. A negative trace alone is not enough, since a saddle can have negative trace.

23  Linear ODE systems and the matrix exponential

title: 23  Linear ODE systems and the matrix exponential
text:
23.5 Key ideas

Coupled linear differential equations can be written as \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\vect{x}\).
Each eigenvector \(\vect{v}\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda\) gives a solution \(e^{\lambda t}\vect{v}\), and the general solution is a combination of these.
Complex eigenvalues \(\alpha \pm \beta i\) give oscillation at frequency \(\beta\), growing or decaying like \(e^{\alpha t}\).
The equilibrium at the origin is stable when every eigenvalue has a negative real part.
The matrix exponential solves every such system at once: \(\vect{x}(t) = e^{\M{A}t}\vect{x}(0)\).

title: 23  Linear ODE systems and the matrix exponential
text:
23.7 In practice

Control engineering: aircraft, robots and power grids are modelled near an operating point by \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\vect{x} + \M{B}\vect{u}\), where \(\vect{u}\) is the control input. Feedback \(\vect{u} = -\M{K}\vect{x}\) changes the matrix to \(\M{A} - \M{B}\M{K}\), and controller design chooses \(\M{K}\) to move its eigenvalues into the left half of the complex plane.
Vibration: undamped structures obey \(\ddot{\vect{x}} = -\M{K}\vect{x}\), and each eigenvector of \(\M{K}\) is a mode shape vibrating at angular frequency \(\sqrt{\lambda}\), as in Chapter 18 exercise 7. Engineers check that these frequencies avoid those of engines, footsteps or wind.
Pharmacokinetics: compartment models like exercise 7, with more compartments, predict drug levels in the body and guide dosing.
Electrical circuits: the currents and voltages in a circuit with resistors, capacitors and inductors obey a linear system, whose eigenvalues give the circuit’s time constants and resonant frequencies (Chapter 32).
Nonlinear systems: near an equilibrium, a nonlinear system \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \vect{f}(\vect{x})\) behaves like \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \M{J}\vect{x}\), where \(\M{J}\) is the Jacobian there (Chapter 22). The eigenvalues of the Jacobian decide whether populations, chemical reactions or orbits are stable.

title: 23  Linear ODE systems and the matrix exponential
text:
23.8 Going further

Proofs that \(\frac{d}{dt}e^{\M{A}t} = \M{A}e^{\M{A}t}\) and that the solution is unique: Section C.16.
A defective matrix, such as \(\mat{\lambda & 1 \\ 0 & \lambda}\), gives solutions containing \(te^{\lambda t}\), as exercise 4(b) shows for \(\lambda = 0\). The Jordan form organises all such cases, but in practice expm handles them without it.
Forced systems \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\vect{x} + \vect{f}(t)\) are solved by \(\vect{x}(t) = e^{\M{A}t}\vect{x}_0 + \int_0^t e^{\M{A}(t - s)}\vect{f}(s)\,ds\), the vector version of the integrating factor method.
When eigenvalues differ hugely in size, as in chemical kinetics, the fast modes die almost at once but force ordinary solvers to take tiny steps. Such stiff systems need special solvers, such as solve_ivp(..., method="BDF") or MATLAB’s ode15s.
