title: 24  Floating point and conditioning
text:
24.1 Build intuition
Further
Builds on Chapter 7, Chapter 11.
Computers almost never do exact arithmetic. Every number is stored to about 16 significant digits, and every result is rounded. Usually this is harmless: 16 digits is far more than any measurement deserves. But some problems magnify small errors enormously, so that a tiny rounding error, or a tiny error in the data, ruins the answer. This chapter explains how to tell when that will happen. The key number is the condition number of a matrix, which says how many digits you can expect to lose when you solve a system with it. You met the warning sign in Chapter 10: lines that are nearly parallel.
The app solves two equations in two unknowns, then nudges the right-hand side \(\vect{b}\) by a small amount in many random directions and plots where the solution goes.
Things to try:

title: 24  Floating point and conditioning
text:
Open the condition explorer in its own tab



Compare Well conditioned, Nearly parallel and Very nearly parallel. How much does a 1% change in \(\vect{b}\) move the solution in each case? Compare that with the angle between the lines and the condition number.
Make the nudge smaller. Does the amplification change, or just the size of the cloud?
In Badly scaled, the lines are at right angles, but the condition number is 100. Why are errors amplified here? (Hint: look at the size of the numbers in the second equation.)
In Nearly parallel, change \(\vect{b}\) to \((2, -2)\). What happens to the cloud, and to the amplification?

title: 24  Floating point and conditioning
text:
24.2 The ideas

Floating-point numbers
Computers store numbers in binary scientific notation, a floating-point number \(\pm m \times 2^e\), with a fixed number of binary digits in \(m\). The standard double precision keeps 53 binary digits, about 16 decimal digits, and allows exponents up to about \(\pm 1000\) (numbers up to about \(10^{308}\)). Python’s float and MATLAB’s default numbers are double precision. Because the digits are fixed and the exponent varies, the gaps between neighbouring floating-point numbers double at each power of 2 (Figure 24.1).






Figure 24.1: All the floating-point numbers from 1 to 8 in a toy system with 3 binary digits. Each power of 2 starts a run of equally spaced numbers, with gaps twice as wide as the run before. Double precision has the same pattern, with 53 digits.



Most numbers, even simple ones like \(0.1\), can’t be stored exactly in binary, so they are rounded to the nearest floating-point number. The gap between 1 and the next larger floating-point number is the machine epsilon \[
\varepsilon = 2^{-52} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-16},
\] and rounding any number changes it by a relative amount of at most \(\varepsilon/2\). The arithmetic operations \(+\), \(-\), \(\times\) and \(\div\) give the exact result, rounded in the same way. Two consequences surprise everyone at first:

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false, because none of the three numbers is stored exactly. Never test floating-point numbers for exact equality; test whether they are close.
1 + 1e-16 == 1 is true: the small number is lost entirely, because it is below the precision of the large one.



Cancellation
Each rounding error is tiny, but some operations magnify errors that are already there. The worst is subtracting two nearly equal numbers. If \(a\) and \(b\) agree to 12 digits, \(a - b\) has only about 4 correct digits left, because the leading digits cancel and only the uncertain ones remain. This is cancellation.
The cure is to rearrange the calculation so that the subtraction doesn’t happen. For example, \(1 - \cos x\) for small \(x\) subtracts two nearly equal numbers, but \(1 - \cos x = 2\sin^2(x/2)\) doesn’t. With \(x = 10^{-8}\), \((1 - \cos x)/x^2\) evaluates to 0 on a computer, while \(2\sin^2(x/2)/x^2\) gives the correct answer, 0.5.






NoteExample 1: avoiding cancellation in the quadratic formula



The equation \(x^2 - 10^8x + 1 = 0\) has roots close to \(10^8\) and \(10^{-8}\). Explain why the formula \(x = \bigl(10^8 - \sqrt{10^{16} - 4}\bigr)/2\) gives a poor value for the small root, and find a better way.
Solution. \(\sqrt{10^{16} - 4}\) is \(10^8\) to about 16 significant digits, so the subtraction cancels almost all the digits. In double precision the formula gives \(7.45 \times 10^{-9}\), which is 25% wrong. The large root, \(\bigl(10^8 + \sqrt{10^{16} - 4}\bigr)/2\), involves no cancellation and is accurate. The product of the roots is \(c/a = 1\), so the small root is \[
x_2 = \frac{1}{x_1} = \frac{1}{10^8} = 10^{-8},
\] correct to full precision. The general rule: compute the root that adds magnitudes with the formula, and the other from \(x_1x_2 = c/a\).




Norms: the size of a vector or matrix
To talk about the size of errors in vectors, we need a measure of size. A norm \(\lVert\vect{x}\rVert\) is a length-like measure; the three in common use are \[
\lVert\vect{x}\rVert_1 = \lvert x_1\rvert + \dots + \lvert x_n\rvert,
\qquad
\lVert\vect{x}\rVert_2 = \sqrt{x_1^2 + \dots + x_n^2},
\qquad
\lVert\vect{x}\rVert_\infty = \max_i\lvert x_i\rvert.
\] The 2-norm is the usual length. The \(\infty\)-norm, the largest entry in size, is often the most natural for errors: “every entry is correct to within \(10^{-6}\)”.
The size of a matrix is measured by how much it can stretch vectors: \[
\lVert\M{A}\rVert = \max_{\vect{x} \neq \zerovec}\frac{\lVert\M{A}\vect{x}\rVert}{\lVert\vect{x}\rVert},
\] so that \(\lVert\M{A}\vect{x}\rVert \le \lVert\M{A}\rVert\,\lVert\vect{x}\rVert\) for every \(\vect{x}\). For each vector norm this gives a matrix norm, and they have simple formulas:

\(\lVert\M{A}\rVert_1\) is the largest column sum of the absolute values of the entries;
\(\lVert\M{A}\rVert_\infty\) is the largest row sum of the absolute values;
\(\lVert\M{A}\rVert_2\) is the largest singular value \(\sigma_1\) (Chapter 21).



The condition number
Suppose the right-hand side of \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) has an error \(\Delta\vect{b}\), from measurement or rounding. The solution then has an error \(\Delta\vect{x} = \M{A}^{-1}\Delta\vect{b}\). Comparing relative errors (Section C.17):






ImportantThe condition number



\[
\frac{\lVert\Delta\vect{x}\rVert}{\lVert\vect{x}\rVert} \le \kappa(\M{A})\,\frac{\lVert\Delta\vect{b}\rVert}{\lVert\vect{b}\rVert},
\qquad\text{where}\qquad
\kappa(\M{A}) = \lVert\M{A}\rVert\,\lVert\M{A}^{-1}\rVert
\] is the condition number of \(\M{A}\). In the 2-norm, \(\kappa(\M{A}) = \sigma_1/\sigma_n\).


The condition number is at least 1. It is 1 for the identity and for any orthogonal matrix, it is large when \(\M{A}\) is close to singular, and it is infinite for a singular matrix. A similar bound holds for errors in the entries of \(\M{A}\).
A useful rule of thumb follows. Double precision stores about 16 digits, and errors can be magnified by \(\kappa(\M{A})\), so






TipRule of thumb



When you solve \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) on a computer, expect to lose about \(\log_{10}\kappa(\M{A})\) of the 16 significant digits.


With \(\kappa = 10^4\) you can trust about 12 digits; with \(\kappa = 10^{12}\), about 4; with \(\kappa = 10^{16}\), perhaps none. The same reasoning applies to errors in the data: if \(\vect{b}\) comes from measurements accurate to 3 digits and \(\kappa = 1000\), the solution may have no correct digits at all, however accurately it is computed.






WarningWatch out: a small determinant is not a warning sign



A small determinant does not mean a large condition number. \(10^{-3}\M{I}\), of size \(100 \times 100\), has determinant \(10^{-300}\) but condition number 1 (Chapter 6). Use the condition number, not the determinant, to judge how much accuracy you can trust.








NoteExample 2: a condition number by hand



Find \(\kappa_\infty(\M{A})\) for \(\M{A} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1.01}\). Then solve \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) for \(\vect{b} = (2, 2.01)\T\) and for \(\vect{b} = (2, 2.02)\T\), and compare the change in \(\vect{x}\) with the bound.
Solution. \(\det\M{A} = 0.01\), so \[
\M{A}^{-1} = \frac{1}{0.01}\mat{1.01 & -1 \\ -1 & 1} = \mat{101 & -100 \\ -100 & 100}.
\] The largest absolute row sums are \(\lVert\M{A}\rVert_\infty = 2.01\) and \(\lVert\M{A}^{-1}\rVert_\infty = 201\), so \(\kappa_\infty(\M{A}) = 2.01 \times 201 = 404.01\).
For \(\vect{b} = (2, 2.01)\T\), \(\vect{x} = (1, 1)\T\). For \(\vect{b} = (2, 2.02)\T\), \(\vect{x} = \M{A}^{-1}\vect{b} = (0, 2)\T\). The relative change in \(\vect{b}\) is \(0.01/2.01 \approx 0.5\%\), but the relative change in \(\vect{x}\) is \(1/1 = 100\%\): an amplification of 201, within the bound of 404. The two lines, \(x + y = 2\) and \(x + 1.01y = 2.01\), are nearly parallel, so a small shift in one moves their crossing point a long way along them.








NoteExample 3: the Hilbert matrix



The \(n \times n\) Hilbert matrix has entries \(h_{ij} = 1/(i + j - 1)\): \[
\M{H}_3 = \mat{1 & \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{3} \\ \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{3} & \tfrac{1}{4} \\ \tfrac{1}{3} & \tfrac{1}{4} & \tfrac{1}{5}}.
\] It arises when fitting polynomials by least squares on \([0, 1]\). Choose \(\vect{x} = (1, 1, \dots, 1)\T\), compute \(\vect{b} = \M{H}\vect{x}\), and solve \(\M{H}\hat{\vect{x}} = \vect{b}\) in double precision. How accurate is \(\hat{\vect{x}}\)?
Solution. The results, from the code below:

Each time, the number of digits lost is about \(\log_{10}\kappa\), as the rule of thumb predicts. The solver is not at fault: it is backward stable, and the residuals are all around \(10^{-16}\). The Hilbert matrix is simply so close to singular that a 16-digit computer cannot tell it apart from many nearby matrices with very different solutions.




Conditioning and stability
Two different things can go wrong, and it helps to keep them apart.

A problem is ill-conditioned if small changes in its data cause large changes in its answer. This is a property of the problem itself, measured by \(\kappa(\M{A})\). No method can fix it; only better data, more digits, or reformulating the problem can.
A method is unstable if it introduces more error than the problem’s conditioning makes unavoidable. Gaussian elimination without row swaps is unstable (Chapter 25); computing \(1 - \cos x\) directly for small \(x\) is unstable.

The standard way to judge a method is backward error analysis. Instead of asking how wrong the computed answer \(\hat{\vect{x}}\) is, ask: is \(\hat{\vect{x}}\) the exact answer to a slightly different problem, \((\M{A} + \delta\M{A})\hat{\vect{x}} = \vect{b}\), with \(\delta\M{A}\) about as small as the rounding errors in storing \(\M{A}\)? If so, the method is backward stable: it has done as well as anyone could, and any remaining error is due to the problem’s conditioning. Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting is backward stable in practice, and so the error in its answer is roughly \(\kappa(\M{A})\,\varepsilon\).
One consequence is easy to miss. The residual \(\vect{r} = \vect{b} - \M{A}\hat{\vect{x}}\) measures how well \(\hat{\vect{x}}\) satisfies the equations, and a stable method always makes it tiny. But a tiny residual doesn’t mean a small error: for an ill-conditioned matrix, a vector far from the solution can still almost satisfy the equations (exercise 6).

title: 24  Floating point and conditioning
text:
24.4 Check your understanding






TipWhat is the condition number of \(\mat{2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2}\)?





1: the matrix scales every vector by 2, so relative errors are not magnified at all, even though the matrix is not the identity.









TipA system has \(\kappa(\M{A}) \approx 10^{9}\). Roughly how many correct digits should you expect in double precision?





About \(16 - 9 = 7\).









TipThe residual \(\M{A}\hat{\vect{x}} - \vect{b}\) is \(10^{-15}\). Is \(\hat{\vect{x}}\) accurate?





Not necessarily. A small residual shows the method was stable, but the error in \(\hat{\vect{x}}\) can still be up to about \(\kappa(\M{A})\) times larger, in relative terms.

title: 24  Floating point and conditioning
text:
24.5 Key ideas

Computers store numbers with about 16 significant digits, so almost every calculation is rounded; machine epsilon, about \(2.2 \times 10^{-16}\), measures the gap.
Subtracting nearly equal numbers (cancellation) loses digits, and can often be avoided by rearranging the formula.
Norms measure the size of vectors and matrices.
The condition number \(\kappa(\M{A}) = \lVert\M{A}\rVert\,\lVert\M{A}^{-1}\rVert\) measures how much errors in the data can be magnified in the solution: expect to lose about \(\log_{10}\kappa\) digits.
Ill-conditioning belongs to the problem, and no method can fix it; instability belongs to the method, and a better method can.

title: 24  Floating point and conditioning
text:
24.7 In practice

Calibration and fitting: fitting a polynomial of high degree with the powers \(1, t, t^2, \dots\) as basis functions leads to Hilbert-like matrices. Using orthogonal polynomials, or centring and scaling the data first, gives much better conditioned problems (Chapter 30).
Structural analysis: a structure with one very stiff member and one very flexible one gives a stiffness matrix with a large condition number. Analysts check condition numbers, or the warnings their software prints, before trusting results.
Statistics: when two explanatory variables in a regression are nearly proportional (collinearity), the fitted coefficients are ill-conditioned: small changes in the data swing them wildly, even though the fitted values hardly change.
Units matter: measuring one quantity in millimetres and another in kilometres can make \(\kappa\) huge for no physical reason. Rescaling the unknowns or equations to similar sizes is cheap and often fixes it.
Money: never store amounts of money as floating-point numbers of pounds or dollars; \(0.1\) can’t be stored exactly. Use whole numbers of pence or cents, or a decimal type.

title: 24  Floating point and conditioning
text:
24.8 Going further

Proofs of the condition number bound and of the formulas for \(\lVert\M{A}\rVert_1\) and \(\lVert\M{A}\rVert_\infty\): Section C.17.
Single precision keeps about 7 digits and is twice as fast, and half precision keeps about 3 and is much faster again. Machine learning uses them heavily, because its problems tolerate low accuracy. Mixed precision methods solve in low precision and then correct the answer in high precision.
Wilkinson’s backward error analysis showed in the 1960s that Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting gives the exact solution of a problem with \(\lVert\delta\M{A}\rVert\) of order \(n\varepsilon\lVert\M{A}\rVert\) times a “growth factor” that is almost always small (Chapter 25). Higham’s Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms is the standard reference.

title: 25  Pivoting
text:
25.1 Build intuition
Further
Builds on Chapter 11, Chapter 13, Chapter 24.
Gaussian elimination, as described in Chapter 11, swaps rows only when a pivot is exactly zero. On a computer that is not enough. A pivot that is merely small produces huge multipliers, which swamp the other numbers in the matrix, and the rounding errors that follow can destroy the answer, even for a perfectly well-conditioned system. The cure is cheap: before each elimination step, swap rows so that the pivot is as large as possible. This is partial pivoting, and every library solver does it.
The app carries out elimination on a pretend computer that keeps only a few significant digits, rounding after every operation, so that the effects of rounding are large enough to see. Real computers keep about 16 digits, and the same things happen to larger systems.
Things to try:

text:

title: 25  Pivoting
text:
25.2 The ideas

When elimination without swaps goes wrong
Consider \[
\begin{aligned}
10^{-20}x + y &= 1, \\
x + y &= 2,
\end{aligned}
\] whose solution is extremely close to \(x = 1\), \(y = 1\). The matrix is well conditioned (\(\kappa \approx 2.6\)). Eliminating without a swap uses the pivot \(10^{-20}\) and the multiplier \(10^{20}\): \[
(1 - 10^{20})\,y = 2 - 10^{20}.
\] In double precision, \(1 - 10^{20}\) and \(2 - 10^{20}\) both round to \(-10^{20}\): the 1 and the 2 are far below the 16 digits kept. So \(y = 1\), and then \(10^{-20}x = 1 - y = 0\) gives \(x = 0\). The second equation has been completely swamped by a huge multiple of the first.
Swapping the equations first uses the pivot 1 and the multiplier \(10^{-20}\): \[
(1 - 10^{-20})\,y = 1 - 2 \times 10^{-20},
\] which rounds to \(y = 1\), and then \(x = 2 - y = 1\). Both answers are correct to 16 digits.
The general lesson: a large multiplier magnifies the rounding errors in the pivot row, and lets them swamp the other rows. Small multipliers keep errors small.


Partial pivoting






ImportantPartial pivoting



At each step \(k\) of elimination, look at the entries in column \(k\) on and below the diagonal. Swap the row containing the largest in size into the pivot position, then eliminate as usual.


The pivot is then at least as large as every entry below it, so every multiplier is at most 1 in size. This doesn’t remove rounding errors, but it stops them from being magnified at each step.
All the row swaps can be collected into a permutation matrix \(\M{P}\), as in Chapter 13, giving \[
\M{P}\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U},
\] with every entry of \(\M{L}\) at most 1 in size. This is what scipy.linalg.lu, MATLAB’s lu, and the solvers behind np.linalg.solve and MATLAB’s backslash compute. The extra cost is tiny: searching a column takes \(n\) comparisons, while eliminating with it takes about \(n^2\) arithmetic operations.






NoteExample 1: four-digit arithmetic, with and without pivoting



Solve \[
\begin{aligned}
0.0003x + 1.566y &= 1.569, \\
0.3454x - 2.436y &= 1.018
\end{aligned}
\] rounding every result to 4 significant digits, first without pivoting and then with partial pivoting. The exact solution is \(x = 10\), \(y = 1\).
Solution. Without pivoting, the multiplier is \(0.3454/0.0003 = 1151.3\ldots\), which rounds to \(1151\). Then, rounding each product and each difference to 4 digits, \[
\begin{aligned}
a_{22} &= -2.436 - 1151 \times 1.566 \\
&= -2.436 - 1802 = -1804, \\
b_2 &= 1.018 - 1151 \times 1.569 \\
&= 1.018 - 1806 = -1805.
\end{aligned}
\] So \(y = 1805/1804 = 1.001\), and \[
x = \frac{1.569 - 1.566 \times 1.001}{0.0003} = \frac{1.569 - 1.568}{0.0003} = 3.333.
\] The small error in \(y\) was divided by the tiny pivot \(0.0003\), giving an answer for \(x\) that is 67% wrong.
With partial pivoting, \(0.3454 > 0.0003\), so swap the equations. The multiplier is \(0.0003/0.3454 = 0.0008686\), and \[
a_{22} = 1.566 + 0.0008686 \times 2.436 = 1.568,
\qquad
b_2 = 1.569 - 0.0008686 \times 1.018 = 1.568,
\] so \(y = 1.000\) and \(x = (1.018 + 2.436 \times 1.000)/0.3454 = 10.00\), correct to all 4 digits.








NoteExample 2: \(\M{P}\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}\) with partial pivoting



Factorise \(\M{A} = \mat{1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 6 & 1 \\ 4 & 8 & 6}\) with partial pivoting, and use the factors to solve \(\M{A}\vect{x} = (4, 9, 18)\T\).
Solution. In column 1 the largest entry is 4, in row 3, so swap rows 1 and 3. The multipliers are \(\ell_{21} = 2/4 = \tfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\ell_{31} = 1/4\): \[
\mat{4 & 8 & 6 \\ 2 & 6 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1}
\;\to\;
\mat{4 & 8 & 6 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -\tfrac{1}{2}}.
\] In column 2 the candidates are 2 and 0, so no swap is needed, and the multiplier is 0. So \[
\M{P} = \mat{0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0},
\qquad
\M{L} = \mat{1 & 0 & 0 \\ \tfrac{1}{2} & 1 & 0 \\ \tfrac{1}{4} & 0 & 1},
\qquad
\M{U} = \mat{4 & 8 & 6 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -\tfrac{1}{2}}.
\] Every multiplier is at most 1 in size, as promised. To solve, reorder \(\vect{b}\) in the same way, \(\M{P}\vect{b} = (18, 9, 4)\T\). Forward substitution with \(\M{L}\) gives \(\vect{y} = (18, 0, -\tfrac{1}{2})\T\), and back substitution with \(\M{U}\) gives \(\vect{x} = (1, 1, 1)\T\).




How well does it work?
Errors can still grow if the entries of the matrix grow during elimination. The growth factor is the largest entry that appears in \(\M{U}\) divided by the largest entry of \(\M{A}\). With partial pivoting it can be as large as \(2^{n-1}\): Wilkinson’s example, with 1s on the diagonal and in the last column and \(-1\)s below the diagonal, achieves it (exercise 4). In practice such matrices essentially never arise: decades of experience show growth factors stay small for real problems, which is why partial pivoting is trusted everywhere.


Scaled and complete pivoting
Partial pivoting compares the sizes of entries in one column, but that comparison can mislead when the rows are on very different scales. Multiplying an equation by \(10^6\) makes its entries look large without changing the system. Two refinements deal with this:

Scaled partial pivoting compares each candidate pivot with the largest entry in its own row, and picks the row where the pivot is largest relative to the rest of its row.
Complete pivoting searches the whole remaining submatrix for the largest entry and swaps both rows and columns to bring it into the pivot position. Its growth factor is much better bounded, but the search costs about \(n^3/3\) comparisons, so it is rarely used.

To see this, go back to the app at the start of the chapter and choose Badly scaled. Partial pivoting doesn’t help: look at the sizes of the numbers in each row, and then try Scaled partial.
A simpler and very effective alternative to scaled pivoting is to equilibrate the system first, dividing each row by its largest entry, so that all rows have similar sizes.






NoteExample 3: when partial pivoting is fooled by scaling



In 4-digit arithmetic, solve \[
\begin{aligned}
30x + 591\,400y &= 591\,700, \\
5.291x - 6.130y &= 46.78,
\end{aligned}
\] whose exact solution is \(x = 10\), \(y = 1\).
Solution. This is Example 1 with the first equation multiplied by \(10^5\). Partial pivoting compares 30 with 5.291 and makes no swap, so it repeats the mistake of Example 1: the 4-digit result is \(x = -10.00\), \(y = 1.001\). The pivot 30 looked large, but it is tiny compared with the rest of its row.
Scaled partial pivoting compares \(30/591\,400 \approx 0.00005\) with \(5.291/6.130 \approx 0.86\), swaps the equations, and gets \(x = 10.00\), \(y = 1.000\). This is Badly scaled in the app.




When pivoting isn’t needed
Two important kinds of matrix are safe without any row swaps:

Symmetric positive definite matrices (Chapter 20). Elimination never meets a small pivot, and the Cholesky factorisation \(\M{L}\M{L}\T\) needs no pivoting.
Diagonally dominant matrices, where each diagonal entry is larger in size than the sum of the other entries in its column. Partial pivoting would make no swaps, so it can be skipped, which matters for the banded systems of Chapter 26: swapping rows can widen the band.

title: 25  Pivoting
text:
25.3 In code

Run this chapter’s code yourself: open the notebook in Colab, or download the Jupyter notebook or the MATLAB script.

Adding partial pivoting to the elimination function from Chapter 11 takes three lines: find the row with the largest entry in the pivot column, and swap it into place, in both \(\M{A}\) and \(\vect{b}\).

PythonMATLAB



import numpy as np
import scipy.linalg

def solve_ge(A, b, pivot=True):
    """Solve Ax = b by Gaussian elimination, with or without partial pivoting."""
    A = np.array(A, dtype=float)
    b = np.array(b, dtype=float)
    n = len(b)
    for k in range(n - 1):
        if pivot:
            p = k + np.argmax(np.abs(A[k:, k]))   # row of the largest entry
            A[[k, p]] = A[[p, k]]                 # swap rows k and p
            b[[k, p]] = b[[p, k]]
        for i in range(k + 1, n):
            m = A[i, k] / A[k, k]
            A[i, k:] -= m * A[k, k:]
            b[i] -= m * b[k]
    x = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        x[i] = (b[i] - A[i, i + 1:] @ x[i + 1:]) / A[i, i]
    return x

A = [[1e-20, 1], [1, 1]]

print(solve_ge(A, b, pivot=True))          # right: [1, 1]

function x = solve_ge(A, b, pivot)
% Solve Ax = b by Gaussian elimination, with or without partial pivoting.
n = length(b);
for k = 1:n-1
    if pivot
        [~, p] = max(abs(A(k:n, k)));   % row of the largest entry
        p = p + k - 1;
        A([k p], :) = A([p k], :);      % swap rows k and p
        b([k p]) = b([p k]);
    end
    for i = k+1:n
        m = A(i,k) / A(k,k);
        A(i,k:n) = A(i,k:n) - m * A(k,k:n);
        b(i) = b(i) - m * b(k);
    end
end
x = zeros(n,1);
for i = n:-1:1
    x(i) = (b(i) - A(i,i+1:n) * x(i+1:n)) / A(i,i);
end
end

title: 25  Pivoting
text:
25.4 Check your understanding






TipWith partial pivoting, can a multiplier ever be larger than 1 in size?





No. The pivot is the largest entry in its column (on and below the diagonal), so each multiplier, an entry divided by the pivot, is at most 1 in size.









TipDoes pivoting help with an ill-conditioned system?





Not with its conditioning. Pivoting stops the method from adding unnecessary error; it can’t remove the sensitivity built into the problem (Chapter 24).









TipWhy doesn’t np.linalg.solve let you turn pivoting off?





Because there is no reason to: pivoting costs almost nothing and protects against disaster. The only common exceptions, symmetric positive definite matrices, have their own solver, Cholesky.

title: 25  Pivoting
text:
25.5 Key ideas

Elimination without row swaps fails at a zero pivot, and can give wildly wrong answers at a small one, because large multipliers magnify rounding errors.
Partial pivoting swaps rows so that each pivot is the largest available in its column, which keeps every multiplier at most 1 in size.
The result is written \(\M{P}\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}\), and it is what library solvers compute.
Badly scaled rows can fool partial pivoting; scaled pivoting, or rescaling the equations first, fixes this.
Symmetric positive definite and diagonally dominant matrices need no pivoting at all.

title: 25  Pivoting
text:
25.7 In practice

Every general-purpose dense solver, in LAPACK and so in NumPy, SciPy, MATLAB, R and Julia, uses partial pivoting. You get it automatically.
Sparse solvers face a trade-off: swapping rows for accuracy can destroy the sparsity that makes them fast (Chapter 26). They often use threshold pivoting, accepting any pivot at least, say, 10% of the largest in its column.
Finite element stiffness matrices are symmetric positive definite, so their solvers use Cholesky and skip pivoting altogether.
Many matrices from physical problems are diagonally dominant: heat conduction, diffusion and circuit equations, for example. Solvers for their banded systems skip pivoting safely.

title: 25  Pivoting
text:
25.8 Going further

Higham’s Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms gives the full backward error analysis of elimination with pivoting, and Trefethen and Bau’s Numerical Linear Algebra discusses why large growth factors are so rare.
Rook pivoting, a compromise between partial and complete pivoting, searches along the pivot’s row and column alternately until it finds an entry largest in both.
For symmetric matrices that are not positive definite, the Bunch–Kaufman method pivots symmetrically, using \(1 \times 1\) and \(2 \times 2\) blocks, to keep the symmetry and halve the work.

title: 26  Cost, banded and sparse systems
text:
26.1 Build intuition
Further
Builds on Chapter 11, Chapter 13.
Engineering and scientific models routinely lead to linear systems with a million unknowns: one for each point of a grid covering a wing, a reservoir or a weather system. Gaussian elimination on a full \(10^6 \times 10^6\) matrix would need about \(7 \times 10^{17}\) operations and 8 terabytes of memory. Yet such systems are solved every day, on ordinary computers, in seconds. The reason is that their matrices are sparse: almost all their entries are zero, because each grid point is connected only to its few neighbours. This chapter shows how to count the cost of a calculation, and how to exploit zeros so that most of that cost disappears.
There is no app for this chapter. Instead, consider the two matrices in Figure 26.1. Both are \(12 \times 12\), with non-zero entries only on the diagonal and in one row and one column, and in fact they are the same system with the unknowns numbered in the opposite order. Before reading the caption, predict: when you carry out elimination on each, which entries that start as zero will become non-zero?
Show the code for this figure
import numpy as np
import scipy.linalg
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

n = 12
A = np.eye(n) * 4
A[0, :] = A[:, 0] = 1
A[0, 0] = 4
B = A[::-1, ::-1]                       # number the unknowns in reverse

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(10, 2.8))
for ax, M, title in [(axes[0], A, "A"), (axes[2], B, "A, reordered")]:
    ax.spy(M, markersize=4, color="#2153b8")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
for ax, M in [(axes[1], A), (axes[3], B)]:
    P, L, U = scipy.linalg.lu(M)
    LU = np.abs(L) + np.abs(U) > 1e-12
    ax.spy(LU, markersize=4, color="#9c5208")
    ax.set_title(f"L and U: {LU.sum()} non-zeros", fontsize=10)
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 26.1: Left pair: an arrow matrix with its full row and column first, and the non-zero entries of its LU factors (L and U drawn together in one square). Elimination fills in the entire matrix. Right pair: the same matrix with the unknowns in the opposite order. Now the factors have no new non-zero entries at all.
crumbs: 26  Cost, banded and sparse systems

title: 26  Cost, banded and sparse systems
text:
26.2 The ideas

Counting operations
The running time of a numerical method is roughly proportional to the number of arithmetic operations it performs, its flops (floating-point operations). Counting them for the basic tasks:







Task
Operations (approximately)




Dot product of two vectors of length \(n\)
\(2n\)


Matrix–vector product \(\M{A}\vect{x}\), \(\M{A}\) of size \(n \times n\)
\(2n^2\)


Matrix–matrix product of two \(n \times n\) matrices
\(2n^3\)


Forward or back substitution with a triangular matrix
\(n^2\)


LU factorisation (Gaussian elimination)
\(\tfrac{2}{3}n^3\)


Inverse \(\M{A}^{-1}\)
\(2n^3\)



Only the leading power of \(n\) matters for large \(n\). An \(n^3\) method gets 8 times slower when \(n\) doubles, and 1000 times slower when \(n\) grows tenfold. A laptop does somewhere around \(10^{10}\) to \(10^{11}\) operations a second, so a dense system with \(n = 1000\) takes a few hundredths of a second, \(n = 10^4\) takes seconds, and \(n = 10^5\) takes hours and needs 80 GB just to store the matrix.
Two practical rules follow from the table.

Factorise once, solve many times. Once \(\M{L}\) and \(\M{U}\) are known, each new right-hand side costs only \(2n^2\). If you need to solve with the same matrix many times, as in a simulation stepping forward in time, keep the factors (Chapter 13).
Don’t compute the inverse to solve a system. Computing \(\M{A}^{-1}\) and then \(\M{A}^{-1}\vect{b}\) costs three times as much as elimination, and is less accurate.







NoteExample 1: how long will it take?



A dense system with \(n = 2000\) takes 0.1 seconds to solve on a certain computer. Estimate the time for \(n = 20\,000\), and the memory needed for its matrix.
Solution. The cost grows like \(n^3\), so ten times as many unknowns take \(10^3 = 1000\) times as long: about 100 seconds. The matrix has \(20\,000^2 = 4 \times 10^8\) entries of 8 bytes each, 3.2 GB. Increasing to \(n = 200\,000\) would take about a day, and 320 GB of memory, which is why large problems need sparse methods.




Banded and tridiagonal matrices
A matrix is banded if its non-zero entries all lie within a distance \(p\) of the main diagonal: \(a_{ij} = 0\) whenever \(\lvert i - j\rvert > p\). Eliminating below a pivot then involves only the \(p\) rows below it, and only the \(p\) entries to its right, so elimination without row swaps never creates non-zeros outside the band. The cost drops from \(\tfrac{2}{3}n^3\) to about \(2np^2\).
The most important case is the tridiagonal matrix, with \(p = 1:\) \[
\mat{d_1 & c_1 & & & \\ a_2 & d_2 & c_2 & & \\ & a_3 & d_3 & \ddots & \\ & & \ddots & \ddots & c_{n-1} \\ & & & a_n & d_n}.
\] Tridiagonal systems come from anything arranged in a line, where each point interacts only with its two neighbours: heat flow along a rod, a hanging cable, a chain of masses and springs, spline curves. Elimination simplifies to the Thomas algorithm: one sweep down, removing each \(a_i\), and one sweep up, back substitution.






ImportantThe Thomas algorithm



Forward sweep. Set \(c'_1 = c_1/d_1\) and \(b'_1 = b_1/d_1\). For \(i = 2, \dots, n\): \[
m = d_i - a_ic'_{i-1},
\qquad
c'_i = c_i/m,
\qquad
b'_i = (b_i - a_ib'_{i-1})/m.
\] Back substitution. Set \(x_n = b'_n\). For \(i = n-1, \dots, 1\): \(x_i = b'_i - c'_ix_{i+1}\).


It needs about \(8n\) operations instead of \(\tfrac{2}{3}n^3\): a million unknowns in a few milliseconds. It uses no pivoting, which is safe when the matrix is diagonally dominant or symmetric positive definite (Chapter 25), as it is in most applications.






NoteExample 2: the Thomas algorithm



Solve \[
\mat{2 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 2}\vect{x} = \mat{1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 1}.
\]
Solution. Here every \(d_i = 2\), \(a_i = -1\) and \(c_i = -1\). The forward sweep gives \[
\begin{aligned}
c'_1 &= -\tfrac{1}{2}, & b'_1 &= \tfrac{1}{2}, \\
m &= 2 - \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{3}{2}, & c'_2 &= -\tfrac{2}{3}, & b'_2 &= \bigl(0 + \tfrac{1}{2}\bigr)\big/\tfrac{3}{2} = \tfrac{1}{3}, \\
m &= 2 - \tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{4}{3}, & c'_3 &= -\tfrac{3}{4}, & b'_3 &= \bigl(0 + \tfrac{1}{3}\bigr)\big/\tfrac{4}{3} = \tfrac{1}{4}, \\
m &= 2 - \tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{5}{4}, & & & b'_4 &= \bigl(1 + \tfrac{1}{4}\bigr)\big/\tfrac{5}{4} = 1.
\end{aligned}
\] Back substitution: \(x_4 = 1\), \(x_3 = \tfrac{1}{4} + \tfrac{3}{4} \cdot 1 = 1\), \(x_2 = \tfrac{1}{3} + \tfrac{2}{3} \cdot 1 = 1\), \(x_1 = \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 1 = 1\). So \(\vect{x} = (1, 1, 1, 1)\T\).




Sparse matrices
A matrix is sparse when most of its entries are zero and it pays to take advantage of that. A grid of \(1000 \times 1000\) points with each point linked to its four neighbours gives a \(10^6 \times 10^6\) matrix with about \(5 \times 10^6\) non-zeros: five per row. Storing all \(10^{12}\) entries would be absurd. Instead, sparse formats store only the non-zeros and their positions. The most common, compressed sparse row (CSR), uses three lists:

the non-zero values, row by row;
the column number of each value;
for each row, where its values start in the first list (with one extra entry at the end).

For example, \[
\M{A} = \mat{5 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 & 7}
\quad\text{is stored as}\quad
\begin{aligned}
\text{values} &= (5, 1, 3, 2, 4, 6, 7), \\
\text{columns} &= (0, 3, 1, 0, 2, 2, 3), \\
\text{row starts} &= (0, 2, 3, 5, 7),
\end{aligned}
\] counting from 0, as Python does. A matrix–vector product then needs only 2 operations per non-zero.






NoteExample 3: storage for a grid problem



Heat flow on a square plate is modelled on a grid of \(500 \times 500\) interior points, each linked to its four neighbours (Figure 26.2 shows a small version). Compare the storage needed for the matrix in dense and sparse form.
Solution. There are \(n = 250\,000\) unknowns. Dense storage needs \(n^2 = 6.25 \times 10^{10}\) numbers, 500 GB. Each row has at most 5 non-zeros, so CSR stores at most \(1.25 \times 10^6\) values and \(1.25 \times 10^6\) column numbers, plus \(n + 1\) row starts: about 20 MB, 25 000 times less.






Figure 26.2: A \(4 \times 4\) version of Example 3. Each unknown is coupled only to itself and its neighbours, so row 7 of the matrix has non-zeros in columns 3, 6, 7, 8 and 11, and the matrix has five diagonals of non-zeros. On a \(500 \times 500\) grid, the proportion of non-zeros is tiny.







Fill-in and reordering
Elimination on a sparse matrix can create new non-zeros where there were zeros, called fill-in. Subtracting a multiple of the pivot row puts non-zeros wherever the pivot row has them. In the arrow matrix of Figure 26.1, the first row is full, so eliminating with it fills in the whole matrix, and the factors are dense. Numbering the unknowns in the reverse order puts the full row last, and there is no fill-in at all.
The order of the unknowns doesn’t change the solution, but it can change the cost of elimination enormously. Sparse direct solvers, such as SciPy’s spsolve and MATLAB’s backslash on a sparse matrix, first reorder the unknowns with fast heuristics (such as approximate minimum degree or nested dissection) designed to keep fill-in small, and only then factorise.
When even the reordered factors are too large, which happens for big three-dimensional problems, iterative methods take over. They need only matrix–vector products, so they never create fill-in (Chapter 27).

title: 26  Cost, banded and sparse systems
text:
26.3 In code

Run this chapter’s code yourself: open the notebook in Colab, or download the Jupyter notebook or the MATLAB script.

SciPy’s scipy.sparse module stores sparse matrices, and scipy.sparse.linalg.spsolve solves sparse systems. In MATLAB, sparse and spdiags create sparse matrices, and backslash automatically uses a sparse solver for them. The example solves \(-u'' = 1\) on \(0 < t < 1\), with \(u = 0\) at both ends, by finite differences (Chapter 33): \(n\) grid points give a tridiagonal system. Its exact solution is \(u = t(1 - t)/2\).

PythonMATLAB



import numpy as np
import scipy.sparse as sp
from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve
import time

def thomas(a, d, c, b):
    """Solve a tridiagonal system: a below, d on and c above the diagonal."""
    n = len(d)
    cp, bp = np.zeros(n), np.zeros(n)
    cp[0], bp[0] = c[0] / d[0], b[0] / d[0]
    for i in range(1, n):
        m = d[i] - a[i] * cp[i - 1]
        cp[i] = c[i] / m if i < n - 1 else 0
        bp[i] = (b[i] - a[i] * bp[i - 1]) / m
    x = np.zeros(n)
    x[-1] = bp[-1]
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        x[i] = bp[i] - cp[i] * x[i + 1]
    return x

print(thomas([0, -1, -1, -1], [2, 2, 2, 2], [-1, -1, -1, 0], [1, 0, 0, 1]))

h = 1 / (n + 1)
A = sp.diags([-1.0, 2.0, -1.0], [-1, 0, 1], shape=(n, n), format="csr")
b = h**2 * np.ones(n)
start = time.perf_counter()
u = spsolve(A, b)
print(f"sparse solve: {time.perf_counter() - start:.3f} s, {A.nnz} non-zeros")
t = np.arange(1, n + 1) * h

title: 26  Cost, banded and sparse systems
text:
26.4 Check your understanding






TipSolving one dense system with \(n = 500\) takes 10 ms. About how long for \(n = 1000\)?





About 80 ms: doubling \(n\) multiplies the \(n^3\) cost by 8.









TipWhy is computing \(\M{A}^{-1}\vect{b}\) a bad way to solve \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\), even for one right-hand side?





It costs about \(2n^3\) operations instead of \(\tfrac{2}{3}n^3\), and it is less accurate. For a sparse matrix it is far worse: the inverse is usually completely full.









TipHow many operations does a matrix–vector product take for a sparse matrix with \(N\) non-zeros?





About \(2N\): one multiplication and one addition per non-zero, whatever the size of the matrix.
crumbs: 26  Cost, banded and sparse systems

title: 26  Cost, banded and sparse systems
text:
26.5 Key ideas

Counting operations predicts running times: dense elimination costs about \(\tfrac{2}{3}n^3\), so it slows down quickly as \(n\) grows.
A tridiagonal system can be solved by the Thomas algorithm in time proportional to \(n\).
Sparse matrices are stored by their non-zero entries only, which can save almost all of the memory and the work.
Elimination can create new non-zeros (fill-in), and reordering the unknowns can reduce it a great deal.
Choose a solver to match the structure: dense for small or full matrices, banded or sparse when most entries are zero.

title: 26  Cost, banded and sparse systems
text:
26.7 In practice

Finite differences and finite elements turn differential equations into sparse systems: tridiagonal for problems in a line, banded or more general sparse patterns in two and three dimensions (Chapter 33).
Circuit simulation packages, such as SPICE, solve sparse systems with one unknown per node, because each component touches only two nodes (Chapter 32).
Networks: the link matrices of road networks, power grids and the web are extremely sparse; the web’s has billions of rows and a few dozen non-zeros in each (Chapter 35).
Splines: drawing a smooth cubic curve through \(n\) points needs a tridiagonal solve, which is why spline routines are so fast.
GPUs do dense matrix multiplication at enormous speed, so for medium-sized problems a dense method on a GPU can beat a sparse one on a CPU. Counting operations is a guide, not the final word.
crumbs: 26  Cost, banded and sparse systems

title: 26  Cost, banded and sparse systems
text:
26.8 Going further

Davis’s Direct Methods for Sparse Linear Systems explains sparse factorisations and the reordering methods behind spsolve and backslash, with code.
Strassen’s algorithm multiplies matrices in about \(n^{2.81}\) operations instead of \(2n^3\), by a clever way of combining \(2 \times 2\) blocks. Methods with even lower powers exist, but only win for impractically large \(n\).
Modern computers are often limited by moving data rather than by arithmetic, so libraries arrange calculations in blocks that fit in fast memory. This is why a library routine can be 100 times faster than the same operation count in a simple loop.

title: 27  Iterative methods
text:
27.1 Build intuition
Further
Builds on Chapter 19, Chapter 26.
Gaussian elimination is a direct method: after a fixed number of steps it gives the answer, up to rounding. For the very large sparse systems of Chapter 26, that fixed number of steps can be too many, because fill-in makes the factors too big to store. Iterative methods take a different approach. They start from a guess and improve it, step after step, using nothing but multiplications by the original sparse matrix, so they never create fill-in. They give an approximate answer, but you choose how accurate, and often a few hundred cheap steps beat one enormous factorisation.
The app solves two equations in two unknowns by three iterative methods: each starts from a guess and improves it, step by step. It draws each guess as a point in the plane; the solution is where the two lines cross. The methods are called Jacobi, Gauss–Seidel and SOR, and this chapter explains how each one works. For now, just watch what they do.
Things to try:

title: 27  Iterative methods

title: 27  Iterative methods
text:
27.2 The ideas

Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel
Solve the \(i\)th equation for the \(i\)th unknown. For the system \[
\begin{aligned}
4x_1 + x_2 &= 5, \\
2x_1 + 5x_2 &= 7,
\end{aligned}
\qquad\text{this gives}\qquad
\begin{aligned}
x_1 &= (5 - x_2)/4, \\
x_2 &= (7 - 2x_1)/5.
\end{aligned}
\] The Jacobi method uses these as update rules: put the current guess into the right-hand sides to get the next guess. The Gauss–Seidel method does the same, but uses each new value as soon as it has been computed: the new \(x_1\) is used straight away to compute the new \(x_2\). Gauss–Seidel usually converges faster, and needs only one copy of the vector in memory.
In matrix form, split \(\M{A} = \M{D} + \M{L} + \M{U}\) into its diagonal \(\M{D}\), its strictly lower triangular part \(\M{L}\) and its strictly upper triangular part \(\M{U}\). (These \(\M{L}\) and \(\M{U}\) are not the LU factors.) Then \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Jacobi:}\quad & \M{D}\vect{x}_{k+1} = \vect{b} - (\M{L} + \M{U})\vect{x}_k, \\
\text{Gauss–Seidel:}\quad & (\M{D} + \M{L})\vect{x}_{k+1} = \vect{b} - \M{U}\vect{x}_k.
\end{aligned}
\] Each step solves a diagonal or triangular system, which is cheap, and multiplies by sparse matrices, which is cheap too.






NoteExample 1: Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel by hand



Take three steps of each method for the system above, starting from \(\vect{x}_0 = (0, 0)\T\). The solution is \((1, 1)\T\).
Solution. Jacobi uses the old values in both formulas: \[
\vect{x}_1 = \mat{5/4 \\ 7/5} = \mat{1.25 \\ 1.4},
\quad
\vect{x}_2 = \mat{(5 - 1.4)/4 \\ (7 - 2.5)/5} = \mat{0.9 \\ 0.9},
\quad
\vect{x}_3 = \mat{1.025 \\ 1.04}.
\] Gauss–Seidel uses the new \(x_1\) at once: \[
\vect{x}_1 = \mat{1.25 \\ (7 - 2.5)/5} = \mat{1.25 \\ 0.9},
\quad
\vect{x}_2 = \mat{(5 - 0.9)/4 \\ (7 - 2.05)/5} = \mat{1.025 \\ 0.99},
\quad
\vect{x}_3 = \mat{1.0025 \\ 0.999}.
\] After three steps, Jacobi’s error is about 0.04 and Gauss–Seidel’s about 0.0025. The matrix is strictly diagonally dominant (\(4 > 1\) and \(5 > 2\)), so both are sure to converge.




When do they converge?
Both methods have the form \(\vect{x}_{k+1} = \M{T}\vect{x}_k + \vect{c}\), for an iteration matrix \(\M{T}\): \(\M{T}_J = -\M{D}^{-1}(\M{L} + \M{U})\) for Jacobi and \(\M{T}_{GS} = -(\M{D} + \M{L})^{-1}\M{U}\) for Gauss–Seidel. The exact solution \(\vect{x}\) satisfies \(\vect{x} = \M{T}\vect{x} + \vect{c}\), so subtracting, the error \(\vect{e}_k = \vect{x}_k - \vect{x}\) obeys \[
\vect{e}_{k+1} = \M{T}\vect{e}_k,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\vect{e}_k = \M{T}^k\vect{e}_0.
\] This is a matrix power again (Chapter 19), and its behaviour is set by the eigenvalues of \(\M{T}\). The spectral radius \(\rho(\M{T})\) is the largest of their absolute values.






ImportantConvergence of an iterative method



The iteration converges from every starting guess if and only if \(\rho(\M{T}) < 1\). The error then shrinks by a factor of about \(\rho(\M{T})\) per step, so gaining one more correct digit takes about \(-1/\log_{10}\rho(\M{T})\) steps.


Finding \(\rho(\M{T})\) is as hard as solving the system, so a simple sufficient condition is useful. A matrix is strictly diagonally dominant if, in every row, the diagonal entry is larger in size than the sum of the sizes of the other entries: \[
\lvert a_{ii}\rvert > \sum_{j \neq i}\lvert a_{ij}\rvert \quad\text{for every } i.
\] For such matrices, both Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel are sure to converge (Section C.18). Gauss–Seidel also always converges for symmetric positive definite matrices. Reordering the equations can sometimes make a matrix diagonally dominant, as Diverges in the app shows.






NoteExample 2: the spectral radius



Find the iteration matrices for Example 1 and their spectral radii.
Solution. Here \(\M{D} = \mat{4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5}\), \(\M{L} = \mat{0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0}\) and \(\M{U} = \mat{0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0}\). For Jacobi, \[
\M{T}_J = -\M{D}^{-1}(\M{L} + \M{U}) = \mat{0 & -\tfrac{1}{4} \\ -\tfrac{2}{5} & 0},
\] with \(\lambda^2 = \tfrac{1}{10}\), so \(\rho(\M{T}_J) = 1/\sqrt{10} \approx 0.316\). For Gauss–Seidel, \[
\M{T}_{GS} = -(\M{D} + \M{L})^{-1}\M{U} = -\mat{4 & 0 \\ 2 & 5}^{-1}\mat{0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0} = \mat{0 & -\tfrac{1}{4} \\ 0 & \tfrac{1}{10}},
\] which is triangular, with eigenvalues 0 and \(\tfrac{1}{10}\), so \(\rho(\M{T}_{GS}) = 0.1 = \rho(\M{T}_J)^2\). Each Gauss–Seidel step gains one correct digit, and each Jacobi step about half a digit, as Example 1 shows.




Successive over-relaxation
When convergence is slow, Gauss–Seidel’s steps all point the right way but are too short. Successive over-relaxation (SOR) stretches each one by a factor \(\omega\): it computes the Gauss–Seidel value for each unknown and then moves \(\omega\) times as far from the old value, \[
x_i^{\text{new}} = (1 - \omega)x_i^{\text{old}} + \omega\,x_i^{\text{Gauss–Seidel}}.
\] With \(\omega = 1\) this is Gauss–Seidel. It converges only for \(0 < \omega < 2\), and the best \(\omega\) is usually between 1 and 2. For many matrices from grid problems, including the examples here, the best value is \[
\omega_{\text{best}} = \frac{2}{1 + \sqrt{1 - \rho(\M{T}_J)^2}},
\] and it can cut the number of steps from thousands to a hundred or so.
Now that you know how the three methods work, go back to the app. Here it is again.

NoteExample 3: a larger problem



The tridiagonal system \(-x_{i-1} + 2x_i - x_{i+1} = b_i\) with \(n = 50\) unknowns models the temperature along a heated rod (Chapter 33). How many steps does each method need to reduce the residual by a factor of \(10^6\)?
Solution. For this matrix \(\rho(\M{T}_J) = \cos\bigl(\pi/(n + 1)\bigr) \approx 0.9981\), desperately close to 1. The code below gives:

The matrix is only just diagonally dominant (2 is equal to, not greater than, \(1 + 1\) in the middle rows), and its condition number grows like \(n^2\), which is why the simple methods are so slow. For this small problem a direct tridiagonal solve (Chapter 26) is better than any of them; the comparison matters for large two- and three-dimensional problems, where direct methods become too expensive.




Conjugate gradients
For symmetric positive definite systems, the most important iterative method is the conjugate gradient method (CG). Chapter 22 showed that solving \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) is the same as minimising \(f(\vect{x}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b}\T\vect{x}\), and that gradient descent zigzags when the contours are long, thin ellipses. CG fixes the zigzag.
Each step searches along a direction chosen to be conjugate to all the earlier ones, \(\vect{p}_i\T\M{A}\vect{p}_j = 0\), which means that minimising along the new direction never spoils the minimisation already done along the old ones.
In exact arithmetic it reaches the solution in at most \(n\) steps, and in practice it gets close far sooner: the number of steps needed grows like \(\sqrt{\kappa(\M{A})}\), compared with \(\kappa(\M{A})\) for Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel. Each step costs one multiplication by \(\M{A}\) and a few vector operations.
For matrices that are not symmetric, GMRES and BiCGSTAB play the same role. Together these are called Krylov methods, because they build their answers from the vectors \(\vect{b}, \M{A}\vect{b}, \M{A}^2\vect{b}, \dots\)


When to stop, and which method to use
An iteration needs a stopping rule. The usual one stops when the residual is small compared with the right-hand side, \(\lVert\vect{b} - \M{A}\vect{x}_k\rVert \le \text{tol} \times \lVert\vect{b}\rVert\). Remember that a small residual means a small error only if \(\M{A}\) is well conditioned (Chapter 24).
As a rough guide:

For small and medium systems (up to perhaps \(10^4\) unknowns, or \(10^5\) to \(10^6\) if sparse in a two-dimensional pattern), use a direct solver: it is reliable and needs no tuning.
For very large sparse systems, especially from three-dimensional problems, use a Krylov method with a good preconditioner (below).
Jacobi, Gauss–Seidel and SOR are rarely used alone today, but they are the building blocks of preconditioners and multigrid methods, and they show how all iterative methods behave.

title: 27  Iterative methods
27  Iterative methods
text:
27.4 Check your understanding






TipIs \(\mat{3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 3}\) strictly diagonally dominant?





Yes: in each row the diagonal entry wins, since \(3 > 1 + 1\), \(4 > 1 + 2\) and \(3 > 0 + 2\).









TipAn iteration has \(\rho(\M{T}) = 0.9\). About how many steps does it need to reduce the error by a factor of \(10^6\)?





About \(6/(-\log_{10}0.9) \approx 131\) steps.









TipWhy don’t iterative methods suffer from fill-in?





They never change the matrix: they only multiply vectors by it (and by its diagonal or triangular parts), so its zeros stay zero.

title: 27  Iterative methods
text:
27.5 Key ideas

Iterative methods improve a guess step by step. Jacobi updates every unknown from the old values; Gauss–Seidel uses each new value as soon as it has it.
Both converge for every starting guess exactly when the spectral radius of their iteration matrix is less than 1; strict diagonal dominance guarantees this.
The closer the spectral radius is to 1, the slower the convergence, and SOR with a well-chosen \(\omega\) can speed it up enormously.
For symmetric positive definite systems, the conjugate gradient method is the method of choice.
Iterative methods pay off for large sparse systems, where direct elimination would fill in.

title: 27  Iterative methods
text:
27.7 In practice

Heat flow, groundwater flow and electrostatics on large two- and three-dimensional grids lead to huge sparse symmetric positive definite systems, usually solved with preconditioned CG.
Multigrid methods use a few Jacobi or Gauss–Seidel steps to remove the rapidly varying part of the error, then correct the slowly varying part on a coarser grid. They can solve grid problems in a number of operations proportional to \(n\), the best possible.
Computational fluid dynamics codes use GMRES and BiCGSTAB with preconditioners for the non-symmetric systems from flow equations.
PageRank and many network calculations are iterative methods applied to enormous sparse matrices (Chapter 35).
Each step is parallel: a Jacobi step updates every unknown independently, which suits graphics cards and supercomputers well.

title: 27  Iterative methods
text:
27.8 Going further

Proofs that \(\rho(\M{T}) < 1\) is needed for convergence, and that Jacobi converges for strictly diagonally dominant matrices: Section C.18.
Preconditioning replaces \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) by \(\M{M}^{-1}\M{A}\vect{x} = \M{M}^{-1}\vect{b}\), where \(\M{M}\) is an approximation to \(\M{A}\) that is easy to solve with, such as its diagonal, or an incomplete LU factorisation that discards fill-in. A good preconditioner makes \(\M{M}^{-1}\M{A}\) close to \(\M{I}\) and so well conditioned, and Krylov methods then converge in a handful of steps.
Saad’s Iterative Methods for Sparse Linear Systems (freely available from the author) and Shewchuk’s An Introduction to the Conjugate Gradient Method Without the Agonizing Pain are good next steps.

title: 28  Newton’s method for nonlinear systems
text:
28.1 Build intuition
Further
Builds on Chapter 11, Chapter 22.
Most of this book is about linear equations, but most of the world is not linear. The angles of a robot arm that put its hand at a given point, the voltages in a circuit with diodes, the concentrations in a chemical equilibrium and the shape of a cable under load all satisfy nonlinear equations. Newton’s method solves them by turning the nonlinear problem into a sequence of linear ones. At each step it replaces the equations by their best linear approximation, the Jacobian of Chapter 22, and solves that linear system. Close to a solution it is astonishingly fast: the number of correct digits roughly doubles at every step.
The app colours each starting point in the plane by the solution that Newton’s method reaches from it. Click anywhere to see the steps from that point, and the table of how quickly they close in.

title: 28  Newton’s method for nonlinear systems
text:
28.2 The ideas

One equation
For one equation \(f(x) = 0\), Newton’s method replaces \(f\) near the current guess \(x_k\) by its tangent line, \(f(x_k) + f'(x_k)(x - x_k)\), and takes the point where the tangent crosses zero as the next guess: \[
x_{k+1} = x_k - \frac{f(x_k)}{f'(x_k)}.
\] For \(f(x) = x^2 - 2\), starting at \(x_0 = 1\), this gives \(1.5\), \(1.41667\), \(1.4142157\) and \(1.41421356237469\): correct digits 0, 1, 3, 6, 12. Each step roughly doubles them.


Systems
For \(n\) equations in \(n\) unknowns, \(\vect{f}(\vect{x}) = \zerovec\), the tangent line becomes the linear approximation of Chapter 22: \[
\vect{f}(\vect{x}_k + \Delta\vect{x}) \approx \vect{f}(\vect{x}_k) + \M{J}(\vect{x}_k)\,\Delta\vect{x},
\] where \(\M{J}\) is the Jacobian, the matrix of partial derivatives \(\partial f_i/\partial x_j\). Setting the approximation to zero gives a linear system for the step.






ImportantNewton’s method for systems



Starting from a guess \(\vect{x}_0\), repeat:

solve the linear system \(\M{J}(\vect{x}_k)\,\Delta\vect{x} = -\vect{f}(\vect{x}_k)\);
set \(\vect{x}_{k+1} = \vect{x}_k + \Delta\vect{x}\);

until \(\lVert\vect{f}(\vect{x}_k)\rVert\) or \(\lVert\Delta\vect{x}\rVert\) is small enough.


Never compute \(\M{J}^{-1}\): solve the system, by elimination for small problems or by the sparse and iterative methods of Chapter 26 and Chapter 27 for large ones. Each Newton step costs one Jacobian and one linear solve, so all of Parts II to V are at work inside it.






NoteExample 1: a circle and a hyperbola



Find where the circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 4\) meets the hyperbola \(xy = 1\), starting from \((2, 0.5)\) (Figure 28.1).






Figure 28.1: The circle and the hyperbola of Example 1 meet at four points (dots). Newton’s method from \((2, 0.5)\) (cross) converges to the nearest one. The steps are too small to see at this scale.



Solution. Write the equations as \(\vect{f}(x, y) = (x^2 + y^2 - 4, \; xy - 1)\T = \zerovec\). The Jacobian is \[
\M{J} = \mat{2x & 2y \\ y & x}.
\] At \((2, 0.5)\), \(\vect{f} = (0.25, 0)\T\) and \(\M{J} = \mat{4 & 1 \\ 0.5 & 2}\), with determinant 7.5. Solving \(\M{J}\,\Delta\vect{x} = -\vect{f}\), \[
\Delta\vect{x} = -\frac{1}{7.5}\mat{2 & -1 \\ -0.5 & 4}\mat{0.25 \\ 0} = \mat{-0.0667 \\ 0.0167},
\qquad
\vect{x}_1 = \mat{1.9333 \\ 0.5167}.
\] Continuing (see the code below):

The residual is roughly squared at each step, and three steps give 12 correct digits. The exact root is \(\bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt{6} + \sqrt{2}}{2}, \tfrac{\sqrt{6} - \sqrt{2}}{2}\bigr)\), which you can find by noticing that \((x + y)^2 = 6\) and \((x - y)^2 = 2\).








NoteExample 2: a robot arm



A planar robot arm has two links of length 1. The first link makes angle \(\theta_1\) with the \(x\) axis, and the second makes angle \(\theta_2\) with the first. Find angles that put the hand at \((1.2, 0.8)\).
Solution. The hand is at \((\cos\theta_1 + \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2), \; \sin\theta_1 + \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2))\), so we solve \[
\vect{f}(\theta_1, \theta_2) = \mat{\cos\theta_1 + \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2) - 1.2 \\ \sin\theta_1 + \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2) - 0.8} = \zerovec,
\] with Jacobian, writing \(s_1 = \sin\theta_1\), \(c_1 = \cos\theta_1\), \(s_{12} = \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)\) and \(c_{12} = \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2)\), \[
\M{J} = \mat{-s_1 - s_{12} & -s_{12} \\ c_1 + c_{12} & c_{12}}.
\] Starting from \((\theta_1, \theta_2) = (0, 1)\), the residual goes \(0.34\), \(0.098\), \(0.0035\), \(5.6 \times 10^{-6}\), \(1.5 \times 10^{-11}\), and the angles converge to \(\theta_1 = -0.1774\) and \(\theta_2 = 1.5308\) radians (\(-10.16°\) and \(87.71°\)). Check with the cosine rule: the distance to the target is \(d = \sqrt{1.2^2 + 0.8^2}\), and \(\cos\theta_2 = (d^2 - 2)/2 = 0.04\), so \(\theta_2 = 1.5308\). ✓ Starting from a negative \(\theta_2\) finds the other solution, with the elbow bent the other way (Figure 28.2). In a robot controller, the starting guess is the arm’s current position, so Newton’s method finds the nearby solution and the arm moves smoothly.






Figure 28.2: The two solutions of Example 2. Newton’s method from \((0, 1)\) finds the solid one, with \(\theta_1 = -10.16°\) (below the \(x\) axis) and \(\theta_2 = 87.71°\); starting with a negative \(\theta_2\) finds the dashed one, with the elbow bent the other way.







Quadratic convergence
Near a root \(\vect{x}^*\) where the Jacobian is invertible, Newton’s method converges quadratically: there is a constant \(C\) with \[
\lVert\vect{x}_{k+1} - \vect{x}^*\rVert \le C\,\lVert\vect{x}_k - \vect{x}^*\rVert^2.
\] If the error is \(10^{-3}\), the next is about \(10^{-6}\), then \(10^{-12}\). The reason is that the linear approximation is wrong only by terms of second order in \(\Delta\vect{x}\), so the step it gives is wrong only by that much (Section C.19). By contrast, the iterations of Chapter 27 converge linearly: the error is multiplied by a fixed factor at each step, adding a fixed number of digits.


When Newton’s method fails
The guarantee holds only near a root. Further away, several things can go wrong:

A singular Jacobian. If \(\M{J}(\vect{x}_k)\) is singular, the linear system has no unique solution and the method breaks down. Near such points the steps are huge and throw the guess far away. In the app’s Circle and hyperbola, the Jacobian is singular along the lines \(y = \pm x\), which is why the colours change there.
A bad start. From a poor starting guess, the steps can wander, cycle or run off to infinity, or reach a different root from the one you wanted. The basins of attraction, the sets of starting points that lead to each root, can have very complicated, fractal boundaries, as Cube roots of 1 shows.
No root nearby. If the equations have no solution near the start, Newton’s method has nothing to converge to, and wanders.
Multiple roots. Where the Jacobian at the root itself is singular, convergence slows to linear.

So a good starting guess matters. In engineering, it usually comes from physical insight, a simplified model, or the solution of a nearby problem: solving a sequence of problems that change gradually from an easy one to the one you want, starting each from the last answer, is called continuation.






NoteExample 3: where the Jacobian is singular



For the system of Example 1, where is the Jacobian singular? What happens if Newton’s method is started at \((1, 1)\)?
Solution. \(\det\M{J} = x^2 - y^2\), which is zero on the lines \(y = x\) and \(y = -x\). At \((1, 1)\), \(\M{J} = \mat{2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1}\) is singular, so the very first step can’t be computed. Here \(\vect{f}(1, 1) = (-2, 0)\T\), and the linear approximations to the two equations are the parallel lines \(2\Delta x + 2\Delta y = 2\) and \(\Delta x + \Delta y = 0\), which never meet. Starting near the line \(y = x\) gives a nearly singular Jacobian and a huge first step. By symmetry, the four roots lie two on each side of each line, so these lines form the boundaries of the basins of attraction in the app.




Practical Newton’s method
Real implementations add three refinements.

Damping. If the full step makes \(\lVert\vect{f}\rVert\) larger, try half the step, then a quarter, and so on, until it decreases. This line search makes the method far more robust from poor starts, and costs nothing near the root, where the full step is always accepted.
Finite-difference Jacobians. If the derivatives are hard to work out, approximate column \(j\) of \(\M{J}\) by \(\bigl(\vect{f}(\vect{x} + h\ue{j}) - \vect{f}(\vect{x})\bigr)/h\) for a small \(h\), typically \(h \approx 10^{-8}\) times the size of \(x_j\). This costs \(n\) extra evaluations of \(\vect{f}\) per step, and convergence is still very fast.
Quasi-Newton methods. Methods such as Broyden’s method avoid computing the Jacobian at every step. They start with an approximation and update it cheaply after each step, using the change in \(\vect{f}\) that the step produced.

Library solvers, scipy.optimize.fsolve and root in Python and fsolve in MATLAB’s Optimization Toolbox, combine all of these.

28.3 In code

Run this chapter’s code yourself: open the notebook in Colab, or download the Jupyter notebook or the MATLAB script.


PythonMATLAB



import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import fsolve

def f(v):
    x, y = v
    return np.array([x**2 + y**2 - 4, x * y - 1])

def J(v):
    x, y = v
    return np.array([[2 * x, 2 * y], [y, x]])

x = np.array([2, 0.5])
for k in range(5):
    print(f"{k}  {x[0]:.12f}  {x[1]:.12f}  {np.linalg.norm(f(x)):.1e}")
    x = x - np.linalg.solve(J(x), f(x))        # solve, don't invert

print(fsolve(f, [2, 0.5]))                     # library solver

title: 28  Newton’s method for nonlinear systems
text:
28.4 Check your understanding






TipThe errors of an iteration are \(10^{-2}\), \(10^{-4}\), \(10^{-8}\). Is the convergence linear or quadratic?





Quadratic: each error is about the square of the one before, so the number of correct digits doubles.









TipWhat is the Jacobian of a linear system \(\vect{f}(\vect{x}) = \M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b}\), and what does Newton’s method do with it?





The Jacobian is \(\M{A}\), and the linear approximation is exact, so Newton’s method lands on the solution in one step, whatever the start.









TipWhy is it a bad idea to stop Newton’s method only when \(\lVert\Delta\vect{x}\rVert\) is small?





A tiny step can also mean the Jacobian is very large, or the method has stalled. It is safer to also check that \(\lVert\vect{f}(\vect{x})\rVert\) is small.
crumbs: 28  Newton's method for nonlinear systems

title: 28  Newton’s method for nonlinear systems
text:
28.5 Key ideas

Newton’s method replaces a nonlinear system by its linear approximation at the current guess, and solves \(\M{J}\,\Delta\vect{x} = -\vect{f}(\vect{x})\) for the step.
Near a solution where the Jacobian is invertible, it converges quadratically: the number of correct digits roughly doubles at each step.
It can fail from a poor starting guess, or where the Jacobian is singular or nearly so.
In practice, damped steps, finite-difference Jacobians and library solvers make it robust.

title: 28  Newton’s method for nonlinear systems
text:
28.7 In practice

Circuit simulation: SPICE and its descendants find the voltages in circuits with diodes and transistors by Newton’s method, solving a sparse linear system at every step (Chapter 32).
Structural mechanics: large deflections and nonlinear materials lead to nonlinear finite element equations, solved by Newton’s method with the tangent stiffness matrix as the Jacobian.
Robotics: inverse kinematics, finding joint angles that place a tool at a target, is solved by Newton-like steps many times a second (Chapter 34).
Chemistry: equilibrium concentrations in reacting mixtures satisfy nonlinear mass-action equations, solved by damped Newton methods.
Implicit time stepping: stiff differential equations (Chapter 23) are stepped forward by solving a nonlinear system at each time step, by Newton’s method.
crumbs: 28  Newton's method for nonlinear systems

title: 28  Newton’s method for nonlinear systems
text:
28.8 Going further

A proof of quadratic convergence: Section C.19.
Applying Newton’s method to \(\nabla g = \zerovec\) gives Newton’s method for optimisation, \(\M{H}\,\Delta\vect{x} = -\nabla g\), which uses the Hessian to choose both the direction and the length of each step and so avoids the zigzag of gradient descent (Chapter 22). Quasi-Newton optimisers, such as BFGS, build up approximations to the Hessian, and are the default in scipy.optimize.minimize.
Kelley’s Solving Nonlinear Equations with Newton’s Method is a short, practical guide; Dennis and Schnabel’s Numerical Methods for Unconstrained Optimization and Nonlinear Equations is the classic.

title: 29  Eigenvalue algorithms
text:
29.1 Build intuition
Further
Builds on Chapter 13, Chapter 18, Chapter 19.
In Chapter 18, eigenvalues were found as the roots of the characteristic polynomial. That works by hand for \(2 \times 2\) and \(3 \times 3\) matrices, but it is useless on a computer: there is no formula for the roots of polynomials of degree 5 or more, and the roots are extremely sensitive to rounding errors in the coefficients. Software instead finds eigenvalues by iteration, improving approximations to eigenvectors step by step. This chapter describes the simplest such method, the power method, its powerful variants, and the QR algorithm that runs inside eig in every numerical library.
The app repeatedly multiplies a vector by a \(2 \times 2\) matrix and rescales the result to length 1, so you can watch the direction settle onto an eigenvector.
Things to try:

title: 29  Eigenvalue algorithms
text:
Open the power method app in its own tab



In Symmetric, take a few steps. Which eigenvector does the direction approach? Compare the column of errors with the factor given below the table.
Compare Symmetric with Close eigenvalues. Which converges faster, and why?
In Negative dominant, the arrow flips at every step. Is it still converging?
In Equal sizes, the two eigenvalues are the same size. What does the power method do?

title: 29  Eigenvalue algorithms
text:
29.2 The ideas

The power method
Chapter 19 showed that multiplying a vector by \(\M{A}\) over and over brings it into line with the eigenvector of the dominant eigenvalue, the one largest in size. Writing \(\vect{x}_0 = c_1\vect{v}_1 + \dots + c_n\vect{v}_n\) in terms of the eigenvectors, \[
\M{A}^k\vect{x}_0 = c_1\lambda_1^k\vect{v}_1 + c_2\lambda_2^k\vect{v}_2 + \dots = \lambda_1^k\left(c_1\vect{v}_1 + c_2\Bigl(\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\Bigr)^k\vect{v}_2 + \cdots\right),
\] and if \(\lvert\lambda_1\rvert > \lvert\lambda_2\rvert \ge \dots\), all the terms but the first die away. The vector itself grows or shrinks like \(\lambda_1^k\), so to stop it overflowing, the power method rescales it to length 1 at every step:






ImportantThe power method



Start with any vector \(\vect{q}_0\) of length 1. Repeat: \[
\vect{y} = \M{A}\vect{q}_k,
\qquad
\vect{q}_{k+1} = \vect{y}/\lVert\vect{y}\rVert.
\] \(\vect{q}_k\) approaches the dominant eigenvector (up to sign), and the error shrinks by a factor of about \(\lvert\lambda_2/\lambda_1\rvert\) per step.


Each step costs one matrix–vector product, cheap even for huge sparse matrices. The weakness is speed: if \(\lvert\lambda_2/\lambda_1\rvert = 0.99\), gaining each digit takes about 230 steps. The method also fails if \(c_1 = 0\) (in practice, rounding errors soon introduce some \(\vect{v}_1\)), and if two eigenvalues share the largest size, as with \(\pm\lambda\) or a complex pair.






NoteExample 1: the power method by hand



Apply the power method to \(\M{A} = \mat{2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3}\), starting from \(\vect{q}_0 = (1, 0)\T\), and estimate the dominant eigenvalue with the Rayleigh quotient.
Solution. The eigenvalues are \((5 \pm \sqrt{5})/2\), about 3.618 and 1.382. \[
\begin{aligned}
\M{A}\vect{q}_0 &= (2, 1)\T, & \vect{q}_1 &= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2, 1)\T, & r &= \tfrac{1}{5}(2, 1)\mat{5 \\ 5} = 3, \\
\M{A}\vect{q}_1 &= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(5, 5)\T, & \vect{q}_2 &= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1)\T, & r &= \tfrac{1}{2}(1, 1)\mat{3 \\ 4} = 3.5, \\
\M{A}\vect{q}_2 &= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(3, 4)\T, & \vect{q}_3 &= (0.6, 0.8)\T, & r &= (0.6, 0.8)\mat{2 \\ 3} = 3.6.
\end{aligned}
\] The next estimates are 3.6154 and 3.6176. The errors in the estimates, 0.618, 0.118, 0.018, 0.0026, shrink by a factor of about 0.146 each step. That is \((1.382/3.618)^2\): the square of the factor for the vectors, because \(\M{A}\) is symmetric.




The Rayleigh quotient
Given an approximate eigenvector \(\vect{q}\) of length 1, the best estimate of its eigenvalue is the Rayleigh quotient \[
r(\vect{q}) = \vect{q}\T\M{A}\vect{q},
\] the number \(\lambda\) that makes \(\M{A}\vect{q} - \lambda\vect{q}\) as short as possible. If \(\vect{q}\) is an exact eigenvector, \(r(\vect{q}) = \lambda\). For a symmetric matrix, the Rayleigh quotient is especially accurate: if \(\vect{q}\) is wrong by a small amount \(\delta\), \(r(\vect{q})\) is wrong only by an amount proportional to \(\delta^2\). So the eigenvalue estimates converge twice as fast as the vectors, gaining digits at twice the rate.


Inverse iteration and shifts
The eigenvalues of \(\M{A}^{-1}\) are \(1/\lambda_i\), with the same eigenvectors (Chapter 18, exercise 4). So the power method applied to \(\M{A}^{-1}\) finds the eigenvalue of \(\M{A}\) smallest in size. This is inverse iteration. Each step needs \(\vect{y} = \M{A}^{-1}\vect{q}_k\), but, as always, don’t form the inverse: factorise \(\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}\) once, and solve \(\M{A}\vect{y} = \vect{q}_k\) with the factors at each step (Chapter 13).
A shift makes this far more useful. The eigenvalues of \(\M{A} - \mu\M{I}\) are \(\lambda_i - \mu\), so inverse iteration with \(\M{A} - \mu\M{I}\) finds the eigenvalue of \(\M{A}\) closest to \(\mu\). The error factor per step is \[
\frac{\lvert\lambda_{\text{closest}} - \mu\rvert}{\lvert\lambda_{\text{next closest}} - \mu\rvert},
\] which is tiny when \(\mu\) is a good guess. Shifted inverse iteration can find any eigenvalue you have a rough estimate of, and is the standard way to find an eigenvector once its eigenvalue is known accurately.
To see it, go back to the app at the start of the chapter and choose Equal sizes, where the power method never settles. Then choose Shifted inverse and move the shift. Which eigenvalue does it find for each shift, and how fast? What happens as the shift gets close to an eigenvalue?
Taking the shift to be the current Rayleigh quotient at every step gives Rayleigh quotient iteration, which, for symmetric matrices, converges cubically: the number of correct digits roughly triples at each step. The price is a new factorisation at every step.






NoteExample 2: shifted inverse iteration



Find the smaller eigenvalue of the matrix in Example 1 by inverse iteration with shift \(\mu = 1\), starting from \((1, 0)\T\).
Solution. \(\M{A} - \M{I} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2}\), whose inverse is \(\mat{2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1}\). (For a \(2 \times 2\) example it is fine to write the inverse down; for a large matrix, use its LU factors.) Then \[
\vect{y} = (2, -1)\T,
\qquad
\vect{q}_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2, -1)\T,
\qquad
r = \tfrac{1}{5}(2, -1)\mat{3 \\ -1} = 1.4.
\] The next estimates are 1.38235, 1.381974 and 1.3819662, converging to \(1.3819660\ldots\) with the error shrinking by a factor of about 0.02 per step. The vector factor is \(\lvert 1.382 - 1\rvert/\lvert 3.618 - 1\rvert \approx 0.146\), and the estimates gain at its square, as in Example 1.




The QR algorithm
To find all the eigenvalues of a dense matrix, libraries use the QR algorithm. Factorise \(\M{A}_0 = \M{A}\) as \(\M{A}_0 = \M{Q}_0\M{R}_0\), with \(\M{Q}_0\) orthogonal and \(\M{R}_0\) upper triangular (introduced in Chapter 17; Chapter 30 shows how to compute it), then multiply the factors in the opposite order, and repeat: \[
\M{A}_k = \M{Q}_k\M{R}_k,
\qquad
\M{A}_{k+1} = \M{R}_k\M{Q}_k.
\] Since \(\M{R}_k = \M{Q}_k\T\M{A}_k\), each new matrix is \(\M{A}_{k+1} = \M{Q}_k\T\M{A}_k\M{Q}_k\): a change of basis by an orthogonal matrix (Chapter 15), so it has the same eigenvalues as \(\M{A}\). Remarkably, the \(\M{A}_k\) converge to an upper triangular matrix (diagonal, if \(\M{A}\) is symmetric), with the eigenvalues on its diagonal. In effect the QR algorithm runs the power method on many vectors at once, keeping them orthogonal, so that each settles onto a different eigenvector.
The basic version converges at the same slow rate as the power method. Production versions, in LAPACK and so in NumPy and MATLAB, add three refinements that make it very fast:

first reduce \(\M{A}\) to Hessenberg form (zero below the first subdiagonal; tridiagonal if \(\M{A}\) is symmetric) by orthogonal changes of basis, so that each QR step costs \(O(n^2)\) instead of \(O(n^3)\);
use shifts, like inverse iteration, so that the last diagonal entry converges in a few steps;
once it has converged, deflate: remove the last row and column and carry on with a smaller matrix.

The total cost is about \(10n^3\) operations for all the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a dense matrix, and the computed eigenvalues are exact for a matrix within rounding error of \(\M{A}\).






NoteExample 3: the QR algorithm



Apply the basic QR algorithm to the matrix of Example 1.
Solution. The first steps give (see the code below) \[
\M{A}_1 = \mat{3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2},
\quad
\M{A}_2 = \mat{3.5 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & 1.5},
\quad
\M{A}_3 = \mat{3.6 & -0.2 \\ -0.2 & 1.4},
\quad
\M{A}_5 \approx \mat{3.6176 & -0.0294 \\ -0.0294 & 1.3824}.
\] Every \(\M{A}_k\) is symmetric with trace 5 and determinant 5, as it must be, since they all have the same eigenvalues. The off-diagonal entries shrink by a factor of about \(1.382/3.618 \approx 0.38\) per step, and the diagonal entries approach the eigenvalues. The top-left entries, 3, 3.5, 3.6, …, are exactly the Rayleigh quotients from the power method in Example 1: the QR algorithm really is the power method in disguise.

title: 29  Eigenvalue algorithms
text:
29.3 In code

Run this chapter’s code yourself: open the notebook in Colab, or download the Jupyter notebook or the MATLAB script.

For large sparse matrices, when only a few eigenvalues are needed, use scipy.sparse.linalg.eigs (or eigsh for symmetric matrices) in Python and eigs in MATLAB. They use Krylov methods, Lanczos and Arnoldi, which extract far more from the sequence \(\vect{q}, \M{A}\vect{q}, \M{A}^2\vect{q}, \dots\) than the power method does, and with the option sigma they use shifted inverse iteration to find the eigenvalues nearest a given value.

PythonMATLAB



import numpy as np
import scipy.linalg

A = np.array([[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 3.0]])

# Power method
q = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
for k in range(1, 6):
    y = A @ q
    q = y / np.linalg.norm(y)
    print(f"{k}  {q @ A @ q:.10f}")          # Rayleigh quotient

# Shifted inverse iteration: factorise once, solve at each step
lu = scipy.linalg.lu_factor(A - 1.0 * np.eye(2))
q = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
for k in range(1, 5):
    y = scipy.linalg.lu_solve(lu, q)
    q = y / np.linalg.norm(y)
    print(f"{k}  {q @ A @ q:.10f}")

# Basic QR algorithm
Ak = A.copy()
for k in range(5):
    Q, R = np.linalg.qr(Ak)
    Ak = R @ Q
print(np.round(Ak, 4))

title: 29  Eigenvalue algorithms
text:
29.4 Check your understanding






TipA matrix has eigenvalues 10, 9 and 1. Will the power method converge quickly?





No: the factor per step is \(9/10 = 0.9\), so each correct digit takes about 22 steps. A shift would help: the power method on \(\M{A} - 5\M{I}\), with eigenvalues 5, 4 and \(-4\), has factor \(0.8\); better still, inverse iteration with a shift near 10.









TipWhat does inverse iteration with shift \(\mu\) find if \(\mu\) is exactly an eigenvalue?





In exact arithmetic \(\M{A} - \mu\M{I}\) is singular and can’t be factorised. In floating point, it is nearly singular, and solving with it gives an enormous vector pointing almost exactly along the eigenvector: one step is enough.









TipWhy does eig not use the characteristic polynomial?





Its roots can be extremely sensitive to small changes in its coefficients, so rounding errors would ruin them; and computing the coefficients is itself expensive and unstable. The QR algorithm works on the matrix directly, with orthogonal transformations that don’t magnify errors.

title: 29  Eigenvalue algorithms
text:
29.5 Key ideas

The power method multiplies a vector by \(\M{A}\) over and over, and converges to the dominant eigenvector at a rate set by \(\lvert\lambda_2/\lambda_1\rvert\).
The Rayleigh quotient \(\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x}/\vect{x}\T\vect{x}\) turns an approximate eigenvector into an accurate eigenvalue.
Inverse iteration with a shift \(\sigma\) finds the eigenvalue closest to \(\sigma\), and converges very fast when \(\sigma\) is close.
The QR algorithm, which eig uses, finds all the eigenvalues together by repeated QR factorisations.

text:
