title: 35  Markov chains and PageRank
text:
35.8 Going further

Absorbing chains are used to price loans that may default, to estimate how long patients stay in each stage of an illness, and to analyse games. Kemeny and Snell’s Finite Markov Chains is the classic account.
Langville and Meyer’s Google’s PageRank and Beyond tells the full story of PageRank, including how it is computed for the whole web and how people tried to manipulate it.
Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, central to modern statistics and physics, design a Markov chain whose steady state is a probability distribution you want to sample from, then simulate it.
Hidden Markov models, in which the states can’t be observed directly, underlie speech recognition and the analysis of DNA sequences.

title: 36  Population models
text:
36.1 The problem
Core
Builds on Chapter 18, Chapter 19.
In the early 1980s, loggerhead sea turtles nesting on the beaches of the south-eastern United States were in decline. Conservation effort had focused on the most visible stage of their lives: protecting eggs on nesting beaches and helping hatchlings reach the sea. But were the eggs the right place to intervene? Loggerheads take decades to mature, and many juveniles drowned in shrimp trawling nets.
In 1987, Deborah Crouse, Larry Crowder and Hal Caswell answered the question with a \(7 \times 7\) matrix. Their model showed that even if every egg survived, the population would still decline, whereas modest improvements in the survival of large juveniles could reverse the decline. The work helped persuade the US government to require turtle excluder devices in shrimp nets, which let turtles escape. This chapter builds the mathematics behind that model.

title: 36  Population models
text:
36.2 The model

Leslie matrices
Divide a population of females into age classes: newborns (age 0 to 1), one-year-olds, and so on, and count them once a year. Two kinds of number describe the life cycle:

the fecundity \(f_i\): the average number of female offspring, surviving to the next count, produced by each female in class \(i\);
the survival rate \(s_i\): the fraction of class \(i\) that survives to join class \(i + 1\) a year later.

If \(\vect{x}_k\) lists the numbers in each class in year \(k\), then next year’s newborns are \(f_1x_1 + f_2x_2 + \dots + f_nx_n\), and each other class is the survivors of the one before. In matrix form, \(\vect{x}_{k+1} = \M{L}\vect{x}_k\), with the Leslie matrix \[
\M{L} = \mat{f_1 & f_2 & \cdots & f_{n-1} & f_n \\ s_1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & s_2 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ \vdots & & \ddots & & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & s_{n-1} & 0}.
\]


Stage-based models
For long-lived species, counting every year of age gives an enormous matrix, and individuals of the same age can be very different in size. Biologists instead group them into stages, such as eggs, juveniles, subadults and adults, each lasting several years. A stage-based (Lefkovitch) matrix has three kinds of entry: fecundities in the first row; \(P_i\) on the diagonal, the probability of surviving and staying in stage \(i\); and \(G_i\) below the diagonal, the probability of surviving and growing into the next stage. If a stage lasts \(D_i\) years and its annual survival is \(s_i\), a standard approximation is \[
P_i = s_i\,\frac{1 - s_i^{D_i - 1}}{1 - s_i^{D_i}},
\qquad
G_i = \frac{s_i^{D_i}(1 - s_i)}{1 - s_i^{D_i}}.
\]


Growth rate and stable distribution
Either way, \(\vect{x}_k = \M{L}^k\vect{x}_0\), and Chapter 19 tells us what happens in the long run. A population matrix has non-negative entries, and if every stage can eventually lead to every other (through births), the Perron–Frobenius theorem says that it has a positive real eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\), larger in size than all the others (in the usual cases), with an eigenvector \(\vect{w}\) of positive entries. Then, for large \(k\), \[
\vect{x}_k \approx c\,\lambda_1^k\vect{w}.
\] So:

\(\lambda_1\) is the long-run growth rate: the population grows by a factor \(\lambda_1\) each year. It increases if \(\lambda_1 > 1\), decreases if \(\lambda_1 < 1\), and holds steady if \(\lambda_1 = 1\). Ecologists usually write \(\lambda\) without the subscript.
\(\vect{w}\), scaled so that its entries add up to 1, is the stable age distribution (or stable stage distribution): the proportions in each class that the population settles into, whatever it started with.
The other eigenvalues decide how quickly it settles: the transient effects die away like \(\lvert\lambda_2/\lambda_1\rvert^k\).







NoteExample 1: a three-class Leslie matrix



An animal lives for at most three years. Half the newborns survive their first year, and a quarter of one-year-olds survive their second. One-year-olds have 4 female young on average and two-year-olds have 3 (Figure 36.1). Find the long-run growth rate and the stable age distribution.






Figure 36.1: The life cycle of Example 1. Straight arrows are survival into the next class, the subdiagonal of \(\M{L}\); curved arrows are births into class 1, its first row.



Solution. \[
\M{L} = \mat{0 & 4 & 3 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.25 & 0}.
\] Expanding \(\det(\M{L} - \lambda\M{I})\) along the first column (Chapter 6), \[
-\lambda(\lambda^2 - 0) - 0.5\,(4\cdot(-\lambda) - 3 \times 0.25) = -\lambda^3 + 2\lambda + 0.375,
\] so the eigenvalues solve \(\lambda^3 - 2\lambda - 0.375 = 0\). Trying \(\lambda = 1.5\): \(3.375 - 3 - 0.375 = 0\). ✓ Dividing out \(\lambda - 1.5\) leaves \(\lambda^2 + 1.5\lambda + 0.25 = 0\), with roots \(-1.309\) and \(-0.191\), so 1.5 is the dominant eigenvalue: in the long run the population grows by 50% a year. For the eigenvector, the second and third rows of \((\M{L} - 1.5\M{I})\vect{w} = \zerovec\) give \(w_2 = w_1/3\) and \(w_3 = w_2/6 = w_1/18\), so \(\vect{w} \propto (18, 6, 1)\), and scaled to add to 1, \(\vect{w} = (0.72, 0.24, 0.04)\): 72% newborns, 24% one-year-olds and 4% two-year-olds.
The second eigenvalue, \(-1.309\), is not much smaller in size than 1.5, so the population takes a long time to settle, oscillating as it does (the ratio \(1.309/1.5 \approx 0.87\) per year). Starting from 100 newborns, after 10 years the proportions are still \((0.81, 0.14, 0.05)\).








NoteExample 2: loggerhead sea turtles



Crouse, Crowder and Caswell divided the loggerhead’s life into seven stages: eggs and hatchlings (H), small juveniles (\(J_s\)), large juveniles (\(J_l\)), subadults (Sub), novice breeders (\(B_1\)), first-year remigrants (\(B_2\)) and mature breeders (M). Their matrix, from field data, is

\[
\M{A} = \left(\begin{array}{ccccccc}
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 127 & 4 & 80 \\
0.6747 & 0.7370 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0.0486 & 0.6610 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0.0147 & 0.6907 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0.0518 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0.8091 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0.8091 & 0.8089
\end{array}\right).
\]

For example, a small juvenile has a 73.7% chance of surviving and staying a small juvenile next year, and a 4.86% chance of surviving and growing into a large juvenile; a mature breeder produces 80 eggs a year, on average. What does the model predict?
Solution. The dominant eigenvalue, from the code below, is \(\lambda = 0.945\): the population shrinks by about 5.5% a year, halving in about 12 years. The stable stage distribution is about 21% eggs and hatchlings, 67% small juveniles, 11% large juveniles, and under 1% in each later stage: only about 2 in 1000 turtles is a mature breeder, because so few survive the long juvenile stages.




Which rates matter most?
A manager can afford to improve only some survival or birth rates. Which change raises \(\lambda\) the most? The sensitivity of \(\lambda\) to the entry \(a_{ij}\) of the matrix is \[
\frac{\partial\lambda}{\partial a_{ij}} = \frac{v_iw_j}{\vect{v} \cdot \vect{w}},
\] where \(\vect{w}\) is the right eigenvector (the stable distribution) and \(\vect{v}\) is the left eigenvector, \(\vect{v}\T\M{L} = \lambda\vect{v}\T\), whose entries are the reproductive values of the stages: how much an individual in each stage will contribute to future generations. Because fecundities and survival rates are on very different scales, ecologists compare elasticities, \(e_{ij} = (a_{ij}/\lambda)\,\partial\lambda/\partial a_{ij}\): the proportional change in \(\lambda\) for a 1% change in \(a_{ij}\). The elasticities add up to 1.






NoteExample 3: eggs or juveniles?



Compare two strategies for the turtles: (a) protecting nests and hatchlings so well that every egg survives its first year; (b) using turtle excluder devices to raise the annual survival of large juveniles from 0.676 to 0.776.
Solution. (a) Changing the entry \(0.6747\) to 1 raises \(\lambda\) from 0.945 to only 0.965: even perfect protection of eggs and hatchlings can’t stop the decline. (b) Raising the large juveniles’ annual survival by 0.1, and recomputing their \(P\) and \(G\) entries with the formulas above (they last about 8 years), raises \(\lambda\) to 1.006: the population grows. The elasticities explain why. Summed over each stage, those for eggs and hatchlings come to about 0.05, while those for the three juvenile and subadult stages come to about 0.6. Large juveniles have a high reproductive value (they are worth about six newly hatched turtles each, for the population’s future), and they spend many years exposed to trawling. This kind of analysis, now routine in conservation biology, is a direct application of eigenvectors.

title: 36  Population models
text:
36.3 Explore
There is no app for this chapter. Figure 36.2 shows how the growth rate \(\lambda\) responds to improving the annual survival of each stage in turn, recomputing its \(P\) and \(G\) entries.


Show the code for this figure
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

A = np.array([[0, 0, 0, 0, 127, 4, 80],
              [0.6747, 0.7370, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0],
              [0, 0.0486, 0.6610, 0, 0, 0, 0],
              [0, 0, 0.0147, 0.6907, 0, 0, 0],
              [0, 0, 0, 0.0518, 0, 0, 0],
              [0, 0, 0, 0, 0.8091, 0, 0],
              [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.8091, 0.8089]])
lam = lambda M: max(np.linalg.eigvals(M).real)

def stage(s, D):
    """Probabilities of staying (P) and growing (G) for annual survival s over D years."""
    return s * (1 - s**(D - 1)) / (1 - s**D), s**D * (1 - s) / (1 - s**D)

increase = np.linspace(0, 0.2, 41)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.6))
values = []
for dx in increase:
    B = A.copy()
    B[1, 0] = 0.6747 + dx            # first-year survival of eggs and hatchlings
    values.append(lam(B))
ax.plot(increase, values, label="eggs and hatchlings", lw=2)
for col, s0, D, name in [(1, 0.7857, 7, "small juveniles"), (2, 0.6758, 8, "large juveniles"),
                         (3, 0.7425, 6, "subadults")]:
    values = []
    for dx in increase:
        B = A.copy()
        B[col, col], B[col + 1, col] = stage(s0 + dx, D)
        values.append(lam(B))
    ax.plot(increase, values, label=name, lw=2)
ax.axhline(1, color="0.4", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("increase in annual survival")
ax.set_ylabel("growth rate λ")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 36.2: Long-run growth rate λ of the loggerhead model as the annual survival of one stage is raised from its current value, the others staying fixed. The population grows only above the dashed line, λ = 1. Raising the first-year survival of eggs and hatchlings barely helps (even 100% survival only gives λ = 0.965); modest improvements for large juveniles are enough.





Things to try, with the code:

Find how much the annual survival of large juveniles must rise for \(\lambda\) to reach exactly 1.
Halve the fecundities of all breeders. How much does \(\lambda\) fall? Compare with halving the survival of mature breeders.
Start from 1000 eggs and project the population for 50 years. How long does it take to settle into the stable stage distribution?

title: 36  Population models
text:
36.5 Check your understanding






TipWhat goes in the first row and the subdiagonal of a Leslie matrix, and why is everything else zero?





The first row holds the fecundities, the births from each age class, and the subdiagonal the survival rates from each class into the next. Nothing else can happen in a year: no one gets younger, stays the same age or skips a class.









TipA population matrix has dominant eigenvalue 0.97. What happens to the population in the long run?





It shrinks by about 3% a year, whatever the starting numbers, so it halves roughly every 23 years (\(0.97^{23} \approx 0.5\)), settling into the stable stage distribution as it does.









TipWhy do ecologists compare elasticities rather than sensitivities?





Fecundities can be large numbers, like 127 eggs, while survival rates are at most 1, so a change of 0.01 means very different things for each. Elasticities measure proportional changes, so they can be compared directly, and they add up to 1.

title: 36  Population models
text:
36.6 Key ideas

A Leslie matrix has birth rates in its first row and survival rates on its subdiagonal; stage-based models also let individuals stay in a class.
The dominant eigenvalue \(\lambda\) is the long-run growth factor per time step: the population grows if \(\lambda > 1\) and declines if \(\lambda < 1\).
Its eigenvector is the stable age (or stage) distribution that every population settles into.
Sensitivities and elasticities show which rates matter most, which guides conservation.

title: 36  Population models
text:
36.8 Going further

Crouse, Crowder and Caswell’s paper, “A stage-based population model for loggerhead sea turtles and implications for conservation” (Ecology, 1987), is short and readable. Caswell’s Matrix Population Models is the standard text on the whole subject.
Real populations fluctuate. Models with random variation in the matrix from year to year, or with matrices that depend on population density, capture this; their long-run behaviour is no longer a single eigenvalue, but eigenvalues remain the starting point.
The same mathematics describes the ageing of a workforce, the turnover of equipment, and the spread of an infection through age groups, where the dominant eigenvalue of the next-generation matrix is the famous reproduction number \(R_0\).

title: 37  Data: regression and dimensionality reduction
text:
37.1 The problem
Further
Builds on Chapter 17, Chapter 21, Chapter 30.
In 1936 the statistician Ronald Fisher published measurements of 150 iris flowers, 50 from each of three species: Iris setosa, Iris versicolor and Iris virginica. For each flower, Edgar Anderson had measured four things, in centimetres: the length and width of a sepal (the green, leaf-like parts under the petals) and of a petal. The data set has been used ever since to teach and test statistical methods, and it raises two questions that run through all of data science:
The first is answered by multiple regression, which is least squares (Chapter 17). The second is answered by principal component analysis, which is the SVD (Chapter 21). Both are matrix calculations on the \(150 \times 4\) table of data.
The data are in the file data/iris.csv in the book’s repository (download it here), one row per flower; the code below reads it from there.

title: 37  Data: regression and dimensionality reduction
text:
37.2 The model

The design matrix
To predict a quantity \(y\) from \(p\) explanatory variables \(x_1, \dots, x_p\), a linear model says \[
y \approx \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots + \beta_px_p.
\] With \(n\) observations, each row of data gives one equation. Collecting them, \[
\vect{y} \approx \M{X}\vect{\beta},
\qquad
\M{X} = \mat{1 & x_{11} & \cdots & x_{1p} \\ 1 & x_{21} & \cdots & x_{2p} \\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ 1 & x_{n1} & \cdots & x_{np}},
\] where \(\M{X}\) is the \(n \times (p + 1)\) design matrix: a column of 1s for the intercept \(\beta_0\), and one column per variable. The model is linear in the coefficients \(\vect{\beta}\), which is all that matters: columns such as \(x_1^2\), \(\log x_2\) or \(x_1x_2\) are allowed, so the same machinery fits curves and interactions.


Multiple regression
There are many more observations than coefficients, so the system has no exact solution, and we choose \(\hat{\vect{\beta}}\) to minimise the sum of squared residuals \(\lVert\vect{y} - \M{X}\vect{\beta}\rVert^2\). That is a least-squares problem, solved by the normal equations \[
\M{X}\T\M{X}\hat{\vect{\beta}} = \M{X}\T\vect{y}
\] (Chapter 17), or more accurately by QR (Chapter 30), which is what statistical software does. The fitted values are \(\hat{\vect{y}} = \M{X}\hat{\vect{\beta}}\), the projection of \(\vect{y}\) onto the column space of \(\M{X}\). How well the model fits is summarised by the coefficient of determination \[
R^2 = 1 - \frac{\lVert\vect{y} - \hat{\vect{y}}\rVert^2}{\lVert\vect{y} - \bar{y}\vect{1}\rVert^2},
\] the fraction of the variation in \(y\) that the model explains. Statistical theory adds a measure of the uncertainty in each coefficient, its standard error, which is proportional to the square root of the corresponding diagonal entry of \((\M{X}\T\M{X})^{-1}\).






NoteExample 1: a regression by hand



In an experiment, two settings \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) were varied, coded as in the table, and a response \(y\) was measured. Fit \(y \approx \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2\).

Solution. The design matrix has columns \(\vect{1}\), \(\vect{x}_1\) and \(\vect{x}_2\). These happen to be orthogonal: \(\vect{1} \cdot \vect{x}_1 = 0\), \(\vect{1} \cdot \vect{x}_2 = 0\) and \(\vect{x}_1 \cdot \vect{x}_2 = -2 + 1 + 0 - 1 + 2 = 0\). So \(\M{X}\T\M{X}\) is diagonal, \[
\M{X}\T\M{X} = \mat{5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4},
\qquad
\M{X}\T\vect{y} = \mat{25 \\ 17 \\ 2},
\] and \(\hat{\vect{\beta}} = (5, 1.7, 0.5)\T\): \(\hat{y} = 5 + 1.7x_1 + 0.5x_2\). Each coefficient is found separately, and adding or removing a variable doesn’t change the others. This is why designed experiments choose their settings to make the columns orthogonal: it is the opposite of collinearity, the subject of the next section.




Collinearity
If two explanatory variables are nearly proportional, the columns of \(\M{X}\) are nearly dependent, and \(\M{X}\) is ill-conditioned (Chapter 24). The data can’t tell their effects apart: many quite different combinations of the two coefficients fit almost equally well. The symptoms are:

large standard errors, because the diagonal of \((\M{X}\T\M{X})^{-1}\) is large;
coefficients that change a lot, even changing sign, when a variable is added or removed, or the data change slightly;
a large condition number of \(\M{X}\) (after scaling its columns to comparable sizes).

This is collinearity (or multicollinearity). The fitted values \(\hat{\vect{y}}\) are still fine, since the column space is still well defined; it is the individual coefficients that become unreliable, and with them any story about which variable “matters”. The remedies are to drop or combine variables, to collect data that separate them, or to use ridge regression (Chapter 22, exercise 6), which adds \(\mu\M{I}\) to \(\M{X}\T\M{X}\).






NoteExample 2: collinearity in the iris data

(The numbers in brackets are standard errors.) On its own, petal width has a clear positive effect: wider petals go with longer sepals. With petal length included, its coefficient turns negative, with a standard error three times as large, while \(R^2\) barely moves. The two petal measurements have correlation 0.963, so the columns are nearly dependent, and the condition number of the design matrix rises from about 4 to 25. The negative coefficient doesn’t mean that wider petals cause shorter sepals; it means that among flowers with the same petal length, which hardly vary in width, the data say little, and the coefficient is poorly determined.




PCA in practice
Chapter 21 showed that the principal components of a data set are the right singular vectors of its centred data matrix. In practice, three decisions come first.

Centre each column, by subtracting its mean. Without this, the first component mostly points towards the mean.
Standardise each column, by dividing by its standard deviation, when the variables are measured in different units or on very different scales. Otherwise the variables with the largest numbers dominate. (For the iris data all four are lengths in centimetres, so either choice is reasonable; standardising is the common default.)
Choose how many components to keep, typically enough to explain 80–95% of the variance, or where a plot of the explained variance against the component number (a scree plot) levels off.

Then interpret the loadings, the entries of each principal component vector, which say how much each original variable contributes; and plot the scores, each item’s coordinates along the first two components.






NoteExample 3: principal components of the iris data



Standardise the four measurements and find the principal components.
Solution. The singular values of the \(150 \times 4\) standardised matrix give the explained variances: 73.0%, 22.9%, 3.7% and 0.5%. Two components capture 96% of the variation, so a two-dimensional plot loses little. The first two loadings are about \[
\vect{v}_1 = (0.52, -0.27, 0.58, 0.56),
\qquad
\vect{v}_2 = (-0.38, -0.92, -0.02, -0.07),
\] in the order sepal length, sepal width, petal length, petal width. The first component is roughly the average of three size measurements, minus a little sepal width: overall flower size. The second is almost entirely sepal width. Figure 37.1 plots the scores: setosa forms a separate cluster on the left, far from the other two species, which overlap slightly. PCA never used the species labels, but it found them.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

data = np.genfromtxt("../data/iris.csv", delimiter=",", skip_header=1, dtype=str)
X = data[:, :4].astype(float)
species = data[:, 4]
Z = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0, ddof=1)
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Z, full_matrices=False)
scores = Z @ Vt[:2].T

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
for name, colour, marker in [("setosa", "#2153b8", "o"), ("versicolor", "#9c5208", "s"),
                             ("virginica", "#0a7050", "^")]:
    pts = scores[species == name]
    ax.scatter(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], s=18, color=colour, marker=marker, label=name, alpha=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel(f"PC1 ({100 * s[0]**2 / np.sum(s**2):.0f}% of variance)")
ax.set_ylabel(f"PC2 ({100 * s[1]**2 / np.sum(s**2):.0f}%)")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

37.5 Check your understanding






TipIs \(y \approx \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \beta_2x^2\) a linear model? What is the row of the design matrix for an observation with \(x = 3\)?





Yes: it is linear in the coefficients, which is all that matters. The row is \((1, 3, 9)\).









TipTwo explanatory variables are nearly proportional. Are the model’s predictions unreliable?





Not for data like the data it was fitted to: the fitted values are a projection onto the column space, which is still well defined. It is the individual coefficients that become unreliable, so don’t read much into their sizes or signs.









TipWhy centre the data before PCA, and when should you also standardise it?





Without centring, the first component mostly points towards the mean of the data, not along its spread. Standardise as well when the variables are in different units or on very different scales, or the variables with the largest numbers dominate.

title: 37  Data: regression and dimensionality reduction
text:
37.6 Key ideas

A regression model is linear in its coefficients, so fitting it is a least-squares problem with a design matrix \(\M{X}\), one row per observation.
Collinear variables make \(\M{X}\) ill-conditioned: predictions can still be good, but individual coefficients become unreliable.
PCA finds the directions of greatest variance from the SVD of the centred (and usually standardised) data.
The squared singular values show how much of the variance each component explains.

title: 37  Data: regression and dimensionality reduction
text:
37.8 Going further

Ridge regression and the lasso add a penalty on the size of the coefficients to the least-squares objective. Ridge regression shrinks the coefficients of collinear variables towards each other; the lasso sets some to exactly zero, choosing variables automatically. Both are central to modern machine learning. Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman’s The Elements of Statistical Learning (free online) covers them, and much more, in depth.
Linear discriminant analysis, another of Fisher’s ideas from the same 1936 paper, finds the directions that best separate known groups, rather than the directions of greatest variance. It leads to a generalised eigenvalue problem.
For data with thousands of variables, such as gene expression or images, PCA is computed with randomised or iterative SVD methods (Chapter 29), which find the first few components without computing all of them.

title: 38  Physics: rotations, inertia and quantum states
text:
38.1 The problem
Further
Builds on Chapter 8, Chapter 20, Chapter 23.
Physics is full of quantities that are not numbers or vectors but linear maps from vectors to vectors. Spin a rigid body about some axis, and its angular momentum generally points in a different direction: the map from angular velocity to angular momentum is a matrix, the inertia tensor. That is why an unbalanced car wheel wobbles, and why a thrown book spins steadily about two of its axes but tumbles about the third. In quantum mechanics, matrices go further still: the state of a system is a vector, every measurable quantity is a symmetric (or more precisely Hermitian) matrix, and the possible results of a measurement are its eigenvalues. This chapter shows three places where the linear algebra of this book is the physics.
crumbs: 38  Physics: rotations, inertia and quantum states

title: 38  Physics: rotations, inertia and quantum states
text:
38.2 The model

The inertia tensor
A rigid body made of point masses \(m_k\) at positions \(\vect{r}_k\) (relative to its centre of mass) rotates with angular velocity \(\vect{\omega}\): the axis of rotation is the direction of \(\vect{\omega}\) and the rate is its length. Each mass moves with velocity \(\vect{\omega} \times \vect{r}_k\), and the total angular momentum works out to be \[
\vect{L} = \M{I}\vect{\omega},
\qquad
\M{I} = \sum_k m_k\left(\lVert\vect{r}_k\rVert^2\M{I}_3 - \vect{r}_k\vect{r}_k\T\right),
\] where \(\M{I}_3\) is the \(3 \times 3\) identity. The inertia tensor \(\M{I}\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite. Its diagonal entries are the familiar moments of inertia about the axes, such as \(I_{xx} = \sum m(y^2 + z^2)\); its off-diagonal entries, the products of inertia such as \(I_{xy} = -\sum mxy\), measure how unbalanced the body is.
Because \(\M{I}\) is symmetric, the spectral theorem (Chapter 20) says that it has three perpendicular eigenvectors: the principal axes. About a principal axis, \(\vect{L} = \lambda\vect{\omega}\) is parallel to \(\vect{\omega}\), and the body spins smoothly; the eigenvalues are the principal moments of inertia. About any other axis, \(\vect{L}\) and \(\vect{\omega}\) point different ways, and keeping the body spinning about that axis needs a constantly changing torque, felt as vibration. Balancing a car wheel means adding small weights to make its axle a principal axis.






NoteExample 1: a dumbbell



Two masses of 1 kg are at \((1, 1, 0)\) and \((-1, -1, 0)\) (in metres), joined by a light rod. Find the inertia tensor and its principal axes. If the dumbbell spins about the \(x\) axis with \(\vect{\omega} = (1, 0, 0)\) rad/s, what is its angular momentum?
Solution. For \(\vect{r} = (1, 1, 0)\), \(\lVert\vect{r}\rVert^2 = 2\) and \[
2\M{I}_3 - \vect{r}\vect{r}\T = \mat{1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2}.
\] The other mass gives the same, so \(\M{I} = \mat{2 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4}\) kg m². Its eigenvalues are 0, with eigenvector \((1, 1, 0)\), along the rod: the point masses don’t resist spinning about their own axis. The other two are both 4, with eigenvectors \((1, -1, 0)\) and \((0, 0, 1)\): any axis perpendicular to the rod.
Spinning about the \(x\) axis, \(\vect{L} = \M{I}\vect{\omega} = (2, -2, 0)\): not along the \(x\) axis at all, but perpendicular to the rod. As the dumbbell turns, \(\vect{L}\) turns with it, so a torque is needed to keep it spinning about \(x\): the bearings would feel a wobble (Figure 38.1).






Figure 38.1: The dumbbell of Example 1, spinning about the \(x\) axis. Its angular momentum \(\vect{L} = (2, -2, 0)\) is not along \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\), but at right angles to the rod.







Rotating frames and angular velocity
A body’s orientation can be described by the rotation matrix \(\M{R}(t)\) that turns its own axes into the fixed ones (Chapter 8). A point fixed in the body, at \(\vect{r}(t) = \M{R}(t)\vect{r}_0\), has velocity \[
\dot{\vect{r}} = \dot{\M{R}}\vect{r}_0 = \dot{\M{R}}\M{R}\T\vect{r},
\] using \(\M{R}\T\M{R} = \M{I}\). Differentiating \(\M{R}\M{R}\T = \M{I}\) shows that \(\M{\Omega} = \dot{\M{R}}\M{R}\T\) satisfies \(\M{\Omega}\T = -\M{\Omega}\): it is skew-symmetric, so it has the form \[
\M{\Omega} = \mat{0 & -\omega_z & \omega_y \\ \omega_z & 0 & -\omega_x \\ -\omega_y & \omega_x & 0},
\qquad
\M{\Omega}\vect{r} = \vect{\omega} \times \vect{r}.
\] So the angular velocity vector is hidden in the three independent entries of a skew-symmetric matrix, and \(\dot{\M{R}} = \M{\Omega}\M{R}\). For a constant \(\vect{\omega}\), this is a linear differential equation with solution \(\M{R}(t) = e^{\M{\Omega}t}\M{R}(0)\) (Chapter 23): the exponential of a skew-symmetric matrix is a rotation. Gyroscopes in phones and aircraft measure \(\vect{\omega}\), and navigation software integrates this equation to track orientation.






NoteExample 2: angular velocity from a rotation



A body rotates about the \(z\) axis at a constant rate \(\omega\): \(\M{R}(t)\) is the rotation by \(\omega t\) about \(z\). Find \(\M{\Omega} = \dot{\M{R}}\M{R}\T\).
Solution. With \(c = \cos\omega t\) and \(s = \sin\omega t\), \[
\M{R} = \mat{c & -s & 0 \\ s & c & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1},
\qquad
\dot{\M{R}} = \omega\mat{-s & -c & 0 \\ c & -s & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0},
\qquad
\dot{\M{R}}\M{R}\T = \omega\mat{0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0},
\] using \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\). Matching the pattern above, \(\vect{\omega} = (0, 0, \omega)\): along the axis of rotation, with length equal to the rate, as it should be. Then, for example, the point \((1, 0, 0)\) has velocity \(\M{\Omega}(1, 0, 0)\T = (0, \omega, 0)\).




Two-state quantum systems
The simplest quantum systems have just two basic states: the spin of an electron (up or down along a chosen axis), the polarisation of a photon, or the two levels of a qubit in a quantum computer. The rules of quantum mechanics, for such a system, are:

States are vectors \(\vect{\psi} = (\alpha, \beta)\T\) of complex numbers, with \(\lvert\alpha\rvert^2 + \lvert\beta\rvert^2 = 1\). The basis states \((1, 0)\T\) and \((0, 1)\T\) are written \(\lvert\uparrow\rangle\) and \(\lvert\downarrow\rangle\).
Measurable quantities are Hermitian matrices, equal to their own conjugate transpose: the complex version of symmetric. Like symmetric matrices, they have real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors (Section C.13).
Measurement: measuring the quantity \(\M{A}\) always gives one of its eigenvalues. The probability of getting the eigenvalue with unit eigenvector \(\vect{e}\) is \(\lvert\vect{e}^*\vect{\psi}\rvert^2\), the squared size of the component of \(\vect{\psi}\) along \(\vect{e}\) (where \(^*\) is the conjugate transpose). After the measurement, the state is that eigenvector.
Time evolution: between measurements, \(\vect{\psi}(t) = e^{-i\M{H}t/\hbar}\vect{\psi}(0)\), where the Hermitian Hamiltonian \(\M{H}\) is the energy, and \(\hbar\) is the reduced Planck constant. This is the solution of the linear system \(i\hbar\,\dot{\vect{\psi}} = \M{H}\vect{\psi}\), the Schrödinger equation (Chapter 23).

For spin, the measurements of spin along the three axes are (in units of \(\hbar/2\)) the Pauli matrices \[
\M{\sigma}_x = \mat{0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0},
\qquad
\M{\sigma}_y = \mat{0 & -i \\ i & 0},
\qquad
\M{\sigma}_z = \mat{1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1},
\] each with eigenvalues \(+1\) and \(-1\): a measurement of spin along any axis gives only “up” or “down”, never anything in between. The three matrices don’t commute, and so they have no common eigenvectors: a state can’t have a definite spin along \(x\) and along \(z\) at once. That is the uncertainty principle, in its simplest form, and it is a statement about matrices.






NoteExample 3: measuring a spin



An electron is prepared spin up along \(z\), \(\vect{\psi} = (1, 0)\T\). Its spin is then measured along \(x\). What results are possible, with what probabilities? What if instead it evolves for a time under \(\M{H} = \tfrac{1}{2}\hbar\omega\M{\sigma}_x\) (a magnetic field along \(x\)) before its spin along \(z\) is measured?
Solution. The eigenvalues of \(\M{\sigma}_x\) are \(+1\) and \(-1\), with eigenvectors \(\vect{e}_\pm = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, \pm 1)\T\). The probabilities are \(\lvert\vect{e}_\pm\T\vect{\psi}\rvert^2 = \bigl(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bigr)^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\) each: knowing the spin along \(z\) exactly means knowing nothing at all about it along \(x\).
For the time evolution, \(\M{\sigma}_x^2 = \M{I}\), so the power series for the matrix exponential (Chapter 23) splits into even and odd terms: \[
e^{-i\omega t\M{\sigma}_x/2} = \cos\frac{\omega t}{2}\,\M{I} - i\sin\frac{\omega t}{2}\,\M{\sigma}_x,
\qquad
\vect{\psi}(t) = \mat{\cos(\omega t/2) \\ -i\sin(\omega t/2)}.
\] Measuring spin along \(z\) gives up with probability \(\cos^2(\omega t/2)\) and down with probability \(\sin^2(\omega t/2)\). The spin flips back and forth: Rabi oscillation, the basis of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and of single-qubit operations in quantum computers. After \(\omega t = \pi\) it is certainly down: a quantum NOT gate.

38.3 Explore
There is no app for this chapter. Figure 38.2 shows the probabilities of Example 3, computed with the matrix exponential, alongside the probabilities for a state that starts tilted from the \(z\) axis.


Show the code for this figure
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.linalg import expm

sx = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]])
t = np.linspace(0, 4 * np.pi, 300)                      # in units of 1/ω
starts = {"spin up": np.array([1, 0]),
          "tilted 60° towards y": np.array([np.cos(np.pi / 6), 1j * np.sin(np.pi / 6)])}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.2))
for (label, psi0), style in zip(starts.items(), ["-", "--"]):
    p = [abs((expm(-1j * sx * tk / 2) @ psi0)[0])**2 for tk in t]
    ax.plot(t, p, style, lw=2, label=label)
ax.set_xlabel("ωt")
ax.set_ylabel("P(spin up along z)")
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(0, 4 * np.pi + 0.1, np.pi), ["0", "π", "2π", "3π", "4π"])
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 38.2: Rabi oscillation: the probability of finding the spin up along z, for a spin evolving under H = ½ħω σₓ, starting spin up (solid) and starting tilted 60° from the z axis towards y (dashed). Each curve comes from applying the 2 × 2 matrix exponential to the starting state.

Replace \(\M{\sigma}_x\) by \(\M{\sigma}_z\) in the Hamiltonian. Why doesn’t the probability change at all now?
Use \(\M{H} = \tfrac{1}{2}\hbar\omega(\M{\sigma}_x + \M{\sigma}_z)/\sqrt{2}\), a field at \(45°\). What is the largest probability of finding the spin down?
Starting spin up, measure along a direction at angle \(\theta\) to \(z\), with \(\M{A} = \cos\theta\,\M{\sigma}_z + \sin\theta\,\M{\sigma}_x\). Check that the probability of “up” is \(\cos^2(\theta/2)\).

text:
38.4 In code

Run this chapter’s code yourself: open the notebook in Colab, or download the Jupyter notebook or the MATLAB script.

The code finds the principal axes of four point masses in an L shape, and applies a quantum time evolution.

PythonMATLAB



import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import expm

# Inertia tensor of four 1 kg masses in an L shape, about their centre of mass
r = np.array([[0, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0], [2, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0]], dtype=float)
m = np.ones(4)
r = r - m @ r / m.sum()                    # positions relative to the centre of mass

title: 38  Physics: rotations, inertia and quantum states
text:
38.5 Check your understanding






TipA wheel spins about an axis that is not one of its principal axes. What do you notice?





Its angular momentum \(\M{I}\vect{\omega}\) isn’t parallel to \(\vect{\omega}\), so keeping it spinning about that axis needs a constantly changing torque from the axle, felt as vibration. Balancing weights fix this by making the axle a principal axis.









TipWhy is \(\M{\Omega} = \dot{\M{R}}\M{R}\T\) always skew-symmetric?





Differentiating \(\M{R}\M{R}\T = \M{I}\) gives \(\dot{\M{R}}\M{R}\T + \M{R}\dot{\M{R}}\T = \M{0}\), which says \(\M{\Omega} + \M{\Omega}\T = \M{0}\).









TipAn electron is in the state \((0.6, 0.8)\T\). Its spin along \(z\) is measured. What are the possible results and their probabilities?





The eigenvalues of \(\M{\sigma}_z\), \(+1\) (up) and \(-1\) (down), with eigenvectors \((1, 0)\T\) and \((0, 1)\T\). The probabilities are \(0.6^2 = 0.36\) and \(0.8^2 = 0.64\), which add up to 1.

title: 38  Physics: rotations, inertia and quantum states
text:
38.6 Key ideas

The inertia tensor is a symmetric matrix; its eigenvectors are the principal axes, about which a body can spin without wobbling.
The rate of change of a rotation matrix gives the skew-symmetric angular velocity matrix \(\M{\Omega} = \dot{\M{R}}\M{R}\T\).
A two-state quantum system is a complex unit vector; measurable quantities are Hermitian matrices, such as the Pauli matrices.
The possible results of a measurement are the eigenvalues, with probabilities given by the squared sizes of the components along the eigenvectors.

text:
38.8 Going further

Why does a book spin stably about its longest and shortest axes but tumble about the middle one? The answer, the tennis racket theorem, comes from linearising Euler’s equations of rigid-body motion about each principal axis and examining the eigenvalues (Chapter 23). Taylor’s Classical Mechanics covers rigid bodies thoroughly.
Special relativity uses a \(4 \times 4\) matrix, the Lorentz transformation, which mixes time and space while preserving \(c^2t^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2\) instead of length. It is a “rotation” in spacetime, with hyperbolic functions in place of sines and cosines.
In quantum mechanics with more than two states, everything above holds with larger matrices, and for continuous systems with infinite-dimensional ones. Nielsen and Chuang’s Quantum Computation and Quantum Information and Susskind and Friedman’s Quantum Mechanics: The Theoretical Minimum are good next steps from here.

title: 39  Cryptography: the Hill cipher
text:
39.1 The problem
Core
Builds on Chapter 3, Chapter 7.
For most of history, secret messages were protected by substitution: replace each letter by another, according to a key. Such ciphers are easily broken by counting letters, because E is the most common letter in English text, so the most common letter in the ciphertext probably stands for E. In 1929 the American mathematician Lester Hill published a cipher that defeats simple letter counting by mixing letters together: each letter of the ciphertext depends on several letters of the message, through a matrix.
The Hill cipher was never widely used, and it is easy to break today. But it is the first cipher built on linear algebra, it shows clearly why invertibility matters, and the weakness that breaks it, linearity, is exactly what modern ciphers are designed to avoid.

title: 39  Cryptography: the Hill cipher
text:
39.2 The model

Arithmetic modulo 26
Number the letters A = 0, B = 1, …, Z = 25. Arithmetic is done modulo 26: after each calculation, keep only the remainder on division by 26, so that the result is again a letter. For example, \(33 \equiv 7 \pmod{26}\) and \(-3 \equiv 23 \pmod{26}\). Addition, subtraction and multiplication work as usual, and matrix multiplication modulo 26 just means multiplying as usual and reducing every entry at the end.
Division is the problem. A number \(a\) has an inverse modulo 26, a number \(a^{-1}\) with \(aa^{-1} \equiv 1\), only if \(a\) and 26 have no common factor: \(\gcd(a, 26) = 1\). So the odd numbers other than 13 have inverses, and the even numbers and 13 don’t. For example, \(3 \times 9 = 27 \equiv 1\), so \(3^{-1} \equiv 9\); but \(2x\) is always even, and so never \(\equiv 1\), since every multiple of 26 is even too.


Encryption by matrix multiplication
Choose a \(2 \times 2\) key matrix \(\M{K}\) with entries from 0 to 25. Split the message into pairs of letters (adding an X if needed), and turn each pair into a vector \(\vect{p}\). The ciphertext pair is \[
\vect{c} \equiv \M{K}\vect{p} \pmod{26}.
\] Each ciphertext letter depends on both letters of the pair, so the same letter is encrypted differently in different pairs, and a single-letter count reveals little. Larger keys, \(3 \times 3\) or more, mix more letters together.






NoteExample 1: encrypting



Encrypt HELP with the key \(\M{K} = \mat{3 & 3 \\ 2 & 5}\).
Solution. HELP is H = 7, E = 4, L = 11, P = 15, giving the pairs \((7, 4)\) and \((11, 15)\). \[
\M{K}\mat{7 \\ 4} = \mat{21 + 12 \\ 14 + 20} = \mat{33 \\ 34} \equiv \mat{7 \\ 8} = \text{HI},
\qquad
\M{K}\mat{11 \\ 15} = \mat{33 + 45 \\ 22 + 75} = \mat{78 \\ 97} \equiv \mat{0 \\ 19} = \text{AT}.
\] The ciphertext is HIAT. The two letters of the second pair are both affected by both letters of the first: changing HELP to HELD would change the AT.
Open this encryption in the Hill cipher machine to see each pair worked through.




Inverses modulo 26
To decrypt, we need a matrix \(\M{K}^{-1}\) with \(\M{K}^{-1}\M{K} \equiv \M{I} \pmod{26}\); then \(\vect{p} \equiv \M{K}^{-1}\vect{c}\). The formula for the inverse of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix (Chapter 7) still works, with division by the determinant replaced by multiplication by its inverse modulo 26: \[
\M{K} = \mat{a & b \\ c & d}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\M{K}^{-1} \equiv (\det\M{K})^{-1}\mat{d & -b \\ -c & a} \pmod{26}.
\] So:






ImportantWhen a Hill key works



\(\M{K}\) has an inverse modulo 26 if and only if \(\gcd(\det\M{K}, 26) = 1\): the determinant, reduced modulo 26, must be odd and not 13.


A non-zero determinant, which is enough over the real numbers, is not enough here. If \(\det\M{K}\) is even, for example, then two different messages encrypt to the same ciphertext (exercise 4), and no one, not even the intended recipient, can tell which was sent. The proof is in Section C.22.






NoteExample 2: decrypting



Find \(\M{K}^{-1}\) modulo 26 and decrypt HIAT.
Solution. \(\det\M{K} = 15 - 6 = 9\), and \(\gcd(9, 26) = 1\), so the key is valid. Since \(9 \times 3 = 27 \equiv 1\), \(9^{-1} \equiv 3\). Then \[
\M{K}^{-1} \equiv 3\mat{5 & -3 \\ -2 & 3} = \mat{15 & -9 \\ -6 & 9} \equiv \mat{15 & 17 \\ 20 & 9} \pmod{26}.
\] Check: \(\M{K}^{-1}\M{K} = \mat{45 + 34 & 45 + 85 \\ 60 + 18 & 60 + 45} = \mat{79 & 130 \\ 78 & 105} \equiv \mat{1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1}\). ✓ Decrypting the first pair, \(\M{K}^{-1}(7, 8)\T = (105 + 136, \; 140 + 72) = (241, 212) \equiv (7, 4)\) = HE, and the second, \(\M{K}^{-1}(0, 19)\T = (323, 171) \equiv (11, 15)\) = LP.
Open this decryption in the Hill cipher machine to see \(\M{K}^{-1}\) and each pair worked through.




Breaking the cipher
The Hill cipher’s weakness is its linearity. Suppose an attacker knows, or guesses, the plaintext of just two pairs of letters, perhaps a standard greeting or the sender’s name. Put the two known plaintext pairs as the columns of \(\M{P}\), and the matching ciphertext pairs as the columns of \(\M{C}\). Then \(\M{C} \equiv \M{K}\M{P}\), and if \(\M{P}\) is invertible modulo 26, \[
\M{K} \equiv \M{C}\M{P}^{-1} \pmod{26}.
\] Four known letters reveal the whole key, and with it every message. This is a known-plaintext attack. For an \(n \times n\) key, \(n\) known pairs of length \(n\) are enough. Even without known plaintext, the attacker can try all \(26^4 = 456\,976\) possible \(2 \times 2\) keys, a moment’s work for a computer, and pick the one that gives readable English.






NoteExample 3: a known-plaintext attack



An attacker intercepts the ciphertext HIAT and correctly guesses that the message is HELP. Find the key.
Solution. The plaintext pairs HE and LP, and the ciphertext pairs HI and AT, as columns: \[
\M{P} = \mat{7 & 11 \\ 4 & 15},
\qquad
\M{C} = \mat{7 & 0 \\ 8 & 19}.
\] \(\det\M{P} = 105 - 44 = 61 \equiv 9\), whose inverse is 3, so \[
\M{P}^{-1} \equiv 3\mat{15 & -11 \\ -4 & 7} \equiv \mat{19 & 19 \\ 14 & 21},
\qquad
\M{K} \equiv \M{C}\M{P}^{-1} = \mat{133 & 133 \\ 418 & 551} \equiv \mat{3 & 3 \\ 2 & 5}.
\] The whole key, from one guessed word.

title: 39  Cryptography: the Hill cipher
text:
39.4 In code

Run this chapter’s code yourself: open the notebook in Colab, or download the Jupyter notebook or the MATLAB script.

Python’s built-in pow(a, -1, 26) finds an inverse modulo 26 (and raises an error if there is none). In MATLAB, [g, u] = gcd(a, 26) gives the greatest common divisor g, and when g is 1, u is an inverse of a.

PythonMATLAB



import numpy as np

def to_nums(text):
    return [ord(ch) - ord("A") for ch in text]

def to_text(nums):
    return "".join(chr(int(n) + ord("A")) for n in nums)

def hill(K, message):
    """Encrypt (or, with the inverse key, decrypt) a message of even length."""
    pairs = np.array(to_nums(message)).reshape(-1, 2).T     # pairs as columns
    return to_text((K @ pairs % 26).T.ravel())

def inverse_mod26(K):
    det = round(np.linalg.det(K)) % 26
    d_inv = pow(det, -1, 26)               # error if gcd(det, 26) != 1
    adj = np.array([[K[1, 1], -K[0, 1]], [-K[1, 0], K[0, 0]]])
    return d_inv * adj % 26

K = np.array([[3, 3], [2, 5]])
c = hill(K, "HELP")
Kinv = inverse_mod26(K)
print(c, hill(Kinv, c))
print(Kinv)

# Known-plaintext attack (Example 3)
P = np.array([[7, 11], [4, 15]])
C = np.array([[7, 0], [8, 19]])
print(C @ inverse_mod26(P) % 26)

p = hill(Kinv, c)

% Known-plaintext attack (Example 3)
P = [7 11; 4 15]; C = [7 0; 8 19];
Kfound = mod(C * inv26(P), 26)

% Encrypt (or, with the inverse key, decrypt) a message of even length.

if g ~= 1, error('Key not invertible mod 26'); end

title: 39  Cryptography: the Hill cipher
text:
39.5 Check your understanding






TipWhich of these keys can be used: \(\mat{2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1}\), \(\mat{3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3}\), \(\mat{5 & 2 \\ 1 & 3}\)?





Only the first. Their determinants are 1, 8 and 13. A key works only if its determinant has no common factor with 26, and 8 is even while 13 divides 26.









TipOver the real numbers a non-zero determinant is enough for an inverse. Why not modulo 26?





The inverse formula divides by the determinant, which modulo 26 means multiplying by its inverse, and only numbers with no common factor with 26 have one. With an even determinant, for example, two different messages encrypt to the same ciphertext, so no one can decrypt reliably.









TipA known-plaintext attack needs the matrix \(\M{P}\) of known plaintext pairs to be invertible modulo 26. What can the attacker do if it isn’t?





Then \(\M{C} \equiv \M{K}\M{P}\) doesn’t fix the key: several keys fit. If more plaintext is known, the attacker picks two other known pairs whose matrix is invertible. Otherwise they try each key that fits the known pairs, far fewer than all 456 976, and keep the one that gives readable text.

title: 39  Cryptography: the Hill cipher
text:
39.6 Key ideas

The Hill cipher encrypts blocks of letters by multiplying by a key matrix, with all arithmetic done modulo 26.
Decrypting needs the inverse of the key modulo 26.
The inverse exists exactly when the determinant has no common factor with 26 (it is odd and not a multiple of 13).
A few known plaintext–ciphertext pairs give a linear system for the key, so the cipher is easily broken.

title: 39  Cryptography: the Hill cipher
text:
39.8 Going further

Modern block ciphers, such as AES, which protects most internet traffic, use a matrix multiplication over a finite field as one step (its MixColumns step is a \(4 \times 4\) matrix acting on bytes), but they combine it with non-linear substitution steps and many rounds, precisely so that no known-plaintext attack like the one above can work.
Public-key cryptography, such as RSA, uses arithmetic modulo very large numbers, and relies on the same fact as this chapter: a number has an inverse modulo \(n\) exactly when it shares no factor with \(n\). Singh’s The Code Book is an entertaining history of codes and ciphers; Hoffstein, Pipher and Silverman’s An Introduction to Mathematical Cryptography covers the mathematics.
Linear algebra over finite fields, where arithmetic is done modulo a prime, is the basis of the error-correcting codes in QR codes, CDs, mobile phones and deep-space communication. Gaussian elimination works there exactly as in Chapter 11, since every non-zero number has an inverse.

title: 40  Vibrations and normal modes
text:
40.1 The problem
Core
Builds on Chapter 18. It also uses three results from Chapter 20 and Chapter 23, given in the box below, so you can read it without those chapters. The stiffness matrix of Chapter 31 helps, but this chapter explains what it needs.
Everything with mass and stiffness vibrates: buildings and bridges, car suspensions, aircraft wings, guitar strings, the atoms in a molecule. Each structure has a few natural frequencies at which it prefers to vibrate, and at each one it moves in a particular pattern, its mode shape. Engineers need to know both. If an earthquake, a machine, the wind or footsteps push a structure at one of its natural frequencies, the vibrations build up: this is resonance, and it can break things. Chemists use the same ideas the other way round: a molecule absorbs infrared light at its natural frequencies, which identifies the molecule.
For a structure with \(n\) moving parts, the natural frequencies and mode shapes come from an \(n \times n\) eigenvalue problem. This chapter sets it up for masses joined by springs, the model behind both a tall building and a vibrating molecule.

title: 40  Vibrations and normal modes
text:
40.2 The model

Equations of motion
Take \(n\) masses \(m_1, \dots, m_n\) in a line, joined to each other and to fixed walls by springs, and let \(x_i\) be the displacement of mass \(i\) from its resting position. A spring of stiffness \(k\) stretched by \(\delta\) pulls with force \(k\delta\), so the spring between masses \(i\) and \(i + 1\) pulls mass \(i\) with force \(k(x_{i+1} - x_i)\), and mass \(i + 1\) with the opposite force. Newton’s second law for each mass gives one equation, and together they form \[
\M{M}\ddot{\vect{x}} + \M{K}\vect{x} = \zerovec,
\tag{40.1}\] where the dots mean derivatives with respect to time, \(\M{M} = \operatorname{diag}(m_1, \dots, m_n)\) is the mass matrix and \(\M{K}\) is the stiffness matrix. For three springs and two masses between walls (Figure 40.1), \[
\M{K} = \mat{k_1 + k_2 & -k_2 \\ -k_2 & k_2 + k_3}.
\] Each mass’s diagonal entry is the total stiffness of the springs attached to it, and each spring joining two masses puts \(-k\) in their off-diagonal entries. As for a truss (Chapter 31), \(\M{K} = \M{B}\T\M{D}\M{B}\), where \(\M{B}\) turns displacements into spring extensions and \(\M{D}\) holds the stiffnesses, so \(\M{K}\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite.






Figure 40.1: Two masses between walls, joined by three springs, and the stiffness matrix they give. Each term in \(\M{K}\) is coloured like the spring it comes from: spring \(k_2\), which joins the masses, appears in all four entries.





Natural frequencies and mode shapes
Look for motions in which every mass moves in step, at the same frequency: \[
\vect{x}(t) = \vect{v}\cos(\omega t).
\] Then \(\ddot{\vect{x}} = -\omega^2\vect{v}\cos(\omega t)\), and Equation 40.1 becomes \((\M{K} - \omega^2\M{M})\vect{v}\cos(\omega t) = \zerovec\) for all \(t\), so \[
\M{K}\vect{v} = \omega^2\M{M}\vect{v}.
\tag{40.2}\] This is a generalised eigenvalue problem: an ordinary one when \(\M{M} = m\M{I}\), but with \(\M{M}\) in place of \(\M{I}\) in general. It has a nonzero solution \(\vect{v}\) only when \[
\det(\M{K} - \omega^2\M{M}) = 0,
\] a polynomial equation of degree \(n\) in \(\omega^2\). Its roots give the natural frequencies \(\omega_1 \le \omega_2 \le \dots \le \omega_n\), in radians per second (\(f = \omega/2\pi\) in hertz, cycles per second), and the solutions \(\vect{v}_i\) are the mode shapes. A mode shape gives the pattern of the motion, not its size: any multiple of \(\vect{v}_i\) is also a mode shape.
Because \(\M{K}\) and \(\M{M}\) are symmetric, and \(\M{M}\) is positive definite, the modes behave like the eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix. Substitute \(\vect{v} = \M{M}^{-1/2}\vect{w}\), where \(\M{M}^{-1/2} = \operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt{m_1}, \dots, 1/\sqrt{m_n})\). Then Equation 40.2 becomes \[
\M{M}^{-1/2}\M{K}\M{M}^{-1/2}\,\vect{w} = \omega^2\vect{w},
\] an ordinary eigenvalue problem for a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix (Chapter 20). So:

every \(\omega^2\) is real and at least 0, so every natural frequency is real;
there are \(n\) independent mode shapes, even when frequencies repeat;
the modes are orthogonal with respect to \(\M{M}\): \(\vect{v}_i\T\M{M}\vect{v}_j = 0\) for \(i \neq j\) (exercise 2), and also \(\vect{v}_i\T\M{K}\vect{v}_j = 0\).

A natural frequency of zero means that \(\M{K}\vect{v} = \zerovec\): the structure can move in the pattern \(\vect{v}\) without stretching any spring. That is a rigid-body mode, such as a molecule drifting through space, or a mechanism (Chapter 31).






NoteExample 1: two masses between walls



Two masses of \(m = 1\) kg are joined to each other and to two walls by three springs of stiffness \(k = 100\) N/m. Find the natural frequencies and mode shapes.
Solution. Here \(\M{M} = \M{I}\) and \[
\M{K} = \mat{200 & -100 \\ -100 & 200},
\qquad
\det(\M{K} - \lambda\M{I}) = (200 - \lambda)^2 - 100^2 = (\lambda - 100)(\lambda - 300),
\] writing \(\lambda = \omega^2\). For \(\lambda = 100\), \(\M{K} - 100\M{I} = \mat{100 & -100 \\ -100 & 100}\) gives \(\vect{v}_1 = (1, 1)\T\): the masses move together, in step, and the middle spring is never stretched. For \(\lambda = 300\), \(\M{K} - 300\M{I} = \mat{-100 & -100 \\ -100 & -100}\) gives \(\vect{v}_2 = (1, -1)\T\): the masses move in opposite directions, stretching and squashing the middle spring as well (Figure 40.2). The natural frequencies are \[
\omega_1 = 10 \text{ rad/s}\;(1.59 \text{ Hz}),
\qquad
\omega_2 = \sqrt{300} \approx 17.3 \text{ rad/s}\;(2.76 \text{ Hz}).
\] The mode that stretches more springs, for the same displacements, is the stiffer one, and so the faster one. That is true in general: higher modes have more changes of direction along the structure.






Figure 40.2: The two mode shapes of Example 1. In mode 1 the masses move together and the middle spring keeps its length; in mode 2 they move in opposite directions, so the middle spring is stretched and squashed too, and the mode is faster.



Open the two masses in the normal modes app to watch each mode on its own.




Building any motion from the modes
The equations are linear, so any combination of modes is also a motion, and every free vibration is one: \[
\vect{x}(t) = \sum_{i=1}^n \vect{v}_i\bigl(a_i\cos(\omega_i t) + b_i\sin(\omega_i t)\bigr).
\tag{40.3}\] This is the same idea as solving \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\vect{x}\) with eigenvectors (Chapter 23); here the equation is second order, so each mode has a cosine and a sine instead of one exponential. The starting displacement \(\vect{x}_0\) and velocity \(\dot{\vect{x}}_0\) fix the coefficients, and \(\M{M}\)-orthogonality gives them directly. Multiplying Equation 40.3 at \(t = 0\) by \(\vect{v}_i\T\M{M}\) kills every term except the \(i\)th: \[
a_i = \frac{\vect{v}_i\T\M{M}\vect{x}_0}{\vect{v}_i\T\M{M}\vect{v}_i},
\qquad
b_i = \frac{\vect{v}_i\T\M{M}\dot{\vect{x}}_0}{\omega_i\,\vect{v}_i\T\M{M}\vect{v}_i}.
\] Each mode then carries on at its own frequency, ignoring the others. The motion as a whole needn’t repeat, because the frequencies needn’t be in simple ratios.






NoteExample 2: pulling one mass and letting go



In Example 1, mass 1 is pulled 2 cm to the right and both masses are released from rest. Describe the motion.
Solution. With \(\M{M} = \M{I}\), the coefficients are \(a_i = \vect{v}_i\T\vect{x}_0/\vect{v}_i\T\vect{v}_i\). For \(\vect{x}_0 = (0.02, 0)\T\), \[
a_1 = \frac{0.02}{2} = 0.01,
\qquad
a_2 = \frac{0.02}{2} = 0.01,
\] and every \(b_i = 0\), since the start is from rest. So \[
\vect{x}(t) = 0.01\cos(10t)\mat{1 \\ 1} + 0.01\cos(17.3t)\mat{1 \\ -1}.
\] Mass 1 moves as \(0.01\bigl(\cos(10t) + \cos(17.3t)\bigr)\) and mass 2 as \(0.01\bigl(\cos(10t) - \cos(17.3t)\bigr)\). Pulling one mass excites both modes equally, and since \(\sqrt{3}\) is irrational the motion never exactly repeats; but it is just two simple vibrations added together.








NoteExample 3: a two-storey building



In a simple model of a two-storey building, each floor is a mass and each storey’s columns are a spring that resists sideways movement. The lower floor has mass \(m_1 = 20\) tonnes and the upper \(m_2 = 10\) tonnes; the lower storey has stiffness \(k_1 = 8\) MN/m and the upper \(k_2 = 4\) MN/m. Find the natural frequencies and mode shapes.
Solution. The ground is fixed and the roof is free, so \[
\M{K} = 10^6\mat{12 & -4 \\ -4 & 4},
\qquad
\M{M} = 10^4\mat{2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1}.
\] Dividing both by \(4 \times 10^6\) and writing \(\mu = \omega^2/400\), \[
\det\mat{3 - 2\mu & -1 \\ -1 & 1 - \mu} = (3 - 2\mu)(1 - \mu) - 1 = 2\mu^2 - 5\mu + 2 = (2\mu - 1)(\mu - 2) = 0.
\] So \(\mu = \tfrac{1}{2}\) or 2, that is \(\omega^2 = 200\) or 800: \[
\omega_1 \approx 14.1 \text{ rad/s}\;(2.25 \text{ Hz}),
\qquad
\omega_2 \approx 28.3 \text{ rad/s}\;(4.50 \text{ Hz}).
\] The first row of \((\M{K} - \omega^2\M{M})\vect{v} = \zerovec\) gives \((3 - 2\mu)v_1 = v_2\). For \(\mu = \tfrac{1}{2}\), \(\vect{v}_1 = (1, 2)\T\): both floors sway the same way, the top one twice as far. For \(\mu = 2\), \(\vect{v}_2 = (1, -1)\T\): the floors sway in opposite directions (Figure 40.3).
These modes are not perpendicular, \((1, 2) \cdot (1, -1) = -1\), but they are \(\M{M}\)-orthogonal: \[
\vect{v}_1\T\M{M}\vect{v}_2 = 10^4(2 \times 1 \times 1 + 1 \times 2 \times (-1)) = 0.
\] Earthquakes often shake the ground strongly at frequencies of a few hertz, close to these, which is why low-rise buildings in earthquake zones need careful design.






Figure 40.3: The two-storey building of Example 3 and its two mode shapes. In mode 1 both floors sway the same way, the top one twice as far; in mode 2 they sway in opposite directions.



Open the building in the normal modes app to watch its two modes.




Forced vibration and resonance
Now push the masses with forces that vary like \(\cos(\Omega t)\), at a driving frequency \(\Omega\): \[
\M{M}\ddot{\vect{x}} + \M{K}\vect{x} = \vect{f}\cos(\Omega t).
\] Trying \(\vect{x} = \vect{X}\cos(\Omega t)\) gives a linear system for the amplitudes, \[
(\M{K} - \Omega^2\M{M})\vect{X} = \vect{f}.
\tag{40.4}\] When \(\Omega\) is close to a natural frequency, the matrix \(\M{K} - \Omega^2\M{M}\) is close to singular, so the amplitudes are huge: resonance. Writing \(\vect{X}\) in terms of the modes, using their \(\M{M}\)-orthogonality, shows exactly how: \[
\vect{X} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\vect{v}_i\T\vect{f}}{(\omega_i^2 - \Omega^2)\,\vect{v}_i\T\M{M}\vect{v}_i}\,\vect{v}_i.
\] Mode \(i\) is amplified by \(1/(\omega_i^2 - \Omega^2)\), which blows up as \(\Omega\) approaches \(\omega_i\). But a mode is not excited at all if \(\vect{v}_i\T\vect{f} = 0\): pushing a structure where a mode doesn’t move, or symmetrically when the mode is antisymmetric, can’t drive it. Real structures have some damping, a friction-like force \(\M{C}\dot{\vect{x}}\), which keeps the peaks finite; but lightly damped structures, which most are, still respond far more strongly near their natural frequencies. Designers move the natural frequencies away from the driving frequencies they expect, add damping, or add a tuned mass damper.






NoteExample 4: shaking one mass



In Example 1, a force \(F\cos(\Omega t)\) pushes mass 1. Find the amplitudes of the two masses, and the driving frequencies at which they become very large. At what frequency does mass 1 not move at all?
Solution. Equation 40.4 is \[
\mat{200 - \Omega^2 & -100 \\ -100 & 200 - \Omega^2}\mat{X_1 \\ X_2} = \mat{F \\ 0}.
\] The determinant is \((200 - \Omega^2)^2 - 100^2 = (100 - \Omega^2)(300 - \Omega^2)\), so by the \(2 \times 2\) inverse formula (Chapter 7), \[
X_1 = \frac{(200 - \Omega^2)F}{(100 - \Omega^2)(300 - \Omega^2)},
\qquad
X_2 = \frac{100F}{(100 - \Omega^2)(300 - \Omega^2)}.
\] Both blow up at \(\Omega = 10\) and \(\Omega = \sqrt{300} \approx 17.3\) rad/s: the natural frequencies. But at \(\Omega = \sqrt{200} \approx 14.1\) rad/s, \(X_1 = 0\): mass 1 stands still, even though it is the one being pushed, while mass 2 moves with amplitude \(X_2 = -F/100\). Mass 2 pulls on mass 1, through the middle spring, with a force that exactly cancels the push.
This is the principle of the tuned mass damper. A large mass attached to a vibrating structure by a spring, tuned to the troublesome frequency, absorbs the vibration. The 101-storey Taipei 101 tower has a 660-tonne steel ball hanging near its top for this reason.
Open the normal modes app shaking mass 1 at 14.14 rad/s to see mass 1 stand almost still, then move the slider towards 10 or 17.3.

title: 40  Vibrations and normal modes
text:
40.4 In code

Run this chapter’s code yourself: open the notebook in Colab, or download the Jupyter notebook or the MATLAB script.

scipy.linalg.eigh and MATLAB’s eig both solve the generalised problem \(\M{K}\vect{v} = \lambda\M{M}\vect{v}\) directly, when given both matrices.

PythonMATLAB



import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import eigh

# Example 3: the two-storey building
K = 1e6 * np.array([[12, -4], [-4, 4]])
M = 1e4 * np.diag([2, 1])
lam, V = eigh(K, M)            # solves K v = lam M v, smallest lam first
omega = np.sqrt(lam)
print(omega, omega / (2 * np.pi))
print(V / V[0])                # scale each mode so that its first entry is 1
print(np.round(V.T @ M @ V, 10))   # M-orthogonal: eigh scales them so this is I

# Example 4: amplitudes when mass 1 is shaken
K1 = np.array([[200, -100], [-100, 200]])
for Om in [5, 10.5, np.sqrt(200), 20]:
    X = np.linalg.solve(K1 - Om**2 * np.eye(2), [1, 0])
    print(round(Om, 2), np.round(X, 4))

title: 40  Vibrations and normal modes
text:
40.5 Check your understanding






TipIf every mass in a structure is doubled, what happens to the natural frequencies?





They are divided by \(\sqrt{2}\). Doubling \(\M{M}\) turns \(\M{K}\vect{v} = \omega^2\M{M}\vect{v}\) into \(\M{K}\vect{v} = \omega^2(2\M{M})\vect{v}\), which has the same mode shapes with \(\omega^2\) halved. Heavier structures vibrate more slowly; stiffer ones more quickly.









TipIn Example 1, can equal forces \(F\cos(\Omega t)\) on both masses make the second mode resonate?





No. The force vector is \(F(1, 1)\), and \(\vect{v}_2\T(1, 1) = 1 - 1 = 0\), so the second mode isn’t excited at all, whatever \(\Omega\) is. Pushing both masses the same way can only drive the mode in which they move together.









TipWhat does a natural frequency of zero mean?





That \(\M{K}\vect{v} = \zerovec\) for the mode shape \(\vect{v}\): the structure can move in that pattern without stretching any spring, so nothing pulls it back. It is a rigid-body motion, such as a whole molecule drifting, or a mechanism.

title: 40  Vibrations and normal modes
text:
40.6 Key ideas

Masses joined by springs obey \(\M{M}\ddot{\vect{x}} + \M{K}\vect{x} = \zerovec\), with a diagonal mass matrix and a symmetric stiffness matrix.
The natural frequencies and mode shapes solve the generalised eigenvalue problem \(\M{K}\vect{v} = \omega^2\M{M}\vect{v}\).
The frequencies are real, and the modes are orthogonal with respect to \(\M{M}\), because the problem is a symmetric eigenvalue problem in disguise.
Every free vibration is a sum of modes, each at its own frequency; \(\M{M}\)-orthogonality gives the amount of each from the starting state.
Forcing at a natural frequency makes the amplitudes grow without limit (resonance), unless the force doesn’t excite that mode. A tuned mass damper uses an added mass and spring to cancel the motion at one frequency.

title: 40  Vibrations and normal modes
text:
40.7 Exercises
Exercises marked † are harder: they take longer, or need an idea that the worked examples don’t show.

Two masses \(m\) hang one below the other from a fixed support: a spring \(k\) joins the support to mass 1, and another spring \(k\) joins mass 1 to mass 2. Find the natural frequencies, as multiples of \(\sqrt{k/m}\), and the mode shapes.
Solution to exercise 1
Suppose \(\M{K}\vect{v} = \lambda\M{M}\vect{v}\) and \(\M{K}\vect{w} = \mu\M{M}\vect{w}\), with \(\M{K}\) and \(\M{M}\) symmetric and \(\lambda \neq \mu\). Show that \(\vect{v}\T\M{M}\vect{w} = 0\) and \(\vect{v}\T\M{K}\vect{w} = 0\). (Hint: compute \(\vect{v}\T\M{K}\vect{w}\) in two ways.)
Solution to exercise 2
†Harder exercise. A diatomic molecule is two atoms of masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) joined by a bond that acts like a spring of stiffness \(k\), with no walls. Write down \(\M{K}\) and \(\M{M}\), and show that one natural frequency is 0 and the other is \(\omega = \sqrt{k(1/m_1 + 1/m_2)}\). Describe both modes. For carbon monoxide, \(k \approx 1900\) N/m, the atoms have masses 12 and 16 atomic mass units, and \(1 \text{ u} = 1.661 \times 10^{-27}\) kg. Find the vibration frequency in hertz. (Hint: with no walls, \(\M{K} = k\mat{1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1}\). Set \(\det(\M{K} - \omega^2\M{M}) = 0\) and take out the factor \(\omega^2\).)
Solution to exercise 3
In Example 1, both masses start at rest in their resting positions, and mass 1 is struck so that it starts with velocity 0.5 m/s. Find \(\vect{x}(t)\).
Solution to exercise 4
The lower storey of the building in Example 3 is stiffened to \(k_1 = 16\) MN/m. Find the new natural frequencies and mode shapes. Which way did the frequencies move, and how did the first mode shape change?
Solution to exercise 5
†Harder exercise. A machine of mass \(m_1\) sits on a mounting of stiffness \(k_1\), and an unbalanced motor shakes it with force \(F\cos(\Omega t)\). A small mass \(m_2\) is attached to it by a spring \(k_2\). Show that the machine doesn’t move at all when \(\Omega^2 = k_2/m_2\), whatever \(m_1\) and \(k_1\) are. If the motor runs at 50 Hz and \(m_2 = 2\) kg, what should \(k_2\) be? (Hint: write the amplitude equations \((\M{K} - \Omega^2\M{M})\vect{X} = (F, 0)\T\) and eliminate \(X_2\): the answer for \(X_1\) has a factor \(k_2 - \Omega^2 m_2\).)
Solution to exercise 6
Code. For \(n\) equal masses \(m\) joined by \(n + 1\) equal springs \(k\) between two walls, the natural frequencies are \[
\omega_j = 2\sqrt{k/m}\,\sin\frac{j\pi}{2(n + 1)},
\qquad j = 1, \dots, n.
\] Check this numerically for \(n = 10\), \(m = 1\) and \(k = 100\). Plot the first three mode shapes for \(n = 30\). What shapes are they, and what physical object does a long chain of masses and springs approximate?
