title: Appendix K — Glossary
text: A

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
Absorbing state

A state of a Markov chain that, once entered, is never left. The other states are transient. See Chapter 35.

Adjacency matrix

A table of connections: entry \((i, j)\) is 1 if item \(i\) is linked to item \(j\), and 0 otherwise. Its powers count routes. See Chapter 1 and Chapter 41.

Adjugate

The transpose of the matrix of cofactors. It gives the inverse as \(\M{A}^{-1} = \operatorname{adj}\M{A} / \det\M{A}\). See Chapter 7.

Admittance

The reciprocal \(Y = 1/Z\) of an impedance: the complex version of a conductance, used in nodal analysis of AC circuits. See Chapter 32.

Affine transformation

A linear transformation followed by a translation, \(\vect{x} \mapsto \M{M}\vect{x} + \vect{t}\). In homogeneous coordinates it is a single matrix. See Chapter 34.

Algebraic connectivity

The second smallest eigenvalue \(\lambda_2\) of a graph Laplacian. It is zero exactly when the network is in more than one piece, and small when the network has a bottleneck. See Chapter 41.

Algebraic multiplicity

The number of times an eigenvalue is repeated as a root of the characteristic polynomial. Compare geometric multiplicity. See Chapter 18.

Angle between vectors

The angle \(\theta\) with \(\vect{x} \cdot \vect{y} = \lVert\vect{x}\rVert\,\lVert\vect{y}\rVert\cos\theta\). It makes sense in any number of dimensions because of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. See Chapter 17.

Approximate minimum degree

A fast way of reordering the unknowns of a sparse system before factorising it, chosen to keep fill-in small. Compare nested dissection. See Chapter 26.

Augmented matrix

The matrix \([\M{A} \mid \vect{b}]\) formed by adding the right-hand side of a linear system as an extra column. See Chapter 10 and Chapter 11.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
B

Back substitution

Solving an upper triangular system from the last equation upwards. See Chapter 11.

Backward error analysis

Judging a method by asking whether its computed answer is the exact answer to a slightly different problem, with a change in the data about as small as the rounding errors in storing it. If so, the method is backward stable. See Chapter 24.

Backward stable

Describes a method whose computed answer is the exact answer to a problem within rounding error of the one posed. Its remaining error is then due only to the problem’s conditioning. See Chapter 24.

Banded matrix

A matrix whose non-zero entries all lie within a fixed distance of the main diagonal. Elimination without row swaps keeps the band. See Chapter 26.

Basin of attraction

The set of starting points from which an iterative method, such as Newton’s method, reaches a particular solution. See Chapter 28.

Basis

A set of linearly independent vectors that spans a subspace. Every vector in the subspace is a combination of them in exactly one way. See Chapter 15.

BiCGSTAB

A Krylov method for large sparse systems whose matrix is not symmetric. See Chapter 27.

Bidiagonal matrix

A matrix whose only non-zero entries are on the main diagonal and just above it. Computing the SVD starts by reducing a matrix to this form with Householder reflections. See Chapter 30.

Block diagonal matrix

A matrix made of square blocks down the main diagonal, with zeros everywhere else. The Laplacian of a network in separate pieces has this form when the nodes of each piece are numbered together. See Chapter 41.

Block tridiagonal matrix

A matrix whose blocks follow a tridiagonal pattern: non-zero blocks only on the diagonal and just above and below it. The five-point stencil gives this form. See Chapter 33.

Broyden’s method

A quasi-Newton method for systems of equations, which avoids computing the Jacobian at every step. See Chapter 28.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
C

Cancellation

The loss of accuracy when two nearly equal numbers are subtracted, leaving only their uncertain digits. See Chapter 24.

Cauchy–Schwarz inequality

\(\lvert\vect{x} \cdot \vect{y}\rvert \le \lVert\vect{x}\rVert\,\lVert\vect{y}\rVert\), in any number of dimensions. See Chapter 17.

Central difference

The approximation \(u''(x) \approx \bigl(u(x - h) - 2u(x) + u(x + h)\bigr)/h^2\) to a second derivative, using a point and its two neighbours. See Chapter 33.

Centre

An equilibrium of \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\vect{x}\) surrounded by closed orbits, which happens when the eigenvalues are purely imaginary. See Chapter 23.

Chain rule

For functions of several variables, the derivative of a composition is the product of the Jacobians: the chain rule becomes matrix multiplication. See Chapter 22.

Characteristic equation

The equation \(\det(\M{A} - \lambda\M{I}) = 0\), whose solutions are the eigenvalues of \(\M{A}\). See Chapter 18.

Characteristic polynomial

The polynomial \(\det(\M{A} - \lambda\M{I})\), whose roots are the eigenvalues of \(\M{A}\). Setting it to zero gives the characteristic equation. See Chapter 18.

Cholesky factorisation

The factorisation \(\M{A} = \M{L}\M{L}\T\) of a symmetric positive definite matrix, with \(\M{L}\) lower triangular with positive diagonal entries. See Chapter 20.

Coefficient of determination

\(R^2\): the fraction of the variation in the data that a regression model explains. See Chapter 37.

Cofactor

The determinant left after crossing out row \(i\) and column \(j\) of a square matrix (the minor), multiplied by \((-1)^{i+j}\). See Chapter 6 and Chapter 7.

Cofactor expansion

Working out a determinant along a row or column: multiply each entry by its cofactor and add. See Chapter 6.

Collinearity

Near-dependence between the explanatory variables in a regression, which makes the design matrix ill-conditioned and the coefficients unreliable. See Chapter 37.

Column space

The span of the columns of a matrix: every vector \(\M{A}\vect{x}\). \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) has a solution exactly when \(\vect{b}\) is in it. See Chapter 16.

Column vector

A matrix with one column. In this book, vectors are columns unless they are transposed. See Chapter 1.

Column-stochastic matrix

A matrix with no negative entries whose columns each add up to 1, such as the transition matrix of a Markov chain. See Chapter 35.

Complete pivoting

Choosing each pivot as the largest entry, in size, in the whole of the remaining submatrix, and swapping both rows and columns to bring it into place. Compare partial pivoting. See Chapter 25.

Composition

Doing one transformation after another. “Apply \(\M{B}\), then \(\M{A}\)” has matrix \(\M{A}\M{B}\). See Chapter 5.

Compressed sparse row (CSR)

The most common way of storing a sparse matrix, using three lists: the non-zero values, their column numbers, and where each row starts. See Chapter 26.

Compression

The state of a truss member that is being pushed along its length. Compare tension. See Chapter 31.

Condition number

For a square matrix, the ratio \(\sigma_1/\sigma_n\) of its largest to smallest singular value. It measures how much errors can be magnified when solving \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\). See Chapter 21 and Chapter 24.

Conductance matrix

The symmetric matrix \(\M{G}\) of nodal analysis, with \(\M{G}\vect{v} = \vect{i}\) relating node voltages to injected currents; \(\M{G} = \M{A}\T\M{C}\M{A}\). See Chapter 32.

Conjugate gradient method

An iterative method for symmetric positive definite systems that minimises \(\tfrac{1}{2}\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b}\T\vect{x}\) along mutually conjugate directions. See Chapter 27.

Conjugate pairs

Complex eigenvalues of a real matrix always come in pairs \(\alpha \pm i\beta\), because the characteristic polynomial has real coefficients. See Chapter 18.

Connected component

A piece of a network in which every node can reach every other by following edges. The number of components is the number of zero eigenvalues of the graph Laplacian. See Chapter 41.

Consistent system

A system of equations with at least one solution. One with no solution is inconsistent. See Chapter 10.

Continuation

Solving a sequence of problems that change gradually from an easy one to the one you want, starting each from the last answer, to give Newton’s method good starting guesses. See Chapter 28.

Coordinates

The coefficients that write a vector as a combination of the vectors of a basis. See Chapter 15.

Covariance matrix

For data with \(p\) variables, the \(p \times p\) symmetric matrix whose entry \((i, j)\) is the covariance of variables \(i\) and \(j\), with the variances on the diagonal. See Chapter 20 and Chapter 21.

Cubic convergence

Convergence in which the number of correct digits roughly triples at each step, as in Rayleigh quotient iteration for symmetric matrices. Compare quadratic convergence. See Chapter 29.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
D

Damping


In PageRank, following a link with probability \(d\) and jumping to a random page otherwise, which makes the chain regular. See Chapter 35. (2) In vibrations, a friction-like force \(\M{C}\dot{\vect{x}}\) that removes energy and keeps resonant peaks finite. See Chapter 40.


Defective matrix

A square matrix without enough independent eigenvectors to form a basis, such as a shear. It can’t be diagonalised. See Chapter 18 and Chapter 19.

Deflation

Once an eigenvalue has converged, removing the last row and column and carrying on with a smaller matrix. See Chapter 29.

Degree

The number of edges at a node of a network: the sum of its row of the adjacency matrix. See Chapter 41.

Denavit–Hartenberg convention

The standard way of setting out a robot arm in three dimensions, with one \(4 \times 4\) matrix per joint. See Chapter 34.

Dependence relation

A combination of vectors that adds up to \(\zerovec\) without all the coefficients being zero. Vectors are linearly dependent exactly when one exists. See Chapter 14.

Design matrix

The matrix \(\M{X}\) of a linear model \(\vect{y} \approx \M{X}\vect{\beta}\): a column of 1s for the intercept and one column per explanatory variable. See Chapter 37.

Determinant

The factor by which a square matrix scales areas (in 2D) or volumes (in 3D), with a negative sign when it reverses orientation. See Chapter 6.

Diagonal matrix

A square matrix whose entries off the main diagonal are all zero. It stretches space along the axes. See Chapter 4.

Diagonalisation

Writing \(\M{A} = \M{P}\M{D}\M{P}^{-1}\), with the eigenvectors of \(\M{A}\) as the columns of \(\M{P}\) and its eigenvalues on the diagonal of \(\M{D}\). See Chapter 19.

Diagonally dominant

Describes a matrix whose diagonal entry in each row is larger in size than the sum of the sizes of the other entries in that row (strictly diagonally dominant), or at least as large. See Chapter 27 and Chapter 25.

Dimension

The number of vectors in any basis of a subspace: 1 for a line, 2 for a plane, \(n\) for \(\R^n\). See Chapter 15.

Direct intensity

The amount of a pollutant, such as carbon dioxide, that a sector emits for each £1 of its own output. Compare footprint. See Chapter 42.

Direct method

A method that gives the answer, up to rounding, after a fixed number of steps, such as Gaussian elimination. Compare iterative method. See Chapter 27.

Distance

The distance between \(\vect{x}\) and \(\vect{y}\) is \(\lVert\vect{x} - \vect{y}\rVert\). See Chapter 17.

Dominant eigenvalue

The eigenvalue of largest absolute value, when it is strictly larger than all the others. It decides the long-run behaviour of \(\M{A}^k\vect{x}\). See Chapter 19.

Dot product

For two lists of numbers of the same length, the sum of the products of matching entries: \((1, 2, 3) \cdot (4, 5, 6) = 4 + 10 + 18 = 32\). See the Refresher and Chapter 3.

Double precision

The standard floating-point format, which keeps 53 binary digits (about 16 decimal digits) and handles numbers up to about \(10^{308}\). See Chapter 24.

Driving frequency

The frequency \(\Omega\) of a force that pushes a structure back and forth, \(\vect{f}\cos(\Omega t)\). See Chapter 40.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
E

Eckart–Young theorem

Keeping the \(k\) largest singular values of the SVD gives the closest matrix of rank \(k\), measuring closeness by the square root of the sum of the squared differences of the entries. See Chapter 21.

Edge

A connection between two nodes of a network. See Chapter 41.

Eigenspace

All the eigenvectors for one eigenvalue \(\lambda\), together with \(\zerovec\): the null space of \(\M{A} - \lambda\M{I}\). See Chapter 18.

Eigenvalue

A number \(\lambda\) for which \(\M{A}\vect{v} = \lambda\vect{v}\) has a non-zero solution \(\vect{v}\), the eigenvector: the factor by which \(\M{A}\) stretches that direction. See Chapter 18.

Eigenvector

A non-zero vector that a matrix only stretches (or flips), so that it stays on the same line through the origin: \(\M{A}\vect{v} = \lambda\vect{v}\). The number \(\lambda\) is the matching eigenvalue. See Chapter 9 and Chapter 18.

Eigenvector centrality

A measure of how important each node of a network is: the entries of the eigenvector of the adjacency matrix for its largest eigenvalue. A node scores highly if its neighbours do. See Chapter 41.

Elasticity

In population models, the proportional change in the growth rate \(\lambda\) for a proportional change in one matrix entry. See Chapter 36.

Enlargement

The transformation \(k\M{I}\), which scales every vector by \(k\) about the origin. See Chapter 4.

Entry

One of the numbers in a matrix. The entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\) of \(\M{A}\) is written \(a_{ij}\). See Chapter 1.

Equal matrices

Two matrices are equal when they have the same size and every pair of corresponding entries is equal. See Chapter 1.

Equilibration

Dividing each row of a system by its largest entry before elimination, so that all rows have similar sizes. See Chapter 25.

Equilibrium

A state that does not change. For \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\vect{x}\), the origin is an equilibrium, and it is stable if every solution tends to it. See Chapter 23.

Equilibrium matrix

The matrix whose columns give the forces that each member force and reaction exerts on the joints of a truss. See Chapter 31.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
F

Fecundity

In a population model, the average number of female offspring, surviving to the next count, produced by each female in a class: the first row of a Leslie matrix. See Chapter 36.

Fiedler vector

The eigenvector of a graph Laplacian for its second smallest eigenvalue. The signs of its entries split the network into two well-separated groups. See Chapter 41.

Fill-in

New non-zero entries created in the factors of a sparse matrix during elimination. See Chapter 26.

Final demand

What households, the government and other countries buy from a sector, as opposed to what other sectors buy. See Chapter 42.

Finite difference

An approximation to a derivative from values at neighbouring grid points, such as \(u'' \approx (u_{i-1} - 2u_i + u_{i+1})/h^2\). See Chapter 33.

Finite difference method

Replacing the derivatives in a differential equation by differences between values on a grid, which turns it into a linear system. See Chapter 33.

Five-point stencil

The finite difference version of Laplace’s equation on a square grid, \(4u_{i,j} - u_{i-1,j} - u_{i+1,j} - u_{i,j-1} - u_{i,j+1} = 0\): each value is the average of its four neighbours. See Chapter 33.

Floating-point number

A number stored as \(\pm m \times 2^e\) with a fixed number of binary digits in \(m\); double precision keeps about 16 significant decimal digits. See Chapter 24.

Flops

Floating-point operations. A method’s running time is roughly proportional to the number of flops it needs. See Chapter 26.

Footprint

The total amount of a pollutant emitted, anywhere in the economy, to deliver £1 of a sector’s product to a final buyer. Compare direct intensity. See Chapter 42.

Forward kinematics

Finding the position and orientation of a robot’s hand from its joint angles, as a product of transformation matrices. The reverse problem is inverse kinematics. See Chapter 34.

Forward substitution

Solving a lower triangular system from the first equation downwards. See Chapter 13.

Free variable

An unknown whose column has no pivot in the reduced row echelon form. It can take any value, and the pivot variables are then found from it. See Chapter 12.

Fundamental matrix

For an absorbing Markov chain, \(\M{N} = (\M{I} - \M{Q})^{-1}\), where \(\M{Q}\) holds the probabilities of moving between transient states. Its entries are expected numbers of visits, its column sums the expected times until absorption. See Chapter 35.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
G

Gauss–Jordan elimination

Elimination continued until the matrix reaches reduced row echelon form, so that the solution can be read straight off. See Chapter 12.

Gauss–Seidel method

An iterative method that solves each equation for its own unknown, using the newest values of the others as soon as they are available. See Chapter 27.

Generalised eigenvalue problem

The problem \(\M{K}\vect{v} = \lambda\M{M}\vect{v}\), with a matrix \(\M{M}\) in place of \(\M{I}\). See Chapter 40.

Geometric multiplicity

The dimension of the eigenspace of an eigenvalue: the number of independent eigenvectors it has. It is never more than the algebraic multiplicity. See Chapter 18.

GMRES

A Krylov method for large sparse systems whose matrix is not symmetric. See Chapter 27.

Google matrix

The matrix \(\M{G} = d\M{M} + \frac{1 - d}{n}\vect{1}\vect{1}\T\) used by PageRank, which mixes following links with jumping to a random page. Its entries are all positive, so it has a unique steady state. See Chapter 35.

Gradient

The column vector \(\nabla f\) of the partial derivatives of a scalar function \(f(\vect{x})\). It points in the direction of steepest increase, perpendicular to the contours. See Chapter 22.

Gradient descent

Minimising a function by repeatedly stepping in the direction of \(-\nabla f\). See Chapter 22.

Gram–Schmidt process

A method for turning independent vectors into orthonormal vectors with the same span. See Chapter 17.

Graph Laplacian

The matrix \(\M{L} = \M{D} - \M{A}\) of a network, with the degrees of the nodes on its diagonal and \(-1\) for each edge. It is symmetric positive semidefinite, with one zero eigenvalue for each piece of the network. See Chapter 41.

Ground

The reference node of a circuit, whose voltage is taken to be 0. See Chapter 32.

Growth factor

The largest entry produced during elimination divided by the largest entry of the original matrix. Large growth magnifies rounding errors. See Chapter 25.

Growth rate

In a population model, the dominant eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\) of the matrix: in the long run the population grows by a factor \(\lambda_1\) each step. See Chapter 36.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
H

Hamiltonian

The Hermitian matrix \(\M{H}\) representing the energy of a quantum system. It determines how the state changes in time, through the Schrödinger equation. See Chapter 38.

Hermitian matrix

A complex square matrix equal to its conjugate transpose: the complex version of a symmetric matrix. Its eigenvalues are real. See Chapter 38.

Hessenberg form

A matrix that is zero below the first subdiagonal (tridiagonal, if the matrix is symmetric). The QR algorithm reduces a matrix to this form first, so that each step is cheaper. See Chapter 29.

Hessian

The symmetric matrix of second partial derivatives \(\partial^2 f/\partial x_i\partial x_j\) of a scalar function. Its eigenvalues classify stationary points. See Chapter 22.

Hilbert matrix

The \(n \times n\) matrix with entries \(h_{ij} = 1/(i + j - 1)\), a standard example of an ill-conditioned matrix. See Chapter 24.

Hill cipher

A cipher that encrypts blocks of letters by multiplying them by a key matrix modulo 26. See Chapter 39.

Homogeneous coordinates

Representing the point \((x, y)\) as \((x, y, 1)\) (or \((x, y, z)\) as \((x, y, z, 1)\)), so that translations and perspective become matrix multiplications. See Chapter 34.

Homogeneous system

A system \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec\), with every right-hand side zero. It always has the solution \(\vect{x} = \zerovec\). See Chapter 10.

Householder QR

Computing a QR factorisation with Householder reflections, the way elimination uses row operations. It is backward stable. See Chapter 30.

Householder reflection

The orthogonal matrix \(\M{I} - 2\vect{v}\vect{v}\T/(\vect{v}\T\vect{v})\), a reflection, chosen to zero all but the first entry of a vector. See Chapter 30.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
I

Identity matrix

The square matrix \(\M{I}\) with 1 on the main diagonal and 0 elsewhere. Multiplying by it changes nothing. See Chapter 3.

Ill-conditioned

Describes a problem whose answer changes a lot when its data change a little, such as a system with a large condition number. See Chapter 24.

Impedance

The complex number that plays the part of resistance for a capacitor or inductor at angular frequency \(\omega\): \(Z_C = 1/(j\omega C)\) and \(Z_L = j\omega L\). See Chapter 32.

Incidence matrix

For a network, the matrix with one row per edge, holding \(+1\) and \(-1\) in the columns of the two nodes it joins. See Chapter 32.

Inconsistent system

A system of equations with no solution. See consistent system and Chapter 10.

Inertia tensor

The symmetric matrix \(\M{I}\) with \(\vect{L} = \M{I}\vect{\omega}\), relating a rigid body’s angular velocity to its angular momentum. Its eigenvectors are the principal axes. See Chapter 38.

Input–output table

A table recording how much each industry buys from every other, the starting point of Leontief’s model of an economy. See Chapter 42.

Invariant line

A line that a transformation maps onto itself, though the points on it may move along it. See Chapter 9.

Invariant point

A point that a transformation leaves where it is: \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{x}\). A whole line of them is a line of invariant points. See Chapter 9.

Inverse

The matrix \(\M{A}^{-1}\) that undoes \(\M{A}\), so that \(\M{A}^{-1}\M{A} = \M{I}\). See Chapter 7.

Inverse iteration

The power method applied to \((\M{A} - \mu\M{I})^{-1}\), which finds the eigenvalue of \(\M{A}\) closest to the shift \(\mu\). See Chapter 29.

Inverse kinematics

Finding the joint angles that put a robot’s hand at a chosen point: the reverse of forward kinematics. It is usually solved by Newton’s method. See Chapter 34.

Inverse modulo n

A number \(a^{-1}\) with \(aa^{-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}\), which exists exactly when \(\gcd(a, n) = 1\). See Chapter 39.

Invertible matrix

A square matrix that has an inverse; the same as a non-singular matrix. See Chapter 7.

Iteration matrix

The matrix \(\M{T}\) in an iteration \(\vect{x}_{k+1} = \M{T}\vect{x}_k + \vect{c}\); the error is multiplied by \(\M{T}\) at each step. See Chapter 27.

Iterative method

A method that starts from a guess and improves it step by step until it is accurate enough, such as Jacobi, Gauss–Seidel or conjugate gradients. Compare direct method. See Chapter 27.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
J

Jacobi method

An iterative method that solves each equation for its own unknown, using the previous values of all the others. See Chapter 27.

Jacobian

The \(m \times n\) matrix of partial derivatives \(\partial f_i/\partial x_j\) of a function from \(\R^n\) to \(\R^m\): the matrix of its best linear approximation at a point. See Chapter 22.

Joint

A point of a truss where members meet. See Chapter 31.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
K

Key matrix

The matrix \(\M{K}\) that a Hill cipher multiplies each block of letters by. See Chapter 39.

Kirchhoff’s current law

At every node of a circuit, the total current flowing out equals the total current flowing in. See Chapter 32.

Kirchhoff’s voltage law

Around any closed loop of a circuit, the voltage changes add up to zero. See Chapter 32.

Known-plaintext attack

Recovering a cipher’s key from a piece of message whose plain and encrypted versions are both known. See Chapter 39.

Kronecker product

The block matrix \(\M{A} \otimes \M{B}\) whose \((i, j)\) block is \(a_{ij}\M{B}\); it builds the matrices of grid problems in two and three dimensions. See Chapter 33.

Krylov method

An iterative method that builds its answer from the vectors \(\vect{b}, \M{A}\vect{b}, \M{A}^2\vect{b}, \dots\), such as conjugate gradients, GMRES and BiCGSTAB for linear systems, and Lanczos and Arnoldi for eigenvalues. See Chapter 27 and Chapter 29.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
L

Laplace’s equation

The equation \(\partial^2 u/\partial x^2 + \partial^2 u/\partial y^2 = 0\), satisfied by the steady temperature in a plate with no heat sources. See Chapter 33.

Leading principal minor

The determinant of a top-left \(k \times k\) block of a matrix. A symmetric matrix is positive definite exactly when all of them are positive. See Chapter 20.

Learning rate

Another name for the step size in gradient descent. See Chapter 22.

Least squares

Choosing \(\vect{x}\) to make the sum of the squares of the errors in \(\M{A}\vect{x} \approx \vect{b}\) as small as possible, by solving the normal equations. See Chapter 17.

Least-squares solution

The vector \(\hat{\vect{x}}\) that makes \(\lVert\M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b}\rVert^2\) as small as possible. See least squares and Chapter 17.

Lefkovitch matrix

A population matrix based on stages (such as eggs, juveniles and adults) rather than ages, with fecundities in the first row, the chances of staying in each stage on the diagonal, and the chances of growing into the next stage below it. See Chapter 36.

Left eigenvector

A non-zero vector \(\vect{v}\) with \(\vect{v}\T\M{A} = \lambda\vect{v}\T\): an eigenvector of \(\M{A}\T\). See Chapter 36.

Left null space

The null space of \(\M{A}\T\): the combinations of the rows of \(\M{A}\) that add up to zero. See Chapter 16.

Left singular vectors

The columns \(\vect{u}_i\) of \(\M{U}\) in the SVD \(\M{A} = \M{U}\M{\Sigma}\M{V}\T\): the perpendicular output directions. See Chapter 21.

Leontief inverse

The matrix \((\M{I} - \M{A})^{-1}\) of an input–output model, giving the total output, direct and indirect, needed from each industry for each £1 of final demand. See Chapter 42.

Leslie matrix

A population projection matrix with fecundities in its first row and survival rates just below the diagonal. See Chapter 19 and Chapter 36.

Line of invariant points

A line every point of which a transformation leaves where it is, such as the mirror of a reflection or the axis of a rotation in three dimensions. A plane of invariant points is the same in a plane. See Chapter 9.

Line search

In Newton’s method, trying half the step, then a quarter, and so on, whenever the full step makes the equations further from being satisfied. See Chapter 28.

Linear combination

A sum of scaled vectors, such as \(s\vect{a} + t\vect{b}\). See Chapter 2.

Linear equation

An equation in which the unknowns are only multiplied by numbers and added, such as \(3x + 2y - z = 1\). See Chapter 1 and Chapter 10.

Linear independence

Vectors are linearly independent if no combination of them gives \(\zerovec\) except the one with all coefficients zero. Otherwise they are linearly dependent, and one of them is a combination of the others. See Chapter 14.

Linear model

A prediction \(y \approx \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \dots + \beta_px_p\) of one quantity from others, fitted by least squares. See Chapter 37.

Linear transformation

A transformation with \(\M{A}(s\vect{x} + t\vect{y}) = s\M{A}\vect{x} + t\M{A}\vect{y}\). Every matrix gives one, and in the plane or space every one is given by a matrix. See Chapter 4.

Linearly dependent

See linear independence and dependence relation.

Loadings

The entries of a principal component, which say how much each original variable contributes to it. See Chapter 37.

Lower triangular matrix

See triangular matrix.

Low-pass filter

A circuit that lets slowly varying signals through but weakens fast ones. See Chapter 32.

Low-rank approximation

A matrix of rank \(k\) close to a given matrix. Keeping the first \(k\) terms of the SVD gives the closest one (the Eckart–Young theorem). See Chapter 21.

LU decomposition

Writing a square matrix as \(\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}\), with \(\M{L}\) lower triangular (holding the multipliers of elimination) and \(\M{U}\) upper triangular. With row swaps, \(\M{P}\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}\). See Chapter 13.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
M

Machine epsilon

The gap between 1 and the next larger floating-point number, about \(2.2 \times 10^{-16}\) in double precision. See Chapter 24.

Main diagonal

The entries \(a_{11}, a_{22}, \dots\) of a square matrix, running from top left to bottom right. See Chapter 1.

Markov chain

A process that moves between states at random, with probabilities that depend only on the current state, described by \(\vect{x}_{k+1} = \M{M}\vect{x}_k\) with a matrix whose columns add to 1. See Chapter 19 and Chapter 35.

Mass matrix

The matrix \(\M{M}\) in \(\M{M}\ddot{\vect{x}} + \M{K}\vect{x} = \zerovec\); for point masses it is \(\operatorname{diag}(m_1, \dots, m_n)\). See Chapter 40.

Matrix

A rectangular array of numbers. An \(m \times n\) matrix has \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns. See Chapter 1.

Matrix exponential

The matrix \(e^{\M{A}t} = \M{I} + \M{A}t + (\M{A}t)^2/2! + \cdots\), which solves \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\vect{x}\) as \(\vect{x}(t) = e^{\M{A}t}\vect{x}_0\). See Chapter 23.

Mechanism

A structure that can move without any member changing length; its equilibrium matrix doesn’t have full row rank, and its stiffness matrix is singular. See Chapter 31.

Member

One of the straight bars of a truss, joined at its ends to joints and carrying only tension or compression. See Chapter 31.

Minor

The determinant of the matrix left when the row and column of an entry are crossed out. With a sign attached, it is the cofactor. See Chapter 6.

Mode

A pattern that evolves on its own in a linear system: an eigenvector, multiplied by \(\lambda^k\) in a discrete process or by \(e^{\lambda t}\) in a continuous one. See Chapter 19 and Chapter 23.

Mode shape

The pattern in which a structure moves when it vibrates at one of its natural frequencies: an eigenvector of \(\M{K}\vect{v} = \omega^2\M{M}\vect{v}\). See Chapter 40.

Model matrix

The matrix that places an object in a 3D scene, setting its position, orientation and size. Compare view matrix. See Chapter 34.

Modified Gram–Schmidt

A rearrangement of the Gram–Schmidt process that subtracts each component from all the remaining columns as soon as it is found. In floating point it keeps the vectors much closer to perpendicular than the classical version. See Chapter 30.

Modified nodal analysis

Nodal analysis extended with the currents through voltage sources as extra unknowns. See Chapter 32.

Modular arithmetic

Arithmetic in which only the remainder on division by a fixed number is kept, as modulo 26 in the Hill cipher. See inverse modulo n and Chapter 39.

Moments of inertia

The diagonal entries of the inertia tensor, such as \(I_{xx} = \sum m(y^2 + z^2)\). The off-diagonal entries are the products of inertia, and the eigenvalues are the principal moments of inertia. See Chapter 38.

Multiple regression

Predicting one quantity from several others with a linear model, fitted by least squares. See Chapter 37.

Multiplier

In Gaussian elimination, the number \(m_{ik} = a_{ik}/a_{kk}\) such that subtracting \(m_{ik}\) times the pivot row clears the entry below the pivot. See Chapter 11.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
N

Natural frequency

A frequency at which a structure vibrates freely when disturbed. The natural frequencies \(\omega\) of a system of masses and springs solve \(\det(\M{K} - \omega^2\M{M}) = 0\). See Chapter 40.

Nested dissection

A way of reordering the unknowns of a sparse system before factorising it, chosen to keep fill-in small. Compare approximate minimum degree. See Chapter 26.

Network

A set of nodes joined by edges, such as friendships, web pages or roads between towns. See Chapter 41.

Newton’s method

Solving \(\vect{f}(\vect{x}) = \zerovec\) by repeatedly solving the linear system \(\M{J}(\vect{x}_k)\,\Delta\vect{x} = -\vect{f}(\vect{x}_k)\) and setting \(\vect{x}_{k+1} = \vect{x}_k + \Delta\vect{x}\). See Chapter 28.

Node


A point of a network or circuit where edges or components join. See Chapter 41 and Chapter 32. (2) An equilibrium of \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\vect{x}\) whose eigenvalues are real with the same sign: stable if both are negative. See Chapter 23.


Norm

A measure of the size of a vector, such as the length \(\lVert\vect{x}\rVert_2\) or the largest entry \(\lVert\vect{x}\rVert_\infty\); for a matrix, the most it stretches any vector. See Chapter 17 and Chapter 24.

Normal equations

\(\M{A}\T\M{A}\hat{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\T\vect{b}\), whose solution is the least-squares solution of \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\). See Chapter 17.

Normal stress

A diagonal entry of a stress matrix: a pull (\(+\)) or push (\(-\)) straight across a surface. Compare shear stress. See Chapter 20.

Null space

All the solutions of \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec\). Its dimension is the nullity. See Chapter 16.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
O

Orientation

Whether a transformation keeps the plane or space the same way round, or turns it into its mirror image. It is recorded by the sign of the determinant. See Chapter 6.

Orthogonal matrix

A square matrix \(\M{Q}\) with \(\M{Q}\T\M{Q} = \M{I}\). It preserves lengths and angles: a rotation or a reflection. See Chapter 7.

Orthogonal vectors

Vectors at right angles: their dot product is zero. Orthonormal vectors are orthogonal and of length 1. See Chapter 17.

Orthonormal vectors

Vectors that each have length 1 and are perpendicular in pairs. See Chapter 17.

Output multiplier

The total output across a whole economy generated by £1 of final demand for one sector: a column sum of the Leontief inverse. See Chapter 42.

Overdetermined system

A system with more equations than unknowns. It usually has no solution, and is solved by least squares instead. Compare underdetermined system. See Chapter 12.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
P

PageRank

The steady state of a random surfer on the web, following links with probability \(d\) and jumping to a random page otherwise. See Chapter 35.

Parallelepiped

The slanted box with three vectors as its edges. The size of the determinant of the matrix with those columns is its volume. See Chapter 6.

Partial pivoting

Swapping rows during elimination so that each pivot is the largest entry, in size, in its column on or below the diagonal. See Chapter 13 and Chapter 25.

Particular solution

Any one solution of \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\). Every solution is a particular solution plus a solution of \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec\). See Chapter 10.

Pauli matrices

The \(2 \times 2\) Hermitian matrices that represent measurements of spin along the three axes in quantum mechanics. See Chapter 38.

Permutation matrix

The identity matrix with its rows in a different order. Multiplying by it reorders the rows of a matrix. See Chapter 13.

Perpendicular axis theorem

For a flat body, the moment of inertia about the axis perpendicular to it is the sum of the moments about two perpendicular axes in its plane. See Chapter 38.

Perspective projection

The projection that makes distant objects look smaller: a point at depth \(-z\) in front of a camera with focal length \(d\) appears at \((dx/(-z), \; dy/(-z))\). See Chapter 34.

Phase portrait

A picture of the paths followed by the solutions of a system of two differential equations in the plane. See Chapter 23.

Phasor

A complex number representing a sinusoidal voltage or current: its size is the amplitude and its angle is the phase. See Chapter 32.

Pin

A truss support that can push in any direction, so it provides two unknown reaction components. Compare roller. See Chapter 31.

Pivot

The entry used to clear the others in its column during elimination: in echelon form, the first non-zero entry of each row. It must not be zero, and in practice should not be small. See Chapter 11 and Chapter 25.

Pivot columns

The columns of a matrix that contain pivots after elimination. The original vectors in these columns form a basis for the column space. See Chapter 15 and Chapter 16.

Pivot variables

The unknowns whose columns contain a pivot, also called basic variables. The others are free variables. See Chapter 12.

Positive definite matrix

A symmetric matrix with \(\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x} > 0\) for every \(\vect{x} \neq \zerovec\); equivalently, with all eigenvalues positive. Positive semidefinite allows \(\ge 0\). See Chapter 20.

Positive semidefinite matrix

A symmetric matrix with \(\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x} \ge 0\) for every \(\vect{x}\): its eigenvalues are all at least 0. \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\) is always positive semidefinite. See Chapter 20.

Power method

Finding the dominant eigenvector by repeatedly multiplying a vector by \(\M{A}\) and rescaling it. See Chapter 29.

Preconditioner

An approximation \(\M{M}\) to \(\M{A}\), easy to solve with, used to transform a system so that iterative methods converge faster. See Chapter 27.

Principal axes

The eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix, such as those of a quadratic form or an inertia tensor: the perpendicular directions along which it acts as a pure stretch. See Chapter 20 and Chapter 38.

Principal component analysis

Describing data by its coordinates along the directions of greatest variance, the principal components: the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, or the right singular vectors of the centred data. See Chapter 21.

Principal components

The directions of greatest spread in a set of data: the eigenvectors of its covariance matrix, or the right singular vectors of the centred data matrix. See Chapter 21.

Principal directions

The eigenvectors of a stress matrix, along which there is no shear stress. See Chapter 20.

Principal stresses

The eigenvalues of a stress matrix: the normal stresses along the perpendicular directions in which there is no shear. See Chapter 20.

Productive economy

An economy in which \(\M{I} - \M{A}\) has an inverse with no negative entries, so that it can meet any final demand. See Chapter 42.

Projection

The closest point to a vector in a line or subspace, found by dropping a perpendicular. See Chapter 4 and Chapter 17.

Projection matrix

The matrix \(\M{P} = \M{A}(\M{A}\T\M{A})^{-1}\M{A}\T\) that projects any vector onto the column space of \(\M{A}\). See Chapter 17.

Pseudoinverse

The matrix \(\M{A}^+ = \M{V}\M{\Sigma}^+\M{U}\T\), built from the SVD by inverting the non-zero singular values. \(\M{A}^+\vect{b}\) is the shortest least-squares solution of \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\). See Chapter 21.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
Q

QR algorithm

The standard method for computing all eigenvalues: factorise \(\M{A}_k = \M{Q}_k\M{R}_k\), set \(\M{A}_{k+1} = \M{R}_k\M{Q}_k\), and repeat. See Chapter 29.

QR factorisation

Writing \(\M{A} = \M{Q}\M{R}\), with \(\M{Q}\) having orthonormal columns and \(\M{R}\) upper triangular. See Chapter 17 and Chapter 30.

Quadratic convergence

Convergence in which each error is roughly proportional to the square of the previous one, so the number of correct digits roughly doubles at each step. See Chapter 28.

Quadratic form

A function \(\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x}\) with \(\M{A}\) symmetric, such as \(ax^2 + 2bxy + cy^2\). See Chapter 20.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
R

\(\R^n\)

The set of all vectors with \(n\) real-number entries: the plane is \(\R^2\) and ordinary space is \(\R^3\). See Chapter 14.

Rabi oscillation

The flipping back and forth of a quantum spin between two states, the basis of MRI and of single-qubit operations in quantum computers. See Chapter 38.

Rank

The number of pivots in the echelon form of a matrix: the number of independent rows. See Chapter 12.

Rank–nullity theorem

For a matrix with \(n\) columns, rank plus nullity equals \(n\). See Chapter 16.

Rayleigh quotient

The estimate \(\vect{q}\T\M{A}\vect{q}\) of an eigenvalue, for an approximate eigenvector \(\vect{q}\) of length 1. See Chapter 29.

Rayleigh quotient iteration

Shifted inverse iteration that uses the current Rayleigh quotient as the shift at every step. For symmetric matrices it converges cubically. See Chapter 29.

Reactions

The forces that a structure’s supports provide. See Chapter 31.

Reduced row echelon form

A row echelon form in which every pivot is 1 and is the only non-zero entry in its column. Each matrix has exactly one. See Chapter 12.

Redundant member

A member of a statically indeterminate truss beyond those needed for equilibrium. A truss with \(m\) members, \(r\) reaction components and \(j\) joints has \(m + r - 2j\) of them. See Chapter 31.

Regular Markov chain

A Markov chain some power of whose transition matrix has all its entries positive. It has a unique steady state, which every starting distribution approaches. See Chapter 35.

Reproductive value

An entry of the left eigenvector of a population matrix: how much an individual in that stage will contribute to the future population. See Chapter 36.

Residual

The vector \(\vect{b} - \M{A}\hat{\vect{x}}\), showing how well an approximate solution \(\hat{\vect{x}}\) satisfies \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\). See Chapter 10 and Chapter 24.

Resonance

The large response of a structure pushed at, or near, one of its natural frequencies. See Chapter 40.

Right singular vectors

The columns \(\vect{v}_i\) of \(\M{V}\) in the SVD \(\M{A} = \M{U}\M{\Sigma}\M{V}\T\): perpendicular input directions that \(\M{A}\) sends to perpendicular output directions. See Chapter 21.

Right-hand rule

The convention that fixes which way a rotation in three dimensions is positive: point your right thumb along the axis, and your fingers curl in the positive direction. See Chapter 8.

Rigid-body mode

A mode with natural frequency zero, in which a structure moves without stretching any spring. See Chapter 40.

Roller

A truss support that can only push perpendicular to the surface it rolls on, so it provides one unknown reaction component. Compare pin. See Chapter 31.

Rotation

The transformation that turns the plane by an angle \(\theta\) about the origin, with matrix \(\mat{\cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta}\) for an anticlockwise turn. See Chapter 4.

Row echelon form

A matrix in which each row’s first non-zero entry is to the right of the one above, so that all entries below the pivots are zero. See Chapter 11 and Chapter 12.

Row operation

Adding a multiple of one row to another, swapping two rows, or multiplying a row by a non-zero number. See Chapter 6 and Chapter 11.

Row space

The span of the rows of a matrix. Its dimension is the rank. See Chapter 16.

Row vector

A matrix with one row. See Chapter 1.

Row-times-column rule

The rule for matrix multiplication: entry \((i, j)\) of \(\M{A}\M{B}\) is row \(i\) of \(\M{A}\) dotted with column \(j\) of \(\M{B}\). See Chapter 3.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
S

Saddle point


A stationary point where the Hessian has both positive and negative eigenvalues, so it is a minimum in some directions and a maximum in others. See Chapter 22. (2) An equilibrium of \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\vect{x}\) whose eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, which is unstable. See Chapter 23.


Scalar

A single number, as opposed to a vector or matrix. Multiplying by a scalar scales every entry. See Chapter 2.

Scalar multiplication

Multiplying every entry of a vector or matrix by the same number. See Chapter 2.

Schrödinger equation

The linear system \(i\hbar\,\dot{\vect{\psi}} = \M{H}\vect{\psi}\) that describes how a quantum state changes in time. See Chapter 38.

Scores

The coordinates of each item along the principal components, \(\M{X}\vect{v}_i\). See Chapter 21.

Scree plot

A plot of the variance explained by each principal component against its number, used to choose how many components to keep. See Chapter 37.

Second-order accurate

Describes an approximation whose error is proportional to \(h^2\), so that halving the grid spacing \(h\) divides the error by 4. See Chapter 33.

Sector

One of the industries into which an input–output model divides an economy. See Chapter 42.

Self-stress

A set of member forces in a truss that balance each other with no load at all: a non-zero vector in the null space of the equilibrium matrix. See Chapter 31.

Sensitivity

In a population model, the rate of change of the growth rate \(\lambda\) with one entry of the matrix, \(\partial\lambda/\partial a_{ij}\). See elasticity and Chapter 36.

Shear

A transformation that slides lines parallel to an axis by amounts proportional to their distance from it, such as \(\mat{1 & k \\ 0 & 1}\). See Chapter 4.

Shear stress

An off-diagonal entry of a stress matrix, which slides one side of a surface past the other. Compare normal stress. See Chapter 20.

Shift

Replacing \(\M{A}\) by \(\M{A} - \mu\M{I}\), which subtracts \(\mu\) from every eigenvalue, so that iterative eigenvalue methods find a chosen eigenvalue or converge faster. See Chapter 29.

Shifted inverse iteration

Inverse iteration with \(\M{A} - \mu\M{I}\), which finds the eigenvalue of \(\M{A}\) closest to \(\mu\), and its eigenvector. See Chapter 29.

Similar matrices

Matrices related by \(\M{B} = \M{P}^{-1}\M{A}\M{P}\): the same transformation described in different bases. See Chapter 15.

Singular matrix

A square matrix with determinant zero. It has no inverse, and \(\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}\) has either no solution or infinitely many. See Chapter 6.

Singular value decomposition

The factorisation \(\M{A} = \M{U}\M{\Sigma}\M{V}\T\) of any matrix, with \(\M{U}\) and \(\M{V}\) orthogonal and the singular values \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge 0\) on the diagonal of \(\M{\Sigma}\): rotate, stretch, rotate. See Chapter 21.

Singular values

The numbers \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge 0\) down the diagonal of \(\M{\Sigma}\) in the SVD: the square roots of the eigenvalues of \(\M{A}\T\M{A}\). They measure how much \(\M{A}\) stretches in each direction. See Chapter 21.

Singularity

A position of a robot arm where its Jacobian is singular, so that the hand can’t move in some direction at all. See Chapter 34.

Skew-symmetric matrix

A square matrix with \(\M{A}\T = -\M{A}\). In three dimensions it represents a cross product with a fixed vector, such as an angular velocity. See Chapter 38.

Span

The set of all linear combinations of some vectors. See Chapter 14.

Sparse matrix

A matrix with so many zero entries that it pays to store and use only the non-zeros. See Chapter 26.

Spectral partitioning

Splitting a network into two groups by the signs of the entries of its Fiedler vector. See Chapter 41.

Spectral radius

The largest absolute value of the eigenvalues of a matrix, written \(\rho(\M{T})\). An iteration with iteration matrix \(\M{T}\) converges if and only if \(\rho(\M{T}) < 1\). See Chapter 27.

Spectral theorem

Every real symmetric matrix can be written \(\M{Q}\M{\Lambda}\M{Q}\T\), with real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors. See Chapter 20.

Spiral

An equilibrium of \(\dot{\vect{x}} = \M{A}\vect{x}\) with complex eigenvalues, around which solutions spiral: inwards (stable) if the real parts are negative, outwards if they are positive. See Chapter 23.

Square matrix

A matrix with as many rows as columns. See Chapter 1.

Stable age distribution

The proportions in each age class or stage that a population settles into: the eigenvector of the dominant eigenvalue of its projection matrix. See Chapter 36.

Standard basis

The columns \(\ue{1}, \dots, \ue{n}\) of the identity matrix; in \(\R^2\) and \(\R^3\) these are \(\ui\), \(\uj\) and \(\uk\). See Chapter 15.

Standard error

A measure of the uncertainty in a fitted regression coefficient, proportional to the square root of the corresponding diagonal entry of \((\M{X}\T\M{X})^{-1}\). See Chapter 37.

Statically determinate

Describes a structure whose member forces are fixed by equilibrium alone: its equilibrium matrix is square and invertible. If there are more unknowns than equations it is statically indeterminate. See Chapter 31.

Statically indeterminate

Describes a structure that can carry every load, but in infinitely many ways, so that equilibrium alone doesn’t fix the member forces. See statically determinate and Chapter 31.

Stationary point

A point where the gradient of a function is zero: a minimum, a maximum or a saddle point. See Chapter 22.

Steady state

A vector left unchanged by a process \(\vect{x}_{k+1} = \M{M}\vect{x}_k\): an eigenvector with eigenvalue 1. See Chapter 19 and Chapter 35.

Step size

The distance \(\alpha\) moved at each step of gradient descent, in the direction of steepest descent; also called the learning rate. See Chapter 22.

Stiffness matrix

The symmetric matrix \(\M{K} = \M{B}\T\M{D}\M{B}\) relating joint displacements to applied loads, \(\M{K}\vect{u} = \vect{p}\). See Chapter 31.

Stress matrix

The symmetric matrix that describes the forces between neighbouring pieces at a point inside a loaded material; also called the stress tensor. See Chapter 20.

Stretch

The transformation \(\mat{a & 0 \\ 0 & b}\), which stretches by a factor \(a\) parallel to the \(x\)-axis and \(b\) parallel to the \(y\)-axis. See Chapter 4.

Stretch factor

The number \(\lambda\) by which a transformation multiplies every point of an invariant line: an eigenvalue. See Chapter 9.

Subspace

A set of vectors that contains \(\zerovec\) and is closed under adding and scaling, such as a line or plane through the origin. See Chapter 14.

Successive over-relaxation

SOR: Gauss–Seidel with each update stretched by a factor \(\omega\) between 0 and 2, usually above 1, to speed convergence. See Chapter 27.

Survival rate

In a population model, the fraction of one age class that survives to join the next a step later. See Chapter 36.

Symmetric matrix

A square matrix equal to its transpose, so that \(a_{ij} = a_{ji}\). See Chapter 1.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
T

Technical coefficients matrix

In an input–output model, the matrix \(\M{A}\) whose entry \(a_{ij}\) is the value of industry \(i\)’s product used to make £1 of industry \(j\)’s product. See Chapter 42.

Tension

The state of a truss member that is being pulled along its length. Compare compression. See Chapter 31.

Thomas algorithm

Gaussian elimination specialised to tridiagonal matrices, needing about \(8n\) operations. See Chapter 26.

Tip to tail

Adding vectors geometrically by placing the tail of the second at the tip of the first. See Chapter 2.

Trace

The sum of the diagonal entries of a square matrix, equal to the sum of its eigenvalues. See Chapter 18.

Transient state

A state of a Markov chain that the chain eventually leaves for good. Compare absorbing state. See Chapter 35.

Transition matrix

The matrix of probabilities \(m_{ij}\) of moving from state \(j\) to state \(i\) in one step of a Markov chain; its columns add to 1 (it is column-stochastic). See Chapter 35.

Translation

Sliding everything by a fixed vector. It isn’t linear, because it moves the origin, but homogeneous coordinates turn it into a matrix multiplication. See Chapter 4 and Chapter 34.

Transpose

The matrix \(\M{A}\T\) whose rows are the columns of \(\M{A}\). See Chapter 1.

Triangular matrix

A square matrix that is zero below the main diagonal (upper triangular) or above it (lower triangular). See Chapter 6.

Tridiagonal matrix

A matrix whose only non-zero entries are on the main diagonal and the diagonals just above and below it. See Chapter 26.

Trivial solution

The solution \(\vect{x} = \zerovec\) that every homogeneous system has. See Chapter 10.

Truss

A structure of straight members joined at their ends to form triangles, as in many bridges, roofs, cranes and pylons. See Chapter 31.

Tuned mass damper

A large mass attached to a structure by a spring tuned to a troublesome natural frequency, which absorbs the vibration. See Chapter 40.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
U

Underdetermined system

A system with fewer equations than unknowns. It usually has infinitely many solutions, but can have none. Compare overdetermined system. See Chapter 12.

Unstable method

A method that introduces more error than the conditioning of the problem makes unavoidable. Compare backward stable. See Chapter 24.

Upper triangular matrix

See triangular matrix.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
V

Value added

The part of each £1 of a sector’s output that is not spent on inputs from other sectors, and so pays for wages, profits and imports. See Chapter 42.

View matrix

The \(4 \times 4\) matrix that moves a 3D scene so that the camera sits at the origin, looking along the negative \(z\) axis. See Chapter 34.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
W

Walk

A sequence of edges in a network, each starting where the last one ended. Entry \((i, j)\) of \(\M{A}^k\) counts the walks of length \(k\) from one node to the other. See Chapter 41.

title: Appendix K — Glossary
text:
Z

Zero matrix

The matrix whose entries are all zero, written \(\M{0}\). See Chapter 2.
